Feudal Manors — fees & the fighting men they buy

An ACKS II house-rule framework inspired by English and Burgundian military tenure.

The assize of the fee

Kept, the manor raises its own watch. Unkept it buys the identical protection at market, month after month — raising is capital, hiring is rent. What "unkept" means turns on the definition of record: under the 1181, 1285 or ordinance definitions it is default — a breach, with distraint at the view and the bond in question. Under the Domesday definition there is no statute to breach: the same box unticked reads no assize yet, the levy simply unraised, and no penalty attaches to the man.

The charter — what the paper itself says

Measured against the definition of record — the “muster demands” chip on the Campaign row above. Where the two disagree, that gap is the deficit the settlement has to close; the assessment chip picks which reading rules.

ACKS II’s nobility stops at the 160-family baron. Beneath it sits the layer feudal armies were actually made of — the knight’s fee. This module prices that layer from the game’s own economics: what a fee earns, what it owes, and what its service is worth.

Two RAW facts carry all the math on this page: domains are priced in gp per peasant family per month, and a sworn man's wage doubles per character level (25 / 50 / 100 / 200 / 400, RR p.168). Know those two and every number here will reconcile.

The idea

Three questions, in the order a new reader has them: what a fee is, what changes if you adopt this, and what the module is made of. Nothing below needs a dial moved, and none of it is arithmetic — the arithmetic starts one tab along.

1 · What a fee is

1 · The grantThe lord grants land — a fee: the smallest estate whose income pays a fighting man’s wage.
→
2 · The serviceThe fee is quit1 of its garrison bill by service — a lance (the knight, mounted and mailed, his squire behind him) and a trained levy.
→
3 · The termOne month of service a year in kind; coin — scutage — where a body cannot ride.
1 · quit, the period’s wordQuit in the period's own sense: discharged of a due, owing service instead of coin — the quittance being the written receipt that says so. Charters made estates quit of geld (the land tax) and of castle-guard in consideration of service kept; quit-rent is the same deal run backward — coin paid to be quit of service.

2 · What changes — one swap, and everything follows from it

RAW puts a monthly garrison line on every domain — 2, 3 or 4 gp per family by district class, the standing cost of keeping the land defended. This module makes the fee quit of that line by service instead of paying it in coin. That is the one structural change, and it is the whole of the module's departure from ACKS II at the level of mechanism. Everything else on these six tabs is a consequence of it, an extension where RAW prices nothing, or a citation.

What that swap buys, in practice: a realm whose military strength is counted in lances rather than budgeted in gold, where the interesting decisions are about land and paper rather than about payroll. What it costs: the lord's largest single expense line stops being an expense, so the enfeoffed share of a realm is rich in men and poor in coin by design. It is a real deviation — argued, bounded and priced in the ⚖ module doctrine table, which is where every other departure is written down too.

And the economy itself is a ruling, not an inheritance. Before any figure here means anything, the module has to answer a question ACKS settles once and for all: what does one peasant family yield its lord? That answer is the custom of record — set at the Dials, and chipped on the writ at the foot of the window — and it is a dial with two settings, of which the module's default is not RAW's. ACKS RAW gives every family 4 gp of service revenue and 2 of tax on top of the land value (RR pp.341–2): a free, taxed, commercial peasantry. Customary — the default — reads the same village as villeins holding by custom of the manor, where the rent is the land: service falls to 1 and tax to 0. The reason is RAW's own wording, which describes service revenue as the licence income of freemen's trades — and a villein renders in land and labour, not in coin from a trade he does not practise.

At average land that nets a fee-holder 4 gp a family customary against 9 under RAW, so the same bachelor's fee is 25 families at the customary rent and 12 under ACKS RAW revenues — the whole rural page, re-scaled by one choice. Every rural figure moves with the dial; the towns do not, a burgess being free and taxed in fact as well as on paper. RAW stands on the dial as a comparison rather than a rival century — no era preset touches it — and the value is derived in full, step by step, in the Custom chapter.

3 · What the module is made of

Six tabs in three registers. This one orients; two do work; three are evidence.

Feudal Manors — the micro, and the new part. One estate at a time: what a fee earns, what it owes, who it can keep, and what happens when the paper and the land stop agreeing. This is the layer ACKS II does not have. Feudal Realms — the macro, and mostly ACKS's own. A whole honour: demesne, vassals and fees, two populations, the garrison composed, the host and the ward. RAW's domain layer with the fee tier fitted underneath it. Officers — the other way to set a man over land. Ministerial and revocable where a fee is heritable. One office is priced — the district officer — because his loyalty is the only one that moves money. Library — the argument. Where every mark on every card leads: the ⚖ doctrine tables that own each deviation, page-exact RAW audits, and the long chapters. Not needed to run the module; needed to check it. Hârn — the proving ground. The setting the module was written for, and the corpus it was tested against. Kept apart from the argument so a setting fact never reads as a design one. And two marks worth knowing now. RAW means ACKS II as written, cited to the page; MODULE means this module's own ruling. The full key is under the terms.
The claim in full — the doctrine stated, with its citations

The claim. A fee is the smallest estate whose income pays its holder's wage (RR p.168) — an operational definition, and the reason every era on this page re-counts the same ladder. Historically a fee was a unit of assessment before it was an estate, and only sometimes both: the crown counted servitia, and what lay under a count was the lord's business. This module prices estates, so it takes the smallest one that pays its man. Everything on this page follows from that one sentence. Because a sworn man's wage doubles per level, the rungs fall straight out of the henchman wage table — ½ / 1 / 2 / 4 fees, retaining L2 / L3 / L4 / L5 — each netting land − 2 gp per family under the customary rent, land + 3 under ACKS RAW revenues, each owing as many lances as it counts fees, and the ladder stops below the barony — which RAW sets at 160 families (RR p.343) and not at any figure of income. Nothing here is a new economy; it is ACKS II's own economy read at one level below the baron.

What the definition does not model. One estate, one charter, one lord — that is the shape the whole engine assumes, and three real arrangements fall outside it. One fee spread across several manors, so that no single estate answers to the paper. One manor carrying several fees held of different lords, each with its own count and its own definition of record. And fractions split among coheirs — tenths and fortieths held by heiresses, wards and burgesses, which the record shows from the mid-13th century on. All three are ordinary history, and none of them is here: modelling them means giving up the one-estate-one-paper assumption the ladder, the muster and the writ are all built on. The module prices the case it can, and names the three it does not. The era table (History chapter, Library) says the same thing about the divorce of fee from knight.

The consideration, precisely. What discharges the garrison line is a lance — the knight himself, mounted and mailed, with his fostered squire and remounts — and a trained levy, both held to written terms (the assize of the fee), with the host service bounded at one month of service a year in kind and extension at the lord's wages. Quit is the period's own word for the arrangement: discharged of a due, owing service instead of coin, the quittance being the written receipt that says so.

Where the argument is kept. Citations read RR = ACKS II Revised Rulebook, JJ = Judges Journal, and every page reference in this module has been checked against the 2nd printing and its Major Errata. The rulings that depart from strict RAW are not buried: each is named, priced, and defended in the ⚖ doctrine tables and the Design chapter. The dated sources sit in the History chapter, and both of those, with Money, Custom and the franchise beside them, are on the Library tab. Hârn, the first application, has a tab of its own. The working numbers are on Feudal Manors and Feudal Realms.

One manor, line by line FIXED EXAMPLE

The Bachelor’s fee — one knight’s fee, the ladder’s unit — walked line by line at the default dials (the customary rent, land 6, borderlands density, distraint century, assize kept, squires ride). Move a dial below and the live cards re-price; the figures here are the defaults’, exactly as the engine computes them.

The estate25 families at the — the smallest estate whose income pays a knight: 25 × 4 gp (land 6 − 2) = 100 gp/mo. Under ACKS RAW revenues the same rung is 12 families at 9 gp = 108 gp/mo.
What he earns100 gp a month against his own 100-gp keep (the L3 henchman wage) — nothing over. The fee pays its man exactly and clears no surplus, which is why a relief is paid by borrowing rather than out of income. Under ACKS RAW revenues, 108 against 100 — 8 gp/mo, less than one family’s output.
What he owesOne lance — himself, mounted and mailed, squire and remounts behind him: one month of service a year in kind, and the quota is met the day he rides.
The levy5 yeomen (2 heavy foot, 3 light foot), trained and kitted once (≈510 gp, heirloom — kit and skills pass to their sons): 42 gp/mo of standing watch, part of the service that keeps the fee quit. Under ACKS RAW revenues the same rung’s 12 families raise 2 yeomen — ≈211 gp once, 18 gp/mo.
What he is quit ofThe garrison line — 50 / 75 / 100 gp a month by district class (civilized / borderlands / outlands) — discharged by that service, never paid in coin. Under ACKS RAW revenues, 24 / 36 / 48 on 12 families.
The callActually mustering the levy costs ≈77 gp for the month of service — 42 gp of wages plus 35 gp of idle ploughs — ≈77% of a month’s income: free to keep, dear to call. Under ACKS RAW revenues, ≈42 gp (18 of wages, 24 of ploughs), ≈39%.
What land makes of himThe fee retains an L3 knight but grows its holder only to L2, in ≈3 years — the dubbed man’s last level is won in the field, never behind a plough.
What breaks his bankAny standing hired man: the fee clears nothing at all, so even the 25-gp L1 wage comes straight out of the holder’s own keep — obligations beyond his own body are met in coin (scutage) or for the term, never by a standing payroll. Under ACKS RAW revenues the same wage dwarfs an 8-gp surplus; the verdict is the reading’s to sharpen, not to change.

Every figure above is the engine’s output at the defaults — see it live on the ladder, and walk a harder estate through the muster.

The terms

words carry the module, and they are the whole of its private vocabulary — everything else on the page is ACKS's or the record's. Plain definitions here, in three groups: the manor's words, the realm's, and the crown's. The doctrine behind each lives in the Library.

The manor's words

the custom of record — what a family yields its lord: villeins by custom of the manor (the default), or RAW’s free taxed peasantry as a comparison. It is a realm’s economy rather than a century’s, and it reprices every rural gp on this page — the towns keep RAW’s own 4 and 2 under either reading.
tenement — a full 30-acre holding, worked by one peasant family: ACKS’s revenue unit, and what every rural gp on this page is counted in. A burgess holds no tenement — the towns count in urban families instead.
household — anyone under a roof. It is what a survey counts, not what a manor rents, and the two are different numbers.
fee — land granted to keep a fighting man: the smallest estate whose income pays his wage.
lance — one knight’s service: the man himself, horsed and mailed, squire and remounts behind him.
quota — how many lances an estate owes: as many as it counts fees.
quittance — the deal itself: the fee is excused its garrison bill because it renders service instead of coin.
the assize of the fee10 — the written terms: mail per fee held, a levy trained and kitted, a view of arms twice a year.
scutage — coin sent in place of a body, when no body can ride.
the levy — the manor’s own yeomen, up to two in ten families, standing the watch.
the definition of record — what the charter says a “lance” must be — and the centuries disagree.
assessment (current vs ancient) — whether the paper is re-surveyed as income grows, or frozen at the grant.
the margin — the income an ancient charter never sees, because the manor grew past the paper. It is what funds a household, and what the crown reaches for by other means.
distraint6 — seizing a man’s goods until he performs what he owes — up to and including knighthood itself.
make-good — the coin that books an old-standard body as the equal of a current one.
the month of service12 — the year’s one month in kind, served at the fee’s own cost (history’s forty days); past it, the lord pays wages.
esquire — an adult armiger holding land: the 60-gp man-at-arms of the half-fee. Not the squire, who is a boy in training; the two words are one letter apart and mean different men.

The realm's words

demesne — land the lord keeps in his own hand. It pays him coin, and it pays its own garrison line; a fee does neither.
vassal — a man granted a domain of his own, who renders tribute in coin (18 gp × families0.6) rather than service. RAW's own tier, above the fee.
honour — the whole of what one lord holds, demesne and vassals and fees together: the unit the Feudal Realms tab prices.
the host — the army the realm musters for its term. Every bodily lance is in it that is not standing ward.
ward (castle-guard) — service owed at a castle's walls rather than in the field. Counted here in lances, not days.
the ward-penny — the tenant's own commutation of ward: a fixed perpetual charge he elects, which is why it funds a garrison where scutage cannot.
serjeanty — land held for a named non-knightly service — the gate, a tower, a watchman — rendered every day of the year rather than for a term.
burgess — a townsman holding his plot by burgage: free, paying money rent, owing no labour on anyone's demesne. The reason a town is priced apart from a manor.
the title population — the figure a lord's rank is read from, which is everyone: rural families and urban together. Not the same as the families in hand.

The crown's words

office — the other way to set a man over land: ministerial and revocable, paid in coin, where a fee is heritable and paid in land. A castellany is a fief; a constable's commission is an office, and crowns staff the second from the men who hold the first.
the fisc — the coin a district renders. RAW's magistrates oversee expense lines only; that a district officer oversees revenue too is this module's extension, and is what the corruption dial prices.
the incidents — the lord's rights arising from the tenure itself rather than from the service: relief (the heir's payment to take up his inheritance), wardship (a minor heir's lands and person), aid (a demand on three named occasions), escheat (the land back, for want of an heir).
tribute inefficiency — RAW's rule that cash tribute decays with vassal count: a third to a half lost to "crime, corruption, or waste". It is why a knight-heavy realm is rich in lances and poor in coin.

The scope rule, in one sentence: convert between the two only where a figure crosses from a source into this page — about 2.5 recorded entries to the family, band 1.5–3.5 — and never inside the page’s own arithmetic, which is in families throughout. The conversion and its band are in the History chapter’s source typing; what the rule is for — a ratio taken across two counting conventions is not a ratio at all — is worked in the Money chapter. Both are in the Library.

And six marks

Every consequential figure on this page is marked with where it comes from. The module is a synthesis — an ACKS II house-rule framework built on English military tenure — and the marks are how a Judge reads the seams between the three. Hover a mark for its meaning; the full argument for every MODULE ruling is in the Library’s ⚖ doctrine tables.

RAW ACKS II as written, cited to the page. RAW-INFORMED RAW motivates the step; the number is still ours. MODULE this module’s ruling — RAW does not say it. HISTORY a historical institution, borrowed — not a game rule. HÂRN setting-specific: Hârn, and Kaldor. DEBATED historians differ — a signpost, not a statute.

What this does not model

This is a subinfeudation and service module, not a domain manager and not a manorial economy. Here is where its edges are.

Not the ACKS domain turn. Tax and morale decisions, population growth and migration, stronghold building, market and urban income, harvest variation, casualties reducing the family base, travel and campaign distance, seasonal service, long-run loyalty drift. RAW handles these; the module holds them still. Not the manor's economy. Demesne against tenant land, free against customary tenure, money rent against produce against labour services, mills, courts and monopolies, meadow and common rights, crop systems, hired labour, market access. A family here is ACKS's family — one revenue number — and every one of those distinctions is folded into it. Not a reconstruction of one place or century. The era presets are composites and say so at the dial; the marks above are how you tell which parts are ACKS, which are borrowed, and which the module invented to join them.

And every figure says per what. 100 gp/mo is a standing rate; 510 gp once is capital paid at the grant and never again; 25 gp for the term falls due when the host is called, and not otherwise. Three different kinds of money — and the module’s hardest question, a levy’s 510 gp once against a bachelor’s fee that clears 0 gp/mo, is only legible once they are told apart. (The same three under ACKS RAW revenues: 108, 211, and 12, against 8 gp/mo of surplus.)

6 · distraint, preciselyDistraint is the period's ordinary legal remedy: the seizure of a man's goods — chattels driven off, profits impounded — to compel performance of an obligation, no court judgment required, only the right. Distraint of knighthood (from 1224; any £20 income from 1241, later £40) is that remedy pointed at rank, with respite purchasable by fine.
10 · hauberk & habergeonThe 1181 assize owed a hauberk — the full mail shirt — per fee held; its 10-mark freeman, a commoner assessed at ~£6⅔ in movable goods, armed at the habergeon, the lighter short mail. The half-fee mapping borrows his kit-grade, not his tenure.
12 · the month of service, and why it needs no free duty RAW's favor⇄duty economy prices relations whose consideration passes repeatedly — the sworn henchman's one free ongoing duty (RR p.345), the outsider's one duty per favor (p.347). The fee is neither. Its service is standing because the tenure is standing, the consideration having passed once and in land at enfeoffment (⚖ the fee's service stands because the fee stands, Library), so the term is what bounds it: one month of service a year — history's forty days rounded to ACKS's month. Both the month-long term and the annual cap are the module's own doctrine: RAW's duties have no duration but revocation.

The eras

The same machinery reads four centuries. Each era defines the required body differently, and every number follows the definition.

A fee is a written thing, and the writing has a date. Found a domain under a century and the module sets its dials to it — what a lance must be,2 whether the assize stands, whether the paper still tracks the land. The requirement drifted by statute and the field standard tightened separately;3 when old charters under-delivered, lords reached for coin4 — until the requirement absorbed the crew whole and the fee itself was commuted.5 Every dial stays live after the preset: touching one returns the century to “dial your own.”

2 · the Domesday milesS. Harvey's ordinary miles ("The Knight and the Knight's Fee in England," Past & Present, 1970): a mailed professional barely above the peasantry, on fees of 1.5–2 hides — a famous argument that drew replies, not a consensus datum; the Domesday-era readings lean on it.
3 · equus coopertusBy the 13th century royal cavalry summonses begin specifying equus coopertus, the covered horse, precisely because men were arriving paper-compliant and obsolete — the definition of record being contested and enforced at the muster itself. DEBATED
4 · Keefe’s cautionHistory ran several engines of commutation at once — fractional fees, campaigns past the forty days, overseas service, the crown's own taste for paid, flexible hosts — Keefe's caution against reading scutage as a single story. The definition lag is one quiet engine in this model, not the whole tale.
5 · the lance fournieThe fifteenth century wrote "lance" into statute: the Burgundian lance fournie (1468: man-at-arms, coustillier, page; Abbeville 1471: those three plus three mounted archers and three foot) — recognizably the fee’s month-of-service muster re-purchased as a paybook unit once tenure had melted to coin. The page rode unpaid and out of the line; the coustillier was a separately paid combatant, never the boy.

Each is a deliberate composite — one century's tendencies gathered into a set of dial positions, not a snapshot of any year. They are starting points a Judge can argue with, and the four names are conveniences: pick the one whose shape matches the realm being run, then move the dials until it is that realm and not England.

The picker lives on the Domains tab, at the foot of the dial panel — because a century is now something a domain is founded under rather than something the whole world is set to. What each one meant is here.

Post-Conquest1066–1100 · the Survey's world

The required bodythe mailed rider — hauberk, horse, spear: a 60-gp man. Knighthood is not yet an income class.
What the fee owesthe fees count in him — a greater estate simply owes more riders (the whole ladder re-counts: 1 / 1⅔ / 3⅓ / 6⅔). No assize yet stands; kit is custom, not statute.
One line of historywasted shires, small grants, the Survey fresh in every hand — the miles barely above the peasantry, on 1.5–2 hides.

Angevin12th c. · Assize of Arms 1181

The required bodythe knight himself — the 100-gp veteran, with mail per fee held: the first statutory kit ladder, the habergeon tier below it.
What the fee owesone knight-service per fee counted; a hauberk per fee held — the second hauberk of a two-fee man is a second man's mail.
One line of historythe hall empties onto the land; the 1166 cartae freeze the counts a generation before the countryside fills — the first margins open, and scutage is already the crown's answer.

Distraint13th c. · Winchester 1285 · Kaldor's home

The required bodythe statute knight — the same 100-gp body, now enforced: wealth-assessed kit and the twice-yearly view of arms, with covered-horse summonses (equus coopertus) pressing past bare paper compliance.
What the fee owesthe full ladder: ½ / 1 / 2 / 4 fees owe ½ / 1 / 2 / 4 lances; mounted serjeants discharge at two-for-one; scutage for the fractions.
One line of historyknighthood dear and honorable, numbers falling — the crown distrains the £20 men into the rank they dodge. The module's default century.

Ordinance14th–15th c. · the lance fournie

The required bodythe ordinance lance — the crew written into the requirement (man-at-arms + coustillier + page, ~145 gp hired), the page an unpaid mouth.
What the fee owescoin — the fee commuted on ancient paper. What the coin buys is the ordinance lance; personal service survives as honor and choice, not obligation.
One line of historyarmies raised by contract and wages, livery in place of tenure — by 1436 the fee holds status land while war goes professional.

The Century preset applies them. The era boxes above (and the era chip in the state bar) move land, density, assize, assessment, and the definition of record to the century's values in one click — a starting point, not a lock: every dial stays live after, and each carries its own reasoning in the Dials. The full era table — the knight of the record, the ladder's reading, and the dials, era by era — is the History chapter in the Library; and played forward, domain-seasons deliver these eras in sequence, no dial set by hand (the three counts of a fee, same chapter).

Setting up — what running this actually takes

Everything above says what the module is. This says what it costs you: what it replaces, the five decisions nothing can be priced until you make, and what actually changes at the table. None of them is a long decision — the page ships with a stated default and the reason for it, and the defaults are a working realm, not a blank form.

What it replaces — and what it leaves alone

This is a supplement to ACKS II's Domains chapter, not a replacement for it. Population growth, morale, tax decisions, stronghold building, urban and market income, the domain turn itself — all of that is still RAW's and is run exactly as written. The module touches three things: it adds a tier below the 160-family baron that ACKS does not have, it makes the fee quit of its garrison line instead of paying it, and it gives the crown a way to reach land it cannot re-rate. A campaign already running can adopt it mid-flight: nothing above the barony changes, and the fees are seated underneath what is already there.

The five decisions

Five settings the rest of the arithmetic hangs on. Each is a real choice with a real consequence, each is argued where it is set, and each has a default with its reasoning beside it. Make these once for the realm, not per manor.

The five decisions a realm must make, what each moves, and the module's default
The decisionWhat it movesThe default, and why
The custom of record — what a family yields MODULE Every rural gp on every tab, by about 2.25× at land 6 — the towns are untouched, and that exemption is itself a ruling (settlements). It decides how many families a knight needs: the same bachelor's fee is 25 families customary and 12 under RAW revenues. Customary. RAW describes service revenue as the income of freemen's trades, and a villein holding by custom renders in land and labour. ACKS RAW is on the same dial as a comparison — the Custom chapter carries the derivation.
The century — when the charters were written HISTORY Four dials at once: what a lance must be, whether the assize stands, whether the paper still tracks the land, and the ground it sits on. The ladder re-counts under each. The distraint century (13th) — knighthood dear and enforced, service still rendered in kind, the crown distraining the £20 men into a rank they dodge. It is where Kaldor sits. The eras are above; every dial stays live after the preset.
The assize of the fee — is the levy raised? MODULE Whether the manor raises its protection or buys it. Kept, one capital bill and a standing credit thereafter; unkept, market wages every month, for ever. Kept. Raising is capital, hiring is rent, and the rent does not stop. Under the 1181 and 1285 definitions "unkept" is a default with distraint attached; under Domesday there is no statute to breach and it reads simply as no assize yet.
The assessment — current or ancient paper HISTORY Whether a growing manor's quota grows with it. Ancient freezes the count at the charter and opens the margin — income the paper never sees, which is what funds a household and what the crown then taxes by other means. Current. It is the simpler campaign and the quieter one. Ancient is where the module gets interesting: it is what turns the grown manor's muster live.
The ward clause — what the charter says about castle-guard HISTORY Whether a lance at the walls is instead of the host or on top of it — and so whether a war year leaves you with bare walls or with a short host. None, until the charter writes one. At the walls, one term — service spent once — and the abating clause (cl. 29) are the two settings, equally historical; lords wrote both as a matter of course. Set in Step 1 of the walk, with the rest of the charter: it is a term of this paper, and the honour's whole reckoning is the ward, on Feudal Realms.

Two more are conventions rather than decisions, and both are a realm's rather than a century's: whether knights raise each other's sons (fosterage) and where the boys end up (placement). They change who stands the watch and on whose ledger it lands; neither changes what a fee is.

What changes at the table

The lord's sheet gains a quota and loses a bill. Instead of a monthly garrison expense he holds a count of lances owed, and the interesting question stops being "can I afford the garrison" and becomes "who owes me, and will he come". Land grants become a rate of exchange. Every family granted away is coin forgone and a body gained, at a price the ladder fixes. A realm's whole character is the mix, and it is visible on one card. Paper becomes a thing that can be wrong. A charter written a century ago against a manor that has grown is the module's central drama — the deficit, the remedy, and who pays for it. It is optional (see assessment above) and it is the best part. Nothing is rolled. This is a design tool: every control is a decision a Judge makes and can defend, and the writ at the foot of the Manors tab is one sentence stating the realm he has chosen. Dice belong at the table, not in the sheet.

Where to go next

To price a manor: Feudal Manors — set the ground, read the ladder, and the four rungs are your fee sizes. To build a realm: Feudal Realms opens with the order to do it in. To check the reasoning: the Library, where every ruling on the page is named, cited and priced. To see it tested: the Hârn tab.

And the practicalities are nil. This is one HTML file: no install, no dependencies, no network, nothing tracked or fetched. It works off a memory stick. The Copy link button on the manor sheet writes the whole dial state into the address, so a realm can be handed to another Judge as a URL.

The fee — one estate, priced

This tab is the module's micro layer, and the part of it that is genuinely new: ACKS II's nobility stops at the 160-family baron, and everything here sits underneath that. One estate at a time — what it earns, what it owes, who it can keep, and what happens when the paper and the land stop agreeing. If you have not read the Overview, read it first: the words below are defined there, and the two dials that reprice every figure on this page are explained there.

A fee is the smallest estate whose income pays its holder's wage (RR p.168) — an operational definition, argued in full on the Overview. Because a sworn man's wage doubles per level, the rungs fall straight out of the henchman wage table: ½ / 1 / 2 / 4 fees, retaining L2 / L3 / L4 / L5, each owing as many lances as it counts fees, and the ladder stops below the barony — which RAW sets at 160 families (RR p.343) and not at any figure of income. The one structural change to RAW is that the fee is quit of its garrison line by service rather than paying it in coin. Everything on this tab descends from those two sentences.

The dials · the ladderWhat does a fee cost? Set the ground and the century, and read the four rungs off the wage table — families, net, quota, levy.
→
The musterWhat does it actually deliver? Where the paper and the land disagree — the grown manor, the deficit, and the remedy the lord chooses.
→
The unitsWhat is it worth in the field? The lance priced as an ACKS battle unit, so a muster can be compared with a mercenary company.

The manor sheet at the head of the dials and the writ pinned at the foot of the window are two readings of the same estate — a sheet to scan and a sentence to argue with. Both are live: every figure moves as you dial. Seating these fees inside a realm is the Feudal Realms tab; the officers who administer them are Officers.

The dials

levers set the world; every card, table, and flag below re-computes as they move. Each carries its plain-language effect up front and its full reasoning — the module's actual argument, unabridged — in a ⚖ Deeper inset. The live readouts (the standing-manor line under the land lever, the parceling check under density, the scutage reading and the era reading) recompute with everything else. You need not scroll back here to move them: the campaign-state bar pinned across the foot of the window carries the that describe the estate, and clicking any chip opens that dial's control beside the manor cards you are reading.

The manor sheet
Land value of the hex RAW
How rich is the dirt? — 3 poor · 6 ordinary · 9 rich
Sets what a family yields — and therefore how big each fresh fee must be: richer dirt, smaller fees. Standing manors never resize; they re-grade (the live line below).
⚖ Deeper — grant-time floors, rich dirt, and the standing manor
3d3 per hex, rolled when the domain is secured (RR p.338) — average 6. What a fee-holder nets from a family depends on the custom of record below — land + 3 under ACKS RAW revenues, land − 2 under the customary rent — and the live figure is printed beside the slider. The slider prices the floor at grant-time: on rich dirt a lord seats the same man on fewer families — and will, since every family he grants away costs him more demesne there. Standing manors don't shrink — moving the slider reprices a fresh grant, it does not follow one manor through changing fortunes; the grown manor (Muster section) does that.
Ground under the fees — population density RAW
How crowded is it? — how much ground one fee takes up
Turns families into ground: how many families a 6-mile hex carries, and how much of a hex each fee occupies (the parceling check below). Doubles as a reading of the century. These are ACKS's own class settings — 185 / 375 / 780 families a hex, RR p.340 — and not demographic estimates of England: the entries that name real places (425, 350, 120) are the module's readings, offered for comparison, and every figure here is a dial the Judge may overrule.
⚖ Deeper — RAW’s hex caps, the class ladder, and the century
RAW caps a 6-mile hex — ~31 sq mi, ~20,000 acres — at 185 / 375 / 780 families for outlands / borderlands / civilized (RR p.340, Limits of Growth). Density turns a fee's families into ground, and ground is what a lord actually parcels out of his hexes. RAW states the limit per 6-mile hex of a domain's territory — a cap on secured land, while land outside any domain carries no one — so realms interleave settled and empty hexes and the figure is never a national average. RAW even advances the classes at these same numbers (185 → borderlands, 375 → civilized, given a road to a small town within 24 miles and a morale of +1 — or by territory instead, 5 hexes and 925 families, 7 and 1,200; or by founding an urban settlement near a friendly city, which asks no family count at all, p.340). The ladder is a ratchet: downward the cap is absolute — a domain “cannot exceed” it — while upward the advance, once made, is permanent “even if the requirements for the classification are no longer being met,” so thin ground under a high class is ordinary and the reverse is illegal. The dial is RAW's own ladder, and it doubles as a reading of the century: the default sits at the 13th-century heartland (the distraint era — History chapter, Library), Domesday England reads ~120, and a manor itself walks the dial as it stocks and fragments (the three counts of a fee, History chapter, Library). The parceling check below reads the dial in those terms — how many ~1,060-acre manor-territories the hex holds, and how full each has filled.
The assize of the fee — terms of enfeoffment MODULE
Does the tenant maintain the local levy? — yes, and the fee is quit of its garrison; no, and the lord hires a watch
Kept, the manor raises its own watch — levy trained & kitted, the fee fully quit. In default, it hires the watch at market and is quit for the lance only.
⚖ Deeper — the assize’s terms, and raising vs. buying protection
The quittance is conditional, and its conditions are written. An assize is a royal ordinance that sets required equipment and inspects for it; this one is written into the fee. Its terms: the count of lances owed (the quota — the charter's servitium, on every card), mail per fee held (Assize of Arms 1181 — a knight owes as many hauberks, full mail shirts, as he holds fees; the sub-knightly man arms at the habergeon, the lighter short mail, the tier the assize set for its 10-mark freeman — a commoner assessed at ~£6⅔ in goods), the levy trained & kitted (the p.341 credit's own wording: "trained and equipped"), and a view of arms twice yearly (Statute of Winchester 1285) — held by the lord's officer under the inspecting-troops delegation (RR p.352–3; the Offices section’s ghost-soldier flag is this view, corrupted). Historically both instruments were national law enforced by royal machinery; writing their content into the fee's charter is this module's deliberate transplant (owned in the ⚖ table). And the assize is era-bound — it is the definition of record's enforcement arm (the definition lever, below): before 1181 there is nothing to keep, kit being custom; 1181 defines and 1285 enforces — the assize written, then the view that polices it; and under the ordinance the fee is commuted and the view survives as the muster commissioner's art. A fee in default is quit for the lance only: it hires the levy's watch until it re-arms.

What the switch actually chooses is not whether the assize stands — the requirement is identical either way — but whether the manor raises its protection or buys it. Kept, the men are its own: a one-time kit bill per man (light foot 88.5 gp, heavy foot 122, the serjeant's 578-gp mounting — RR p.431's Training and Equipment table; note RAW's own worked example on p.432 prices the same two foot at 94.5 and 124, contradicting its table, and this module follows the table, which is internally consistent: 0.5 + 3 + 85 and 1 + 6 + 115), paid once for each man's place in the levy and not again, since his arms and skills pass to his heir (p.432) and the martial tradition carries the place forward. Thereafter their wage-value stands against the garrison line every month, called out or not (p.341), and the mounted serjeant discharges half a lance of the quota besides. In default, the identical protection is bought at market instead: troops at mercenary wage, month after month, for as long as the manor wants a watch at all — and none of it credits toward the lances, which must still be found in bodies or coin. Raising is capital; hiring is rent, and the rent does not stop.
Fosterage (squiring) — a squire rides with the lance HISTORY
Do knights raise each other's sons? — a realm's custom, free to both sides
Adds each knight’s fostered squire — +45 gp of watch-and-train value at zero land cost, where a boy actually rides. Every lance keeps an attendant; fosterage decides whether it is a boy of the class or a hired groom. A realm’s custom, not a century’s.
⚖ Deeper — fosterage: the heir’s education as the lance’s train
Knights place their sons in other knights' households at ~14 — typically up the ladder, in the hall of the father's own lord, whose court is the clearinghouse. Fosterage is the ordinary word for it (Old English fōstor), and is used here rather than squiring because it names the arrangement between two households instead of the boy's job inside one; attested up the aristocracy, extended here to the whole class as a norm. The heir earns his levels before he inherits, and every lance gains a squire (~45 gp of medium-horse wage-value, RR p.169) at zero land cost — the boy's wage is his education. He keeps his knight horsed and stands the manor's watch, but takes no place in the line of battle. Reciprocal, so it nets out realm-wide. The boy is not a henchman and takes no slot — fosterage is a placement between households, not a retainer's contract, and the contract that carries his knight disowns the slot machinery outright (⚖ the bundle is closed). Every knight in the field keeps an attendant regardless: three or four horses and sixty pounds of mail are not a one-man job. What fosterage decides is which kind — a boy of the class, who costs nothing and can stand the manor's watch, or a hired groom, who costs coin and cannot. So the limit is supply, not permission: all knights may squire, and there are not enough boys to go round — the class carries well under one boy of squiring age per lance (the supply of boys, Design chapter, Library), so a realm at canon's paper rate of one squire per lance is describing its assessment, not its muster. A practice, not an entitlement: the toggle sets the realm's custom, but at any given hour not every lance has a boy in it — heirs come of age, fosterings lapse between sons — and the Judge should feel free to leave particular manors empty. The +45 rides only where a squire actually does.
The assessment — when is the paper written? HISTORY
Does the quota change as the estate grows? — current re-counts it, ancient keeps the old charter
Current: the paper tracks income — the default. Ancient: counts freeze at the charter while incomes grow — the margin opens, and the household lives in it.
⚖ Deeper — surveys, escheat, inquest, and the margin
A fee's count is written at the grant and polices kit, not wealth: the view of arms inspects mail against the charter, and no one re-rates a manor for prospering. The paper is rewritten at escheat and re-grant, at new enfeoffment, or on the record of a royal inquest (Domesday, the cartae of 1166, Kirkby's Quest — the inquiry finds the facts and the new paper follows it; generational, resisted, dear). Current assumes the survey is fresh: assessments track income, the module's default behavior. Ancient freezes the counts at the charter while incomes grow past them — the standing-manor line (land lever, above) then shows the margin, the income the paper never sees. The margin is the household's funding (Muster section), distraint is the crown taxing it by income instead of re-surveying, and a realm where the margin is universal has aged into livery (the era table, History chapter, Library). And the count is not all the paper writes — the definition of the lance rides the same charter (the definition lever, below).
The definition of record — what a lance must be MODULE
What counts as one fee's service? — a Domesday rider, an Angevin knight, a statute knight, or an ordinance lance
Sets what the charter’s “lance” must be — the 60-gp Domesday rider, the 100-gp knight (1181 / 1285), or the commuted ordinance crew. Fee-counts, quotas, and the discharge menu re-price with it. This is the calling domain’s standard of demand — what the summons this fee answers actually asks for, and the domain’s era in the only form the module needs. It used to be a setting of the world; it belongs to the domain, because two domains in one realm can be a century apart. A charter keeps its own definition (Muster), and the distance between the two is the lag.
⚖ Deeper — kit inflation, the covered horse, and the definition lag
The charter writes three things: the count of lances, the definition of a lance, and the term — and all three reset only when the paper does (the assessment lever, above). The definition drifted by statute: the 1181 Assize of Arms wrote the first kit ladder into law (mail per fee held), and Winchester 1285 enforced it — not a new price but an enforcement overlay: wealth-assessed kit and the twice-yearly view of arms policing the same body the 1181 assize defined. The field standard tightened separately: by the 13th century royal cavalry summonses begin specifying equus coopertus, the covered horse, precisely because men were arriving paper-compliant and obsolete. Kit inflation ran ahead of old charters, old fees under-delivered by current standards, and lords preferred coin and modern hires — the definition lag is one quiet engine of commutation in this model; history ran several at once (fractional fees, campaigns past the forty days, overseas service, the crown's own taste for paid, flexible hosts — Keefe's caution against reading scutage as a single story). This dial re-prices the requirement: fee-counts, quotas, and the discharge menu all follow it. And because a charter keeps its own definition, paper and muster can disagree: the grown manor (Muster section) carries a charter-definition dial, and the lag is computed there, not narrated. Distraint — the seizure of a man's goods until he performs what he owes — is the crown's definition-reset aimed at the man rather than the manor: distraint of knighthood compels the income-qualified to take up current-standard arms and dubbing (defined in full on the Library’s History chapter).
The custom of record — what a family yields RAW-INFORMED MODULE
Is this a manor, or a taxed province?
The definition of record above says what body the charter names. This says what a family yields — and it is the same thesis one level down: a fixed paper, with the land drifting away from it. Customary is a villein population holding by custom of the manor: the rent is the land, and service falls to the seigneurial monopolies alone. ACKS RAW is the rulebook as printed — a free, taxed, commercial peasantry, and it is offered here as a comparison, not as a rival century: no era preset selects it, and picking a century never moves it. Urban settlements are untouched either way: a borough really is free, taxed and commercial, which is exactly why the manor is not.
Why service is 1 and tax is 0 — one derivation, and every step a number
One residual allocation inside a calibrated model. Every step is a number, and the calibration target is the one that moves the rest.

At land value 6 the customary profile is calibrated to a net receipt of 4 gp per full-tenement unit — that is the historical input, drawn from the manorial record (see the evidence in the Library). The ledger then closes itself: 4 = 6 + service + tax − 3, so service + tax = 1. At ACKS's whole-gold-piece resolution there is exactly one point of non-land recurring revenue left to place, and the only question is where it sits.

RAW answers that: service revenue is the licence income of skilled freemen — "Most of these services are provided by freemen who offer a portion of their labor to the ruler in exchange for the right to practise their trade on his domain" (RR p.341) — and a customary manor still has mills, smiths, bakehouses and brewing. So the residual is not zero, and it belongs on the service line. Tax takes what remains, which is nothing.

What tax 0 says, precisely. Heriot, merchet, entry fines, court profits, tolls and assized rent were all real and all collected. The claim is that this profile resolves no separate whole-gp monthly tax line beyond a total recurring receipt that is already calibrated — a claim about what earns a line of its own, not about what the dues were worth. It does not run the other way: every individual due being smaller than RAW's smallest digit would not make their sum smaller than it.

What is booked where. Agricultural week-work is represented through the land line, because that labour produces the demesne output RAW's land line already collects — so labour-rent is not priced twice. That is a bookkeeping convention, and these are its limits: customary tenants commonly owed works and a fixed money rent on the same holding. The thirteenth-century Extenta Manerii asks its surveyors for "how much rent of assize be paid yearly besides the works and customs" — so cash rent and labour service were two obligations, not one, and this module folds them into a single calibrated receipt rather than resolving them apart.

Relief, aid and wardship are a different layer entirely — they run from the fee-holder up to his liege and replace recurring tribute at that level. They neither duplicate nor excuse peasant dues below it.

How to falsify this. Move the calibration target and the allocation moves with it. If rural service ought to round to nothing, then tax is 1 and service 0. If local cash dues demonstrably need another whole gold piece, then either the target net is too low or this decomposition is wrong. Every step is a number you can argue with.

Tax 0 is in any case RAW's own dial at its floor (p.349) — and it pays the domain nothing for sitting there. Regard is measured from the custom of record, not from RAW's 2, because the custom is what the peasantry expects; a profile resting at its own custom is at ±0 in both readings, and RAW's ±1 a gp then prices travel from that anchor. This page used to print +2 here, and the withdrawal is argued in the Custom chapter under the anchor of regard. The lord's own line follows: where he hires the garrison instead of receiving it in service he nets feeNet − 2/3/4 by district, so at the customary rent an outlands demesne nets exactly nothing — the frontier held in hand pays for its own protection and no more.
The scutage rate — what coin buys off a lance MODULE
What does it cost to commute one missing lance?
What a fee pays when no body rides. RAW anchor: the estate's own Call-to-Arms value, 1 gp a family — the default, and RAW exactly. Customary Angevin, John's and later negotiated price the century's postures, from John's half of the recorded requirement — raised, resisted, and a cause of 1215 — through the customary quarter down to a decayed seventh. The requirement in full: the crown charges the whole recorded requirement, and commutation stops being a bargain — though under the ordinance even that buys no lance, the paper standing at 100 and the lance costing 145. The four settings are postures, not measurements — the period table on the Muster section says why, and shows what the RAW anchor itself is worth in each of them.
⚖ Deeper — why the cheap rate is the interesting one
Scutage is not priced at what it replaces, and that gap is the whole institution. English scutage ran about 20s per fee — and what that was a share of is a question this module will not answer by division: the pay-roll knight at 2s a day is the module's own wage anchor and the History chapter dates it to the 13th–14th century, a century after the customary rate. The familiar quarter is a posture adopted, not a ratio measured, and the period table on the Muster section is where that is laid out figure by figure. What is not in doubt is the shape: the crown took the coin and still had to find the man; the difference came from fines for respite, aids at the three occasions, wardships, and reliefs — which is why a king's military finance is never one line in a ledger, and why barons fought over the rate rather than the principle. Set the dial to the requirement in full and the argument disappears wherever the paper and the hire agree: no lord would ever prefer coin, commutation dies, and the fee stays a body forever. Under the ordinance it does not disappear — the requirement is still the Angevin 100 while the lance it must replace costs 145, so rendering the paper in full leaves the crown 45 gp short of a man. That residue is the ordinance's whole bargain. Set it to the RAW anchor and the rate stops being a setting at all: it becomes the estate's own prosperity read backwards — the reciprocal of what one family nets its lord — so how cheap the coin is depends entirely on the land value, and the Muster section's period table walks the whole range. Keefe's caution applies: scutage was never one story, and the rate moved by reign, by campaign, and by who was arguing. The dial does not model that drift; it lets a Judge pick a century's posture and hold it.
The domain's template — the century it was founded under HISTORY
What century is this domain?
One click sets density, district class, the assize, the assessment custom, and this domain's standard of demand — five dials of the six a century touches. The sixth, land value, it only suggests: the dirt is a fact about this ground and not about the century, so the template offers its figure and leaves the slider where you put it. Everything stays live afterwards, and moving any one of the five by hand returns the chip to dials set by hand. The centuries argued in full: The eras.
⚖ Deeper — what a template writes, what it suggests, and what it never touches
The era table (History chapter, Library) read as dial settings — but read as a founding document rather than a world switch. Writes five: density, district class, the assize standing, the assessment custom, and the standard of demand. Suggests one: land value, which is a domain fact — standing manors don't shrink, and a century cannot make the dirt richer. Never touches two: the custom of record, because the economy belongs to the realm and not to the century (a reader comparing this estate against ACKS RAW revenues has not left the 13th century); and fosterage, a realm's custom for the same reason. Kaldor's own founding is the distraint century.

The ladder

Four rungs — ½, 1, 2, and 4 fees — priced live at the dials above (or from the state bar's chips, without leaving these cards). All four are fresh grants at the wage-parity floor — the smallest estate that keeps its man, sized by the land's yield;7 the holder's wage-grade is his keep, and the difference is the estate's whole spending power.11 Half a fee seats the landed man-at-arms; one the knight bachelor; two the county knight;8 four the castellan.9 The glance table compares them; each card carries its annotations folded at the foot.

7 · the hideFees were income assessments, and the hide — the old English tax-assessment unit of land, notionally 120 acres — was itself physically smaller in fertile shires: richer land shrinks the floors, as it should. A standing manor never resizes for it — it re-grades.
11 · two wage laddersTwo wage ladders meet here. The mercenary table (60 gp regular / 100 gp veteran heavy horse) prices a soldier on the open market; the henchman table (25/50/100/200/400) prices the stipend of a sworn man, whose loot-share and heritable tenure are the rest of his pay. They cross at 100 gp — a dubbed knight's market floor equals an L3 stipend — and the tenure is the discount.
8 · vavasour"Vavasour" is attested in English law for exactly this stratum — the substantial county knight at ~2× the minimal fee, where typical working manors actually sat — though its continental cousin could mean a far more modest rear-vassal: the estate-scale is solid, the word is slippery.
9 · castellariaA castellany is a fief, not an office — territory, as a barony is territory: the multi-manor estate gathered about a castle, held and inherited like any fee (Domesday's castellaria; the French châtellenie, often hereditary). Historical castleries often ran far larger — Richmondshire counted its fees in hundreds; the module borrows the name for its top knightly rung. The constable's commission is the neighbouring, different thing — the Offices section.

Manors at a glance

Cost to lord = income he'd net keeping the land in demesne — the land a lord keeps and runs himself; with the garrison hired for cash that is the fee-holder's net less 2 / 3 / 4 per family at civilized / borderlands / outlands (the c/b/o triplets used throughout — the district popover prints the sum at your current dials). Lord's net = retainer-equivalent − cost. Read it as a comparison and never as coin: what the same men would cost as standing hires, set against the income he gave up to have them instead. The cards split it into the three ledgers it was hiding — a garrison bill avoided monthly, a body owed once a year, and a wage not being paid — because those are three different kinds of number and only the first is a saving that recurs. The surplus of enfeoffment is largely the garrison bill he no longer pays, which is why knights profit a lord most on the frontier — and why the militia table below, where he pays that bill in yeomen instead, is the comparison that actually decides it. Each rung ≈ 2× the one below (wages double per level), so fees count in powers of two in the grade they retain: 1 fee keeps an L3, 2 an L4, 4 an L5 — what the fee grows unaided is one level shy (the knight's contract, ⚖ below).

Reading the manors — recruits, wage-grades, XP plateaus, and the two wage ladders

Recruits is market logic — but it is consulted only at escheat: line extinct, fee forfeit, or new land enfeoffed. In the steady state the fee is heritable and reproduces its own holder — the heir squires out at ~14, inherits at L1–L2, and grows into his grade. Primogeniture's landless younger sons are, in turn, exactly the pool of market knights the recruitment logic prices. Wage-grade is the henchman rate the fee must cover to keep him once he holds it. Raises to is XP logic — RAW pays rulers campaign XP each month from domain income above a level-based threshold (p.423), so land literally levels its holder over the years — and the dubbing decides the ledger. A dubbed knight is on the knight's contract (⚖ table below): his expected wage comes off domain income before the XP threshold applies (RR p.342 + Major Errata r4), so the fee grows him to one level below what it can retain — the last level is won in the field, never behind a plough. The undubbed esquire deducts nothing (p.423) and is the one man land alone completes. Knights are made by war; the fee only keeps them.

And that is an incentive to refuse the belt — put it on the table. On the ledger alone, staying an esquire is worth a level: the undubbed man deducts nothing, so land completes him where it stops his dubbed neighbour one grade short. What stands against it is not arithmetic and is not in these cards — it is distraint of knighthood (the crown compels the belt and fines the refusal; the Crown-follow-up selector in the Muster is that writ), exclusion from the offices and the commissions that only a knight holds, a worse hand in every marriage and wardship negotiation, and the plain fact that a lord chooses which of his men to seat on the better fee. The ledger advantage is real and it is meant to be; it is priced in standing, and standing is the Judge's to charge.

Granting land away can raise Personal Authority, and the module rules what that is. RAW measures PA against the domain a ruler personally administers, so enfeoffing land off the demesne can improve the number while the realm is unchanged. Read it as an administratively costly restructuring: enfeoffment is heritable, hard to reverse, creates a man with claims of his own, and Quia Emptores 1290 is the record's own comment on it — on a narrower point than the statute is usually given. It did not forbid a tenant to alienate his land; it forbade him to subinfeudate when he did, and the mischief it was aimed at was the dilution of a lord's incidents down a lengthening chain of tenures. Granting away stayed lawful. A smaller personal domain genuinely is easier to hold in one man's hand — and a lord who grants to game his PA has bought the number with land he cannot get back.

Two wage ladders meet here — know which is which. The mercenary table (60 gp regular / 100 gp veteran heavy horse) prices a soldier on the open market: kit, remounts, and no tenure. The henchman table (25 / 50 / 100 / 200 / 400) prices the stipend of a sworn man, whose loot-share and heritable tenure are the rest of his pay. They cross at 100 gp — a dubbed knight's market floor (the F1 veteran) equals an L3 stipend — which is exactly why one bachelor's rung (25 families at the customary rent, 12 at ACKS RAW revenues) serves knights of L1–L3, and why the esquire's fee keeps an L2 veteran on the half-fee’s 63 gp at ACKS RAW revenues — 60 at the customary rent — who would cost 100 as a hired lance: the tenure is the discount.

The muster

Walk one estate through a muster. Three campaign dials stand at its head — they decide which steps have anything to settle, and they are the same dials as the chips on the writ at the foot of the window. Then four steps — the estate, its serjeants, the settlement of the count, and the crown’s follow-up. Every choice is a box that says what choosing it means; the card below prices whichever ones are lit, and the household’s full doctrine is folded beneath it. The month of service rides on the knight’s purse and the field supply on the lord’s.13

13 · provider-paysRAW's military economy is provider-pays: the called vassal must muster an army with troop wages equal to 1 gp per family at his own cost, while the Troops favor runs the other way and has the lord pay for what he sends down (RR p.345–6). So the month of service rides on the knight's purse, and the field supply — about 16 gp a month a body, 4 gp a week (RR p.442) — rides on the lord's. Months 2+ the wages shift to the lord as well, at the muster-roll rate.

Paper against muster is not only this page's idea. The charter-versus-assessment model below was built from English evidence and the module's own doctrine — but Hârnic canon, written decades later by different authors, assesses knight service two ways at once (one knight per manor, and one knight per 1,200 gross acres) and leaves the two unreconciled. The mean Kaldoric manor sits 1.40× its paper, and two canon holdings work the whole argument out in print. Full treatment on the Hârn tab, at Canon's two rules; it is made once, there, rather than twice. HÂRN

The men around the man — why the hall matters (the full introduction)

The men around the man. The Ladder section prices what land keeps; this section prices what the hall keeps — the household, the period's mesnie. The fee ladder alone cannot see these men: it is a land-assessment engine, dirt in and one knight per rung out, and household men are unlanded — not a rung but a spending category. They matter twice over. Obligation sets the floor: the quota (on every Ladder card) makes a multi-fee holder owe more lances than his own body, and whatever his dirt cannot grow he must find — coin, term-hire, or retained men. Ambition sets the ceiling: above the floor a lord keeps men because the following is what surplus is for (worship, below). Everything here runs on numbers already in the module — the henchman wage (RR p.168), the supply rate (4 gp/wk), the XP threshold (p.423), and the henchman cap (4 + CHA).

Three populations — who owes, who rides, who is paid
