The populations convert: the household youth who proves out is enfeoffed at escheat or new land — population two feeding population one, the fosterage loop run forward. And history ran the current the other way in the end: as enfeoffment died, the obligation migrated from the first population to the second — the great retinues of the later centuries were retained and paid, not seated on fees (the era table, History chapter, Library).

The ledger — what a holder can keep (how to read the card below)

Every verdict below measures one number: the surplus — what the estate's income clears above the holder's own wage-grade keep (income − anchor). A man whose monthly cost sits inside the surplus is affordable; a man who costs more than it eats into the holder's own keep, and the estate can no longer sustain his grade — it slides toward the threadbare fee (Design chapter, Library). Pick a holder: the quota ledger applies the levy's credit and shows what is still owed, and the menu prices every way of adding a fighting man — per man and for the whole remaining count — at the land value set in the Dials section. The grown manor takes its families and charter from the fields above; the assessment lever (Dials section) picks which of its two readings rules.

What the campaign has already decided — the same three dials as the chips on the writ at the foot of the window: move either hand and both follow
The charter names its own lance in Step 1. This is what the host measures it against — and where the two disagree, that gap is what the settlement has to close.
Current — the paper tracks the land, nothing is owed beyond it, and Steps 3 and 4 stand idle. Ancient freezes the charter's count while the estate grew: the margin opens and the settlement goes live.
Kept, a qualifying multi-fee estate mounts serjeants and Step 2 goes live. In default it buys the identical watch at market instead, month after month.
Step 1

The estate

Who holds, and what the paper says. A fee of the ladder is its charter — its families are the fewest that pay it, and follow the land value. The grown manor is the estate that outgrew its grant, and the grant it outgrew is its identity: set its charter below, because the same families on a heavier paper are a poorer knight.

The holder (a fee’s families are derived; the grown manor sets its own)

— and its charter (fees written at the grant — the half of its identity that is not its size; inert while the assessment reads current, since the survey re-anchors to income)

— and its charter’s definition (the lance the paper names — written when the charter was; the definition of record is the muster’s standard, and the two may disagree)

— and its ward clause (castle-guard, as this charter writes it. The honour's whole reckoning is the ward on Feudal Realms; what a fee owes at a named castle is a term of its own paper, and it is set here)

— the body the clause names (the ward's own definition of record, and it is not the muster's: a charter can bind a watchman to a wall and a knight to the host in the same sentence)

— and who bore the founding capital (the kit is bought once and is an heirloom (p.432), and at every floor on the ladder it costs more than the estate clears in a year — so somebody bore it, and the charter can say who. Stocking is defined by headroom, not by patience: an estate at exact parity accumulates nothing, ever)

— and whether a view has certified it (until the first view, nobody has seen the watch stand, so the fee is not fully quit of its garrison line — though the holder's own lance discharges its part if he is present. This is incapacity, not contumacy: it hires the same watch as an assize in default and is in no way in breach)

Step 2

The serjeants

The assize’s mounted serjeants: ride against the count, or remain with the manor while their share settles below. Readiness is the assize’s; deployment is the muster’s choice — qualifying multi-fee estates only.

— and the ground they leave (a serjeant presented to the host is not standing on the manor: readiness is a question about arms and is unaffected, protection is a question about bodies and is not)

Idle here — this estate mounts no serjeant against the count, or its paper needs no settling.

Step 3

The settlement

How the count is actually discharged — the holder’s own share first, then everything owed beyond him. Live for the grown manor under an ancient assessment; elsewhere the paper needs no remedy and every box stands idle.

— the personal share (the holder's own lance-equivalent; grown manor, ancient reading)

— the additional quota (beyond holder and levy credit; multi-fee charters only)

Idle here — take the grown manor (Step 1) and set the assessment to ancient (the dials at the head of this walk) to settle a count against its old paper.

Step 4

Crown follow-up

After the host rides — the crown’s move against the man or the paper, on its own timescale, never this year’s muster.

Idle here — nothing to pursue while the paper is current.

Step 5

What the field took

The levy after the fighting. RAW says in as many words that a leader should track militia casualties (p.432) — and the module had never rendered what tracking them costs. Nothing here is a new obligation: the count the fee owes does not move, only its ability to discharge it.

— and how the place is read (⚠ the strict reading is the harsher one, not the cheaper: it charges nothing because it offers no remedy. The kit is assumed lost with the man — RAW's heirloom clause covers the man who wears out, not the man who is killed)

— and what the holder does about it (a casualty is incapacity. Only the last of these is contumacy, and only it puts the bond in question)

Idle here — a lordship holds no fee, so the assize reaches its levy neither as credit nor as breach.

Step 6

The view of arms

The ordinary cadence, twice a year — where the lord learns what he has. Four of the seven articles are already settled by the walk above; what the court needs from a Judge is whether the man came, and what convened it.

The holder at the view (⚠ the one article whose grade is a ruling and not a constant: absence with a cause of record is incapacity, absence without one is not)

— and what else the court found (⚠ these two are the Judge's facts and not the page's. The first wiring of this step derived them from the charter ladder — arrears from "the residual settles out of the margin", the watch from "the year's call is set aside" — which reads two capacity facts as a withholding, and priced prudence not laid by as a default against the module's own ruling that only failure to answer is one. The module's headline fee stood in contumacy on an ordinary view)

— and what convened the court (the spec lists these as one thing and they are three: a defect that is already graded, a condition that broke nobody's article, and a change of person — which stays the ladder, because a child cannot be in contempt of a court)

— where the roll stood at the last view (the record carries one view of memory, which is exactly the spec's own threshold: two failed views, or an unremedied refusal)

— and the lord's election now (grace is a favour, offered at the first view and not renewable. Step 5's "grace to the next view" is the holder asking; this is the lord answering, and an election is not a favour)

Idle here — a lordship holds no fee, and the articles of the view are a fee’s.

Step 7

The homage

The other end of Step 6’s stay. Four of the view’s triggers are changes of person — the holder dead, the heir a minor, the line extinct, the fee alienated — and at each of them the court takes the roll and holds the ladder, because a grade is a fact about the fee and the homage is a fact about a man. What convened the court is not asked again here: this step reads it from Step 6, and what it needs from a Judge is what happened at the lord’s court afterwards.

The heir at the lord’s court (the act itself: he kneels, hands between the lord’s hands, and the lord confirms the charter — succession with homage does not rewrite the paper, which is why an heir inherits the count his grandfather was assessed at. The term is the view’s own, and the module declares no second clock)

— and whether he is yet a knight (⚠ three roads lead out of the knight’s contract and all three end on the same −2. This is the second of them, and it is nobody’s fault: an undubbed heir stands where the esquire stands, and the remedy is the lord’s — he dubs him, at his own convenience)

— and the relief (paid at the homage: the two incidents are one scene. ⚠ a relief unpaid is not automatically arrears — the Library’s own worked table finds that at the default land value no rung of this ladder can pay it out of income, and arrears is graded contumacy, so wiring the two together would put every heir in the module in contempt. History’s instrument is the third option)

— and, at an alienation, the licence (Step 6 hands this question over unanswered by design: whether the licence was had is succession’s question, not the view’s. Licensed, the grantee holds by his own charter; unlicensed, nothing has been conveyed that the lord need write down, and the man before him is still the one who granted it away)

— and where the manor lies (RR p.347’s second figure: a man outside the contract stands at −2, and at −4 if his manor lies beyond the range of trade of the lord’s largest town — the range itself JJ p.203, so the trade maps double as loyalty maps. It moves nothing while the contract holds, which is the point)

Idle here — a lordship answers to nobody on this page, so there is no homage to do and no relief to pay.

The rate, by period — and the one quarter that is the game's

Scutage is a share of something, and which something is the whole question. This module's rate lever offers a century's posture; the postures are adopted, not measured, and the block below shows the difference figure by figure. The rule it is built on is short: a period is part of a quantity's dimension — a due from one reign divided by a wage from the next is not a share of anything, whatever the arithmetic says.

What breaks the bank

The finding, plainly: at the wage-parity floor no rung of the knight's ladder keeps a standing fighting man on wages — structurally so: a fresh floor's rounding surplus is always less than one family's output, at most 11 gp under any land value, and can never meet even the 25-gp L1 wage. The quota above one lance is affordable only in coin or for the term, and that is the record's own answer (scutage, the term sergeant). The standing mesnie lives in two places only: the margin — the grown manor whose ancient assessment never caught up, which is why distraint hunts exactly those men — and the barony, where RAW's henchman roster simply resumes. Between the floor and the margin stands the household every knight does keep: the domestic establishment inside his threshold, below.

The two cost regimes — keep in peace, wages in war

A retained man is never priced as a standing mercenary, and the mistake of doing so is what makes households look impossible. In peace he is kept, not hired: the fighting household man is a henchman at his own wage (25/50/100 by level) — part of it rendered as the hall's board in kind (~16 gp/mo of the supply rate, man and mount) — and the bond, not the board, is the discount: a 25-gp L1 henchman stands where a hired sergeant costs 60. Below him the valet draws no wage at all — he is the domestic establishment, inside the threshold (next section): his wage is his place, as the squire's is his education. (The fifteenth-century paybooks kept the same two lines: the ordinance lance paid its coustillier — a fighting rider, this ladder's man-at-arms — and carried its page unpaid; the Library’s History chapter’s lance note has the whole arc.) In war the split follows RAW's own favor-and-duty law (p.345–6) — two RAW halves and one transplant. RAW's halves: a Call to Arms is provider-pays — the called vassal musters at his own wage cost, so the fee’s month of service rides on the knight's purse (priced live on every Ladder card, once a year: at the module's defaults it runs from about three-quarters of the fee's income at the lower rungs to more than the whole of it at the castellany. The share swings with the land value and the custom of record, so every card computes its own rung's figure); and the Troops favor runs the other way — what the lord sends, the lord pays. The transplant (owned in the ⚖ table, Library): RAW bounds duties by count — one per favor, no free service — never by days; the module reads the land as the standing favor that earns one month of service a year, and prices anything beyond it as new consideration at the muster-roll wage — the lord's coin. So the estate carries the term and nothing past it: the keep is why a hall could hold men a wage-ledger says it cannot; the lord's wage past the forty days is why a thin fee could stay in the field beyond them at all. One boundary note: host supply is the lord's line throughout (Units section), so a term-hire's bill on the fee is the wage alone — the ledger shows both the month-of-service sum and the monthly reserve it implies.

The household inside the threshold

Before any wage is paid, every knight already keeps a household — inside his cost of living. RAW prices a level's expected living at its own wage line ("living expenses… equal to the wages of a henchman of the same level" — 25 / 50 / 100 / 200 / 400 gp/mo, p.173), and counts what that spending buys: servants, stabling, an implicit rent of the hall itself (p.173). The XP threshold above it (25 / 75 / 150 / 300 / 600 gp/mo, p.423) is a different ladder — the income a man of each level should command with ease, half again the spending from L2 up — so the establishment fits inside the threshold with headroom. That spending is the domestic establishment — grooms, a porter, a huntsman, men who take up a bill when the manor is entered. So the bank-breaking table above is not "knights had no households"; it is the sharper claim that matches the record: servants who could fight were universal; fighting men on wages were magnate practice. The armed valet lives on the living-expense line, below the threshold; the household knight lives in the margin.

The warded walls — castle-guard

The castellany's arithmetic looks like a paradox — a castle-holder who cannot pay watchmen — until the period's own answer is priced: the castle is warded by other men's service, not the castellan's purse. Castle-guard was a render like any other: fees bound to a castle owed ward in rotation (the honour of Wallingford's fees, History chapter, Library), and serjeanties — small tenures held by the service of a man at the walls — clustered at castles because the castle-holder is the one lord land-rich enough to carve them. This is the quittance doctrine pointed at the walls: the ward is discharged in kind by tenure, and the garrison line the castellan would pay is quit by the same instrument that quits his own. Enfeoffing is the land-rich lord's move; retaining is the land-poor knight's — a bachelor never carves an esquire's half-fee out of his own: at the customary rent that is 15 families out of 25 (under ACKS RAW revenues, 7 out of 12). The ratio that survives every reading is in the anchors — 60 against 100, three to five exactly — and the realised counts sit a little either side of it, because each rung rounds its own remainder up.

And this is where the doctrine is argued; it is priced in two places, at two scales. The clause is a term of this fee's charter and is set in Step 1 above — how many of its own lances stand at the walls, what body the clause names, and what the tenant renders when one does not appear. What a whole honour's walls actually received is the realm's reckoning: the ward, on Feudal Realms. (Ruling T4-R1 — the charter to the charter's tab, the aggregate above it to the realm's.) Either way, what the ledger does with a ward-bound lance depends on what the charter says. Under a substitution charter — the default — it takes them out of the host and puts their service against the castellan's garrison: the service is spent once, which makes ward a decision rather than a second bill. Under an abating charter they owe the walls and the field, so they ride anyway and the ward abates by the months they served (Magna Carta cl. 29) — and it is the walls that go short. The dial is in lances, not days either way: this module keeps one calendar, the month of service. Both readings are in the ⚖ doctrine table, which is where the ruling is declared.

At the barony, RAW resumes

The quota is a doctrine of the knight's ladder only — ACKS RAW gives barons no fee-count; their duties run by favors, tribute, and the Call to Arms as written. And the baron needs no household rules either, because RAW already has them: the mesnie is the henchman roster — 4 + CHA sworn men at the wage table's rates, the 9th-level magnate adding companions who take no slot (p.334–6). How full the hall runs is a matter of demesne: at average land a 160-family barony's demesne clears nothing above the L6 wage in any district under the customary rent — 320 / 160 / 0 gp/mo of demesne against an 800-gp keep — while under ACKS RAW revenues the same 160 families clear ~320 gp/mo above that wage when civilized, ~160 at borderlands, and exactly nothing at outlands. A hall full of sworn men is RAW's economy talking, and the customary reading answers that a barony of this size is a knight's estate with a title on it, not a household. The district selector above prices it, and note what does not move: a fee's own net is class-free (land+3 under ACKS RAW revenues, land−2 customary) — the quittance's quiet gift, and it is the class-freeness rather than the figure that is the point: it is why marcher realms ran on fees while their barons' demesnes ran thin. Where the surplus exists, the binding constraint is never coin but Charisma: the sworn household ends at the cap, and past it stand non-henchman retainers at base −2 — annuitants, liveried men, the bought and re-bought. The affinity begins where Charisma runs out.

Worship — why the surplus becomes men

"Worship" is the period's word for standing, and it worked like a credit rating. In a world with no police, no bureaucracy at the village, and royal courts that could not enforce their own judgments, protection and justice were private goods, produced by networks of lordship — your rights were worth exactly the following that would turn out for you. From that one fact the whole economy of lordship follows. Coin that stays coin cannot defend itself: the rich man with no following is the one whose manor is entered, whose suit is lost to a packed jury, whose heiress is married away — prey. Coin converted into men is security, litigation-power, marriage-market weight, and the only ladder toward lordship — which is why the moral literature praised largesse and damned avarice: it was encoding a political truth. So above the quota's floor, the margin does not accumulate; it recruits. A lord offers good lordship — protection, advancement, offices, his weight at law — and receives service, counsel, arms, and presence; followers wear his badge so that all men know who would come if they were crossed; and the fatal thing said of any lord is that he could not keep his men.

In the module's terms worship is not a new mechanic — it is why the existing ones point the way they do. The loyalty ladder (Design chapter, Library) is the asset being purchased: household henchmen at 0, companions at +2, the affinity's annuitants held near 0 only by continuous good lordship — service must be continuously bought, one favor per duty, and the household's keep is that purchase made monthly. Arbitration is its exercise: most disputes ended not in a verdict but in a loveday — a settlement imposed by a respected lord under the implicit weight of both followings — and being asked to arbitrate is itself worship, the castellan's unofficial office (his official ones are the Offices section’s). And the corruption dial has its mirror here: the unsworn officer converts the crown's revenue into his own level; the lord converts his own revenue into men — one is graft, the other lordship, and both are the same arithmetic of income made into power.

The assessment — when the paper is written

The margin that funds all of this has a legal engine, and the module dials it (the assessment lever, Dials section). A charter writes three things — the count of lances, the definition of a lance, and the term — once, at the grant ("holds by the service of N knights," priced from the land's income by this module's own table), and the assize then polices kit against the paper, never wealth: no one re-rates a manor for prospering. The paper is rewritten at exactly three events: escheat and re-grant (the new charter prices at current income — the same event where recruitment logic runs, Ladder section); new enfeoffment, including subinfeudation; and royal inquest (Domesday, the cartae of 1166, Kirkby's Quest — generational, resisted, dear). Distraint is the crown's cheap workaround and is deliberately not on that list: it rewrites nothing and instead taxes income directly (the £20/£40 lines), forcing the dubbing and with it the knight's ledger, converting the holder's margin from household money into the crown's service. Under current assessments the survey is fresh and the module behaves as it always has. Under ancient, counts — and the definition with them — freeze while incomes grow, and the margin opens — at average land, 100 gp/mo on the 50-family manor the module opens on, still charted at one fee: a household knight, or a few men-at-arms. (The growth is the point, not the size. At average land the customary rent puts a 23-family manor below the one-fee anchor — no margin at all, and it stays below until land 7 — while under ACKS RAW revenues at that same average land those 23 families clear 107 gp/mo. Both halves of that sentence are pinned to land 6.) Distraint is the crown noticing; the era where the margin is universal is bastard feudalism (the recovered layer, History chapter, Library) — frozen quotas, grown incomes, and every margin wearing livery. One cross-current runs the other way: the frozen count capped the crown's scutage basis too, which is why crowns abandoned the fee for the income tax; and a holder might seek re-assessment upward — banner eligibility, a marriage, worship — the social pressure against pocketing the margin quietly forever.

Knight units

Muster the fees into the field. Pick the level of the knights, how many ride, and the banneret who leads them; the calculator organizes them into ACKS units (RR p.435–7), prices the muster (RR p.442), and rates them for the battles system (BR — Battle Rating — is ACKS's unit-strength number for mass battles; 60 ordinary heavy cavalry rate BR 6). The banneret serves as his unit's lieutenant — division command belongs to the lord (commanders must be L6+ at company scale: baron-grade, RR p.435; the officer ladder and the manor grades are the same scale). Leveled knights are priced as heroic units (RR p.466): BR = (AC+1) × HD × (HD+1) × (1+specials) ÷ 960 per man — a unit of true knights is worth several times its weight in hired horse.14

14 · the heroic-unit formulaThe troop tables stop at veteran F1, so RAW prices no L2+ non-hero unit. This module prices every leveled unit by the heroic-unit formula — BR = (AC+1) × HD × (HD+1) × (1+specials) ÷ 960 per man (RR p.466) — floored at veteran heavy cavalry (0.169) and displayed ÷960 throughout so knights, troop tables, and the "≈ N companies" line stay comparable. Hero status gates forays, not unit pricing.
The banneret's qualities
Officer characteristics (RR p.435–6). Defaults are a plain man — a real banneret likely carries Command and a rank of Military Strategy.

The Judge's sheet LIVE · TWO PAGES

Six procedures, in the order a table meets them, with this estate's answers already in them. Every record on this page answers one occasion; what the sheet adds is the arrows — what each procedure hands the next, and what is written down and carried to the sitting after.

The office — a district, and the man who holds it

A fee is heritable and paid in land; an office is revocable and paid in coin. That is the whole distinction, and it is why crowns ran castles by commission while seating knights on fees. This tab prices one office — the district officer, the sheriff or castle-constable — because his is the only loyalty that moves the crown's money. The roster below names every other office the module mentions and says who prices it. Used from both sides: a realm built on Feudal Realms is administered through these men, and they are drawn from the bench the ladder builds.

The office is the other way to set a man over land. RAW prices it already: a ruler may appoint magistrates (RR p.342) — captain of the guard, chaplain, munerator, steward — each overseeing one line of the domain's expenses and keeping 12.5% of the line he oversees as salary. The salary is carved out of the line itself (the ruler pays nothing extra and the troops are not reduced), it counts as the magistrate's own domain income for campaign XP, and RAW wants him sworn: magistrates are "usually fellow adventurers, followers, or henchmen," and "non-henchman magistrates might be susceptible to corruption or treachery." The sheriff and the constable of a royal castle are this machinery set over a district rather than the ruler's whole domain, overseeing two lines: the crown's tribute gathered through the castle, and the garrison it pays for. Command rides with the second line — the captain-of-the-guard delegations are inspecting troops, overseeing training, training troops, and waging war (RR p.352–3).15

15 · office is not tenureA castellany is a fief; the constable's commission is an office — ministerial, revocable, staffed from exactly that bench. RAW's only officer machinery is the four expense-line magistrates at 12.5% (RR p.342); the fisc oversight is this module's extension of that rate, at Call-to-Arms parity (1 gp per family, p.345–6). The fee-farm pole — the governor who keeps what he collects above the farm — is JJ p.405–6.
The fisc, the corruption dial, and the office as anti-fee — the full doctrine

This is doctrine, declared: RAW's four magistrates oversee expense lines only, and none collects revenue — we add the fisc as a fifth oversight for district officers. RAW rewards the extension twice. Cash tribute decays with vassal count (Tribute Inefficiency, RR p.347): a third to half of every payment is lost to "crime, corruption, or waste" — and a sworn collector on a lawful 12.5% is exactly the cure the period applied. And the office is the anti-fee: paid in coin not land, revocable not heritable, loyal at 0 + the crown's CHA — the dubbed knight holds the same base 0, but his bond rides a heritable fee, where the office can be resumed with a word (only the undubbed and the defaulted sit at −2) — which is why crowns ran castles by commission while seating knights on fees. The opposite pole — the officer who keeps everything above a fixed render, as the early English sheriffs farmed their shires — is the Judges Journal's landowner/governor split (JJ p.405–6); this section prices the reformed, salaried custodian instead. And where the office is not held by a sworn man, RAW's warning gets numbers: the appointee skims a share of the spread — the gap between his lawful fee and the district's inefficiency band — sliding the crown's take from 87.5% back down toward the band itself. The two RAW tables are the endpoints; loyalty is the dial between them.

How much fisc can one man administer? — the bound, and why it is RAW's own rate backwards

The extension above has a hole in it, and it is worth naming before the dials do. A sworn officer recovering 87.5% of whatever passes through him recovers it at any scale: one honest sheriff administers a shire, a kingdom or a continent for the same salary, and Tribute Inefficiency — which the Judges Journal describes as load-bearing realm structure, the thing that "prevents realms from being divided up between too many vassals" — is abolished for one appointment. RAW cannot settle it, because RAW's magistrate never touches revenue: the question does not exist in the book. So the bound has to come from somewhere, and there is only one honest place to get it — the magistrate's own rate, read backwards.

He is paid an eighth of the line he oversees. So the line whose eighth pays his wage is wage ÷ ⅛: an L5 at 400 gp carries 3,200 gp/mo of fisc, and at full stretch his lawful salary is exactly his own wage. No number is invented — the 8 is the reciprocal of the eighth, and the bench is self-financing by construction: covering a fisc F needs a wage bill of at least F ÷ 8, which is 12.5% of F, which is the salary. That identity is the whole argument. Beyond his reach the coin does not vanish — it falls back to RAW's band, computed on the remitters he does not answer for, so the inefficiency re-emerges exactly where no seatable man is big enough. That is JJ's design intent restored at scale rather than engineered away.

Three consequences the dials will show you, and one of them is the opposite of what a reader expects. The district is a roster, not a heap of coin: a payer is an immediate remitter — a mesne lord bundling ten fees is one payer — so the officer either answers for a remitter or he does not, and a sheriff too small to answer for a great honour answers for none of it. Deputies buy reach, not salary: the eighth is invariant in officer count, so a bench of five divides exactly what one man would have drawn, and splitting changes who must exist rather than what it costs — so what binds a crown is not the payroll but the supply of graded men, and the slots it has to bind them with. (The slot is cited here of the officer, who is sworn at henchman grade and not enfeoffed — RAW's own "usually … henchmen," p.342. What a slot means for a knight on a fee is settled in the Manors tab's bundle, and nothing here reaches it.) The partition is where the interest lies: a 12,800-gp line is one L7, or two L6, or eight L4 — the same salary every time, and three quite different exposures, because one loyalty score spans a man's whole standing and a great sheriff who falls takes his district with him. These dials price the bench as one head and his deputies; several independent sheriffs over several rosters cost the crown exactly the same and differ only in that blast radius, which is a Judge's call and not an arithmetic one. And below nine remitters the office is a loss: the band pays in full there, so there is no inefficiency to cure and the eighth is simply spent — a spread of −12.5%. The fisc office is therefore a top-tier instrument. A feudal county with mesne lords bundling beneath it never has enough direct remitters to be worth a sheriff's percentage; its officer earns his keep on the demesne lines and the arrears, and the crown that needs the office is the one answering to a hundred tenants-in-chief at once. History agrees: the great vassals met the sheriff as an enforcement arm, and the barons ran their honours with stewards and bailiffs — RAW's own expense-side magistrates.

⚠ One line of this is not negotiable, and it is the line that makes the bound a bound. Capacity follows the officer's actual level, never the level his proceeds imply. Grade the man by his take and then let that grade license the take, and you have written a warning wearing a bound's clothes: it can never bind, because the quantity it caps is the quantity that sets it. The card reports what the office would pay for, beside the man who is in it. The reporting is the useful part; the direction is the whole point.

The dial at a glance — this district, the whole loyalty ladder

A vocabulary note first: the dial runs on the officer's loyalty — the man's stat (base −2 unsworn, −4 beyond the range of trade, RR p.347; "hostile" is the Hostility result of the Henchman Loyalty table) — not morale, which in ACKS II belongs to the district's population (base morale score, RR p.347–8). We read the base loyalty score itself as the dial position — RAW uses it as a roll modifier; the dial treats the −6…+2 axis as a scale of how bought the man is. Read the endpoints: the sworn man costs the lawful 12.5% (RR p.342); the hostile man delivers the crown exactly the inefficiency band (RR p.347) — RAW resumes when governance fails. Loyalty prices everything between. And because the salary is the officer's income for XP by RAW (p.342/423) — and the dial rules the skim the same way, its own extension — corruption levels the man: the unsworn officer grows himself out of the crown's own revenue stream — a self-funded villain, which is how a Sheriff of Nottingham happens. The gap between any row and the sworn man's row is what the bond is worth: closing it is what fosterage and household office-holding are for. The ladder is generated by one rule — an unsworn officer's skim share is (2 − loyalty) ÷ 8, clamped 0–1: at +2 good lordship collects like the sworn man, and by −6 the band has returned without waiting for a Hostility roll. And mind the render rate: the spread scales with the take, so the unsworn officer who exacts 2 gp/family where custom says 1 doubles fee and skim alike — raising the taxes can raise the man a level. Nottingham squeezed the shire for a reason.

The roster — every office this module names, and who prices it

This tab prices one office: the district officer — the sheriff, or the constable of a royal castle — because that is the one whose loyalty changes the crown's revenue. The rest of the page names a dozen more, and this is the boundary: which are RAW's, which are the module's, which are canon's, and which are named for texture and priced by nobody.

Every office this module names, what it oversees, what it is paid, and where it is priced

RAW's own delegations: inspecting troops, overseeing training, training troops, and waging war 12.5% of the line, out of the line — the ruler's costs do not rise RAW prices him (RR p.342). Why only one office gets a dial. Every other line above is either a fixed price (RAW's 12.5%, canon's wages) or a tenure rather than a commission. The district officer is the one whose loyalty moves money — because he stands between the crown and revenue it cannot otherwise reach, and RAW says outright that an unsworn one is "susceptible to corruption" without ever saying what that costs. This tab is the answer to that sentence, and nothing more.

The office in history — how a commission becomes a dynasty

The fee is heritable by design; the office is revocable by design. Nearly the whole medieval history of office is the second trying to become the first — and the dial on this page is that story compressed into one loyalty setting.

Start where the drift is clearest. A Carolingian comes was a royal officer: he held an honor — the office together with the lands that paid for it — at the king’s pleasure, and could in principle be moved or removed. In practice a man who commanded his district’s fighting men, in a century of raids and weak kings, was not easily dislodged; and a king who needed the district defended had every reason to leave a competent son in his father’s place. The Capitulary of Quierzy (877) is the marker usually reached for17. Within a few generations the countship is patrimony, and the office has become a fee. That is this tab’s warning case, not its model: everything below is about the technologies that hold the drift off.

England ran the same institution with the brake on. The sheriff — vicecomes — answered at the Exchequer for the firma comitatus, the county farm: a fixed annual sum for the shire’s revenues, the surplus his to keep. That is exactly the fee-farm pole of the dial (JJ p.405–6): the crown takes a known figure, and hands the risk, the effort and the squeeze to the man on the ground. It is cheap, it is administratively simple, and it is corrupting by construction — the officer’s income is the gap between what he collects and what he renders. Sheriffs grew rich enough that Henry II swept them out wholesale in the Inquest of Sheriffs (1170); later the counties were allowed to farm themselves and cut the middleman out of his own margin.

What kept an office an office was never the officer’s virtue. It was audit and term: the Exchequer’s twice-yearly account, the general eyre and the itinerant justices, the Provisions of Oxford (1258) demanding sheriffs drawn from the county and changed yearly, the elected hundred-constables of Winchester (1285). Rotation and accounting are the counter-technology to heredity, and both are expensive. Where a crown could not pay for them it farmed instead — and where it farmed long enough, it lost the office. The end of that road is venality: the office sold outright as property, and in France the paulette of 1604 letting a holder make his office heritable for an annual premium. At that point the crown has sold its own administration, and the journey from commission to estate is complete.

17 · Quierzy, 877 — a marker, not a moment DEBATED Charles the Bald, leaving for Italy, provided that if a count died in his absence the son might hold his father’s honor pending the king’s decision. It is routinely quoted as the birth of hereditary office, and it is not that: modern scholarship reads it as acknowledging a practice already running, not creating a right. Contested — cite it as a signpost on a slope, not a statute that made fiefs heritable. The direction of travel is what matters here, and on that the record is not divided.

Four stages, and where the dial sits on them

Four stages of an office, and where the corruption dial sits on them
StageThe officer keepsHistorical markerOn this page
Commission — office at pleasureA salary, audited The Carolingian comes at his height; the audited English sheriff Sworn henchman — the lawful 12.5% and nothing else
Farm — office at a priceThe gap between collection and render Firma comitatus; the shrieval farm (JJ p.405–6) The skimming settings — a quarter, a half, three-quarters of the spread
Patrimony — office in the familyThe district itself, in all but name Quierzy 877 and after; the countship become a county Hostile — the band returns entire, and the crown holds a title over a stranger
Property — office as capitalThe office, saleable and heritable Venality; the French paulette, 1604 Off the dial. Not modelled — see the ruling below

The module’s ruling, and its cost. Offices here are never heritable: a district is granted, held, and revoked, and no son inherits a shrievalty. That is a deliberate simplification and the history says it is the unstable case — left alone, offices drift into patrimony, which is precisely why crowns spent so much on audit. So a Judge who lets an office pass to a son has not house-ruled a detail; he has converted the office into a fee, and should price it on the Feudal Manors tab instead, where heritable tenure is what the whole engine is for. Note too what the level counter on this page already models without naming it: an unsworn officer whose skim grows him a level is stage two becoming stage three, at the table, in a few years of play. The corruption dial is not a flavour setting — it is the rate of that drift.

Building a realm — the order to do it in

This tab is the module's macro layer, and most of it is ACKS's own: a domain with a population, expenses, vassals and tribute. What the module adds is the tier underneath — land granted for service rather than for coin — and the arithmetic that follows from it. Six steps below, in the order the sections come. The page opens on a worked realm, so nothing here is blank: change what you need and leave the rest.

Step 1 · The realm

The ground and the lord

Rural families, land value, district class, the lord's level.

Type the rural family count only — towns are counted separately in step 2, and pooling the two is the one mistake this tab will not let you make silently. The lord's level caps how much realm he can hold without a vassal beneath him.

Step 2 · Settlements

The second population

Burgesses — a different people, priced differently.

Towns earn by trade, not by land; they carry a flat garrison of 2 whatever the district; and they keep RAW's own 4-and-2 under either custom of record. Found one per market — two towns are two markets, never one bigger one.

Step 3 · Vassals & fees

How the land is held

The decision this whole module is about.

Three ways, and a realm is the mix: keep it in demesne and take coin, grant it to a vassal and take tribute, grant it as a fee and take service. Fee sizes are the ladder's, not yours — they come off the Feudal Manors tab and move with the same dials.

Step 4 · The ward

Where the service is spent

Castle-guard, the ward-penny, serjeanty.

Whether a lance at the walls is instead of the host or on top of it is what the charter says — and that is what decides which of the two goes short in a war year. This is also where a castle stops being a line item: ward-penny is a standing income against a standing bill, which scutage never was.

Step 5 · The garrison

Men, and where they stand

The first section that builds rather than prices.

The coin garrison left over from steps 3 and 4, spent on actual bodies in actual places. It opens on a derived establishment — the Statute of Winchester's own coefficients over this realm's vills and boroughs — so there is something to argue with rather than a blank matrix.

Step 6 · The reckoning

What it all comes to

Income, host, ward, and the flags.

Read the cards, then read the writ at the foot of the section — one sentence, rebuilt on every dial move. The flags are where the realm tells you it is illegal, over its ceiling, or paying for something twice.

And then the officers. A realm of any size is not administered by its lord in person: districts are held by sheriffs and castle-constables, and what they cost — and what an unsworn one skims — is the Officers tab. It is priced separately because an office is not tenure: revocable where a fee is heritable, paid in coin where a fee is paid in land. Two dials on this tab are set by convention rather than by arithmetic — fosterage and where the boys go — and both are argued at the fields themselves.

⚠ The two tabs are not wired together, and here is what to carry across. The Officers tab holds its own dials so that a district can be priced without a realm behind it — a crown officer is often set over land the player never designs. Building both, you type four figures over by hand: the district's crown demesne (its families in hand), its class, the coin-paying families bound to the office — demesne manors and commuted fees, never knight-fees, which render lances — and the render rate. Everything else on that tab is derived. Nothing on this tab changes when you do: an officer's salary is carved out of the line he oversees, so the reckoning above is already net of him.

The realm

Three ways to hold land, and a realm is the choice between them: keep it in demesne and take coin, grant it to a vassal and take tribute, grant it as a fee and take service. Two populations hold that land — the rural families here and the settlements below — and the honour musters a ward as well as a host. The tables are yours to type into: the honour is a design, not a roll.

Market class — RAW's size grade for a settlement (VI up to I). A label on the market: the population band is what sets the trade rate, and three classes share one.
The ceiling — the largest realm the lord's own level can hold without a vassal beneath him. A bound on the design, not a tax.
⚠ "Settlement" means two things in this module, and they are unrelated. Here it is a town — RAW's second population. On Feudal Manors, Muster Step 3 settles the count, which is an act of bookkeeping: fixing how many lances the paper owes.
The rest of this tab's vocabulary — demesne, honour, vassal and tribute, the host, ward, the ward-penny, serjeanty, burgess, the title population — is defined once, with the manor's and the crown's, at the terms on the Overview.

⚖ Deeper — where one boy per three households comes from
The band is demography, not doctrine. A seven-year window (14–21) over a generation of about 30, times roughly 1.4 sons reaching adolescence per inheriting son, gives about one boy of squiring age per three households of the class. That is the default, and it is the reason "one combatant squire per knight, always" is a convention rather than a demographic fact — the boys do not exist in those numbers. Canon legislates the older shape and says so in its own words. Hârn defines the spear as "one knight, one squire and four yeomen", and the phrase is "has traditionally been set at" — assessment language, a servitium debitum, which is a statement about what a holding OWES and not about who rides out of its gate. Selecting 1 per household is therefore selecting canon's paper, deliberately; the realm then musters its assessment rather than its population, and the module's own default sits lower because in the century it otherwise targets the knight's attendant is commonly a page or a valet, the "esquire" having hardened into a rank of independent combatants. The other realm rate has this same shape — the yeoman at acres ÷ 300 in Kaldor and Chybisa, one per 600 in Melderyn — and for the same reason. What the boy is worth is on the Feudal Manors tab's fosterage lever: +45 gp of watch-and-train value at zero land cost, no place in the line of battle, and reciprocal, so it nets out realm-wide.
⚖ Deeper — the law moves the boys, and the ledger follows them
A flat "+45 per lance" is wrong in shape, not merely in level. The boys do not spread evenly; they pool — and they pool because the law moves them. A lord held the wardship of a tenant's minor heir and commonly raised him in his own household, and the great halls — royal, comital, episcopal — were the training schools of the class. So the halls draw first, by standing, with wardships ahead of placements. Canon prices the office that runs them, and the comparison is canon against canon: Master of Squires at 324 d/mo (Kaldor 17), above a Constable of Keeps at 300 d — printed beside "Squires (unpaid)" in the same table. Kept in pence on purpose: no coin anchor is needed for one canon figure to be read against another, and this module has ruled that there is no single d/gp rate to convert them by. And the consequence is a ledger consequence, not a flavour one. A boy in the earl's hall stands the castle's watch, not a manor's — so the watch-and-train value lands where the boy is, and choosing evenly over the fees moves it back out to the manors, which is the flat assumption stated as a choice rather than made silently.
⚖ Deeper — why a clock, and why never at the fee
This dial belongs to the realm and to nothing else. RAW's scutage is a standing monthly rate on a tribute vassal (RR p.346) — it does not have a term, it runs until the duty is revoked. So "how long does it stand" is a real question here, and RAW answers it with a clock rather than a term: the Favor/Duty table gives a 16.7% chance per month that the most recent duty is revoked, which makes about six months the expectation. The default is 1, which prices a single month and changes no figure that was on this card before the dial existed. ⚠ It must never be offered at the fee tier, and that is a ruling with three reasons. The fee does not hold a levy that stands: it commutes one month of service a year, and it is quit of the very garrison line RAW's monthly rate is netted against. A months multiplier there would double-charge the fee, invert the rate lever — cheaper scutage would start costing more — and price out the wardships and widows the quittance exists to protect. The argument in full is the scutage section of the Design chapter.

Settlements — the realm's second population · RAW's own tier RAW

RAW gives a domain two populations, and this is the other one: burgesses — townsmen holding by burgage, free, paying a money rent for their plot and owing no labour on anyone's demesne. Not peasants, and priced apart from them. The rural field above counts the first population; nothing here is counted twice. Six rulings this section makes are stated on it, because the arithmetic a Judge types depends on them.

A settlement is not a big village: its own revenue line (trade, by its population band — the market class printed beside it is a label, and three classes share one rate), its own expenses, and a flat garrison of 2 whatever the district class. Below 75 families RAW dissolves it into the peasantry, so the editor will not let one exist — those families belong in the rural field above, and moving them is yours to do rather than the page's to do quietly.

Three rulings this section makes. In demesne only — a town in a vassal's realm is his, and reaches you through his tribute, already keyed on the family count you typed for him. Many, never pooled — market class is per settlement: two towns of 200 are two Class VI markets, not one Class V. The realm's morale, not its own — a settlement shares the base and current morale of the domain it sits in, and that domain is yours.

The manorial reading stops at the town wall. Whatever the custom of record says, an urban family yields RAW's own 4 gp of service and 2 gp of tax: the repricing that moves every rural figure on this page is an argument about villeins, and a burgess owes none of it. A deviation, not an omission MODULE — RAW has the domain's tax setting carry over to its urban families (RR p.352), and this module declines to carry the manorial reading across the wall. The argument is the Library's franchise chapter. And the boundary the module rules on does not move your money: Classes V, IV and III all trade at the same rate, so a 2,000-family town earns the same whether it is Class IV or Class III.

Vassals — land that renders tribute · RAW's own tier

A vassal rules his own domain, pays his own garrison, and renders tribute in coin — 18 gp × families0.6 (RR p.344). Grant him families and his grade follows; RAW's Titles of Nobility table names him. What he does inside his realm is his business — run this page again on his families to find out. And a vassal may hold vassals of his own: press ↓ to seat one under another, and each lord is banded only on the men directly under him16 — which is why the pyramid pays.

16 · Quia Emptores, 1290 — the escape has an expiry date The ↓ button models sub-infeudation, and this page rewards it: push a man down a level and he leaves your tribute count entirely. England legislated against exactly that, for exactly that reason. Sub-infeudation stripped a lord of his incidents — wardship, marriage, relief, escheat — because the new mesne lord collected them instead, and Quia Emptores ended the creation of new sub-fees: land could thereafter be substituted, one tenant for another, but not layered. So the pyramid this tool builds is the pre-1290 shape. Run the dial freely for the Post-Conquest, Angevin and distraint centuries; past 1290 the ladder is frozen and a lord who wants fewer direct vassals must grant away rather than interpose. Argued in full in the History chapter, Feudal Manors.

Fees — land that renders service

Each fee is a holding at the ladder's own size: the smallest estate whose income pays its grade of man, wherever that land lies. Sizes are the ladder's law; the counts are yours — and so is how many of each grade render coin instead of a body.

The bargain at the grant — what one fee costs, and what it brings

Every row above is a transaction, and only one side of it has ever been on this page. A grant gives up land and gets service back. The two are in different units, so this block converts them into the one unit that answers the question a lord actually has — months of lance-service a year — using the module's own ward-penny arithmetic: a fee's lance rides one month in twelve, and a month of a lance is worth its wage.

The ward — service spent at the walls · the module's own line MODULE

Castle-guard is the one render RAW does not price, and the one the castellany's arithmetic cannot do without: the castle is warded by other men's service, not the castellan's purse. The doctrine is argued on Feudal Manors — see the warded walls — and this is where it costs something. What the charter says decides whether the walls or the host goes short — and in a war year, under the commonest clause of all, it is the walls.

⚖ Deeper — lances, not days, and the one calendar
The dial is in lances, and that is the ruling. This module keeps exactly one calendar — the month of service, history's forty days rounded to ACKS's month — and a "ward days" input would smuggle a second one in through the reader's own hand. Priced by the day at days ÷ 365 a lance reads 10.96 gp/mo against 8.75 — a 25% swing on every ward line, and a second calendar sitting two cards from the term the rest of the module prices, argues and names. So the ward is counted in lances. ⚠ cl. 29 proportions in days, and this module answers in months. That quantisation is the module's own step, not the charter's — the rule is Magna Carta's, the rounding is ours.
⚖ Deeper — the two charter forms, and what each conserves
The two settings conserve different things, and each is right about its own charter. Under substitution — the first setting above — the service is spent once: a lance on ward is a lance not in the host, and the charter offers the walls instead of the field. That reading cannot describe the two-clause charter, where a fee owes the field and the walls: there the pool is the year, not the month, and Magna Carta cl. 29 settles the collision in the knight's favour — "if we have led or sent him on military service, he shall be excused guard in proportion to the time in service." Serve the field and the ward abates by what was served. Peace year, the lord has his full ward; war year, he has the host and bare walls. It is a hedge, not a dominance — which is why lords wrote both clauses as a matter of course.

⚠ And the honour holds ONE clause at a time — say it, because the sentence above invites the opposite. If lords wrote both routinely, a real honour's ward-bound fees were a mixed population: some substituting, some abating. This dial sets the clause for all the fees bound to the walls, and the ledger reads a single charter population. That is a modelling boundary, not a claim about the record — the same "one estate, one charter, one lord" simplification the fee definition makes (the idea), reappearing at realm scale. To reason about a mixed honour, price each clause's fees in a separate pass — the service is additive, since each fee stands in exactly one of the two. The garrison credit is not: ward is capped by whatever is left of the line after militia, ward-boys and serjeanties, so two passes' credits must be checked against that one remaining line rather than summed. The muster arithmetic underneath already takes a list of charter populations — this is a limit of what the dial offers, not of what the model can express.
⚖ Deeper — why this, and not scutage, pays for a castle
The two commutations are structurally different animals. Scutage is an occasional imposition, levied per campaign, at a rate the lord sets when he chooses. Ward-penny is a fixed perpetual charge attached to the tenure, and the tenant elects it — cl. 29 forbids a constable to distrain money from a knight willing to serve in person. And the fit with the arithmetic is exact. A garrison is a standing monthly bill; ward-penny is a standing monthly income; they match in kind. Scutage does not — it is an occasional lump against a perpetual expense, which is why it covers barely a twentieth of this realm's coin garrison. This is the row that makes a castle payable, and it is why castle-guard rent funded garrisons while scutage funded campaigns. The rate is not a dial: real ward rents were fixed customary conversions of whole honours, not annual optimisations.
⚖ Deeper — twelve times the land, and why that is arithmetic
A fee renders a lance for a month. A serjeanty renders a body at the gate, every day of the year — and it is the answer to "who opens the gate on an ordinary Tuesday", which the ward dial cannot reach. Land paid as a wage at par: the holding's whole net is the standing body — so at the customary net of 4 gp a family, 3 families carry a 12-gp watchman where 15 carry the 60-gp man-at-arms who serves one month in twelve. Under ACKS RAW revenues a family nets 9, and the same two men want 1⅓ and 6⅔ families. The dial above divides by whichever reading is in force, and says so. ⚠ The 12× is construction, not convergence. Land at par means the wage cancels — families per gp of standing body is 12 ÷ months for any wage whatever. It is the definition of serving twelve times the months, not two sources agreeing. What it does establish is the institution's whole selling line: year-round petty service is twelve times cheaper in land than termed service.
A body costs — families' worth of land, which is rarely a whole family — so a grant almost always leaves a fraction of one holding over. It stands nobody under any reading. The first two agree in the lord's purse and are stated as agreeing rather than given a manufactured difference: either way the land has left the fisc and no body came of it. They part company when the Judge asks whom he would be taking it back from. Only the third moves a number, and it moves several — the parcel never leaves the demesne, so it keeps its revenue and its protection line.
⚖ Deeper — where the loyalty roll actually fires
RR p.345 says a vassal can be safely asked for one ongoing duty in a month. Ward in one season and host in another are never concurrent, so they are free. And once cl. 29 abates by right, the two never overlap of their own accord either — so a roll keyed on the calendar would be pricing nothing. Abatement is the default of law; the roll prices the demand beyond it. A lord who wants his walls manned and his host full is asking for two duties at once, and forty ward-bound knights is forty exposures at exactly the moment he needs them to come. That is the grievance cl. 29 was written to remedy, priced in ACKS's own currency. ⚠ Era-gated by custom rather than by code: the distraint century — Kaldor's — takes abatement as settled law, and the demand belongs to the centuries before the charter.
⚖ Deeper — what a counterfactual owes the reader, and the two ways this one nearly lied

The serjeanty row printed one figure for as long as it existed: the garrison credit the standing bodies earned. A credit with no cost beside it reads as free protection, and the question any reader actually has — what did the lord give up to get it? — had no line anywhere on this tab. The ledger above is the answer, and it is six lines because five of them can be made to flatter.

The first flattery is par itself. Land at par means the holding's whole net is the wage, so line 1 and line 3 are the same number reached two different ways — families times the net a family clears on one side, bodies times RAW's wage on the other. They cancel. And when they cancel, whatever is left in line 5 came from somewhere else: here, from line 2, the protection line the granted families no longer carry. That is a genuine gift and it needed naming. A serjeant's three families are quit of the lord's garrison at his class rate, and the same man is credited his whole wage against what remains of it — so the lord books more protection than the land is worth. Three readings were open: leave it, charge the body for the land it stands on, or keep the serjeanty's families on the protection line though off the income. The last two conserve exactly and both were rejected: this module's standing rule about legal fictions is that an additional benefit survives priced and labelled, not deleted — and the grounds are the module's own history, that serjeanties clustered at castles, which is to say the land sits inside the ward its tenant garrisons. The circle is real. What was wrong was that it was invisible.

The second flattery was ours, and it was live for about an hour. Line 5 was first written as lines 1, 2 and 4 added up — the difference between granting and keeping, all else held. The module's own test then measured the two states instead of restating the rule, and they did not agree: at the opening realm the formula said +90 and the purse said +36. "All else held" is false here. The demesne militia is raised on the demesne, so the land that leaves takes its militia with it, and the credit those men stood on the line goes with them. The ward-boys and the castle-guard move for the same reason — a shorter line leaves them less room. So the fifth line runs the whole garrison cascade twice, once as the realm stands and once as it would stand had the land never been granted, and prints the difference the lord's coin actually shows. The formula survives beside it, named as a formula, and the gap between them is attributed.

Line 6 is there because line 4 is capped. A lord cannot bank garrison credit against an obligation he does not have. Grant enough land and the militia already covers the line, the serjeants' service meets nothing, and every hour of it is given — real render, arriving every day of the year, financing nothing. That case is not exotic: it is what happens to any lord who answers "how do I build a garrison that costs nothing" by granting more.

And the parcel. A body costs a fraction of a family's holding, so a grant almost always leaves a piece over. Where it goes is a term of the charter and not a fact of the record, so the dial reports the choice: it over-endows the serjeanties, it lies idle, or the lord never granted it. The first two agree in the lord's purse, and the module says so rather than inventing a difference to justify offering both — they part company only when the Judge asks whom he would be taking it back from.

The garrison composed — men, and where they stand · the first section that builds RAW

RAW says outright that a domain's garrison is "some mix of followers, mercenaries, conscripts, and militia" and that the mix is the ruler's to choose (RR p.434). Until now this module handed you a gp figure and stopped. One row is a kind of man; one column is a place — because a crossbowman stands on the castle's towers and at the town gate, and the count belongs in the cell rather than the row.

The reckoning

One realm, line by line

The honour below is the page as it opens — no dial touched, and it stays that way however far you dial. Read down and the argument is the arithmetic.

The honour4,600 families on the land, and 550 more in two towns — 5,150 all told, which is what the rank is read from. Land worth 6, in the borderlands, under a lord of level 9.
How it is held780 in hand — barely 17% — 2,240 under vassals, 1,580 in fees. The lord of a great honour holds almost none of it, and that is the finding, not a mis-set dial.
What the fees are48 estates owing 63 lances. Of those, 44.5 serve in kind and 18.5 render coin — the fraction is real: a half-fee owes joint service, and half a lance is what the paper says.
What comes inDemesne 2,319 net of its own expenses, tribute from the vassals 2,728, and the two towns 1,300 — 6,347 gp a month in hand. Scutage brings 39 more, and it is deliberately not in that total: a lord who takes scutage must spend it on troops or face loyalty rolls at −4 (RR p.346), so it is reported against the garrison and never as money he may spend. The smallest of the four lines is the one every rules argument is about, and it is the one line that is not his.
And why two townsBecause they are two markets, not one. 400 families band as Class V and 150 as Class VI; a single town of 550 would band as Class IV and trade the whole of it at the higher rate. So the towns render 1,300 where a pooled one would claim 1,375 — the ruling costs this realm 75 gp a month, and it is right to. Those last two are arithmetic you can do from the figure on screen, not numbers the page prints, so they are not set as claims; the self-test holds them. And unlike every rural figure above, these do not move with the custom of record: the town stands on ACKS RAW's own 4 and 2 under either reading.
What the walls costThe garrison line asks 2,340. The demesne militia — 156 men, trained — carries 1,404 of it, the ward-boys 135, and 801 gp is left to pay in coin. Those last two read 180 and 756 until #33 corrected the ward-boys' derivation — three boys in hand, not four.
And what it never asks4,740 gp a month: the garrison line the enfeoffed families would have carried, quit by service. It is the largest number on this page and it is never billed — the quittance, which is the module's largest single departure from RAW but not the only one; the ⚖ table has the rest.
