This is where the marks lead. Every MODULE on the page is argued in the ⚖ tables below; every RAW is verified against the rulebook in the audits; every HISTORY has its record in the History chapter. Nothing here is needed to run the module — it is here so that a Judge who wants to check the reasoning can, and so that the places the module argues against itself are on the same page as the places it does not.

Doctrine — where this module departs, and why

The deviations, stated and priced. Two tables and an FAQ: module doctrine is the rulings that change what RAW does, each with RAW's own words beside it; household doctrine is the further rulings the muster machinery needs, which RAW supplies none of. A ruling not in one of these tables is not a ruling this module has made.

⚖ Module doctrine — where we deviate from RAW, and why MODULE

Module doctrine — where this module deviates from RAW, and why
RulingWhat RAW saysWhy we rule it
The fee is QUIT of the garrison line by service — the lance and the trained levy discharge it in kind, and the fee keeps its whole net — land+3 under ACKS RAW revenues, land−2 under the customary rent. Nothing and no one is priced onto the line. The garrison line is a protection-value floor, not a payroll: RAW itself meets it with unpaid value — trained militia "even if the militia is not called up," scutage, a lord's troops (p.341–2) — though "garrison cost cannot be paid with expenditure on henchman… except actual troops." And the scutage duty (p.346) grants its garrison credit and says "in some realms, a vassal may send troops instead of gp" in the same entry — the cash/kind equivalence is printed, realm-conditional; this module's realms are declared such realms, which is the whole of the Library’s History chapter’s era claim. RAW's channel for the vassal's person is Call to Council, unpriced (p.346) This is the module's structural deviation — owned, bounded, priced (the p.342 aside about "spending only the minimum 2gp" reads the line as payable, not zeroable, and we zero it). The form is a quittance, the period's own instrument: charters made estates quit of geld (the land tax) and of castle-guard in consideration of service kept, and quit-rent is the same deal run backward — coin paid to be quit of service. The fee exercises the scutage entry's equivalence standing: troops instead of gp, permanently. Because the discharge is contractual, no valuation of the knight is ever needed — asked who actually defends the manor, the answer is the consideration itself: one knight, his squire, and his armed yeomen (in the yard, the knight is still the garrison — the quittance is how the ledger says it). The quittance is conditional — see the assize row below: a fee in default is quit for the lance only and hires its missing watch. The bound against strict RAW is small: full militia credit already equals the RAW fee-holder's net land+3 at civilized; the residue is the frontier increment, 1–2 gp/family — and it expires: the fee's own maturation walks it to the civilized reading (the three counts of a fee, History chapter, Library), amortizing the concession over the manor's life. Equivalently, at realm scale: land held by knight-service carries no garrison line — enfeoffed families garrisoned in men, demesne families in coin; the per-fee quittance and the class exemption are one fact in two ledgers.
The assize of the fee — the levy is a term of enfeoffment: mail per fee held, yeomen trained & kitted, view of arms twice yearly; a fee in default hires the levy's watch until re-armed RAW militia is optional — a ruler may levy up to 2 per 10 families (p.432) — but the garrison credit's own wording sets the standard: "trained and equipped" (p.341–2), with kit heritable (p.432). The officer delegations include inspecting troops (p.352–3) The Assize of Arms (1181) owed a hauberk per fee held — mail scaling with fee-count in statute — with its 10-mark freeman at the habergeon tier (his was a chattels assessment — movable goods, not land: the half-fee mapping borrows the kit-grade, not the tenure); the Statute of Winchester (1285) added the twice-yearly view of arms. Both were national legislation on all free men, enforced by royal machinery — juries and itinerant justices in 1181, elected hundred-constables in 1285. Writing their content into the charter of the fee, and their enforcement into the lord's household, is this module's deliberate transplant. Hârn's yeomen (double tenancy, own kit) are the same custom in canon. Age works against the assize, too: the mail-grade yeomen are precisely the whole-holding tenants, and fragmentation thins that stratum (the three counts of a fee, History chapter, Library) — the old subdivided manor is where the view finds habergeons pawned and the fee slides toward default. The convergence is a calibration, not a law — and it is a calibration of ONE reading. Under ACKS RAW revenues at land 6 — RAW's own average — the rungs' heavy-foot ceilings count 1 / 2 / 4 mail-grade yeomen on the 1-, 2-, and 4-fee rungs, the statute's scaling out of RAW's qualifying numbers, the esquire at the habergeon tier (0). At the customary rent the same rungs are larger and the same land value counts 2 / 5 / 10, with the esquire at 1: the counts still rise with the fee-count, but they no longer equal it, and the resonance is RAW's alone. Richer or poorer hexes shift both. Default is priced, not forbidden: −levy-credit gp/mo of hired watch until the one-time re-arming is paid — distraint (the seizure of goods to compel a defaulter) as texture, on RAW numbers. And so is delivery: when the service is called, the knight pays his men's wages himself (provider-pays — Call to Arms, p.345–6); the month-of-service bill is on every card, and it cuts into the fee's net for the term — one month of service a year; past the forty days the lord's wages carry the host.
The quota — a fee owes as many lances as it counts fees: ½ owes joint service, 1 its holder, 2 and 4 the holder and the count beside him. A lance is one knight-service, and discharge is by body: a heavy horseman serves a lance whole, a medium-horse serjeant at two-for-one, light horse and foot not at all, coin at the scutage rate — the assize's mounted serjeants credit ½ each while it is kept. And the definition of a lance is itself the charter's, drifting by era (the definition lever): the Survey's mailed rider (60 gp — the fees re-count in him), the 1181 knight (mail per fee), the statute knight of 1285 (Winchester's enforcement overlay on the same body; the covered-horse summonses pressing past it), and the ordinance lance that absorbed the crew — the fee by then commuted. Priced on every card and in full on the Muster section RAW's Call to Arms prices the duty in gp — troops worth 1 gp/family (p.346) — and never counts lances; the wage ladder alone would read "4 fees = one L5 knight" and stop there The servitium debitum counted knights — one fee, one knight's service; two fees, two — and the Assize of Arms scaled mail with fee-count: the second hauberk of a two-fee man was a second man-at-arms's mail, not a better coat for the first. The module keeps both truths: the fee retains a grade (the wage ladder) and owes a count (the quota) — the gap between them is where scutage, the term-hire market, and the household live. The discharge is priced, not assumed: at wage-parity floors the count above one is affordable only in coin or for the term, which is the record's own answer — real multi-fee holders scutaged and hired; standing retinues awaited the margin (Muster section). The 2:1 substitution is the servitium's own record — two serjeants accepted for a knight (Pollock & Maitland carry the cases) — but the pinning is the module's calibration, owned here: the historical serjeant was a social and tenurial category, not an equipment tier. We map him to the ACKS medium-horse body, and rule the 60-gp heavy-cavalry man sufficiently equipped to discharge a service whole, as the pay rolls' esquire-grade men-at-arms did.
The knight's contract — dubbing puts the fee-holder on the henchman XP ledger (expected wage deducted before the threshold) and raises his base loyalty from −2 to 0 for as long as the fee's service is kept — the same conditions the quittance already audits: homage at succession, the assize, the render. There is no separate bond to track: the loyalty rides the fee. A fee in default of its service is a bond in question — −2 until it re-arms, and still deducted. The esquire's fee sits outside the contract: RAW's plain vassal, undeducted, base −2 RAW keys the wage deduction to henchman status: "henchmen vassals subtract their expected monthly wage from domain income for purposes of calculating XP" (p.342, Major Errata r4 form); a non-henchman vassal deducts nothing. Base 0, by contrast, it keys to nothing at all: "most henchmen, mercenaries, specialists, and followers begin with a loyalty of 0" (p.166), the same page that modifies every loyalty score by Charisma alike — neither is a henchman perk. The exception is the −2, which p.347 attaches to a non-henchman assigned to rule a vassal domain ("instead of 0"), −4 beyond the range of trade (the range itself defined JJ p.203) Two transplanted clauses, each with a RAW precedent of exactly its shape. The ledger: companions "function as henchmen for all purposes… but do not take up henchmen slots" (p.334–6) — the book's own proof that henchman accounting detaches from the slot system and travels; we move one clause of that bundle onto the dubbed fee-holder. The loyalty: note first what this clause is not — it grants no bonus. 0 is p.166's ordinary baseline for hired men of every sort; the module's move is to decline the −2 that p.347 alone attaches, and it takes RAW's own waiver of that penalty as its warrant — senatorial republics give "non-henchmen assigned to rule vassal domains base loyalty scores of 0 instead of −2" because the institution commands the loyalty (p.355), and tenure by knight-service is feudal monarchy's same institution. The loyalty attaches to the position, not the person, which is why the heiress's husband who renders the service is as sworn as the man born to it — the exact shape of the senate parallel. The clauses ship together because RAW never sells them apart: nowhere does the book pair the wage deduction with negative base loyalty (henchman 0, companion +2) — a deducted man at −2 would kneel to be made strictly worse off, and no one kneels for that. Dubbing is thus a real exchange: the knight's last level moves to the battlefield, his lord's hall moves closer. What falls out downstream — the esquire as the one man land alone completes, and distraint of knighthood emerging from the arithmetic — has its own section on the Library’s History chapter.
The bundle is closed — the fee makes a sworn fee-holder, and he carries two clauses of RAW's henchman machinery and no others. Scope: this defines what the fee does to the man who holds it. A knight without a fee is not a lesser sworn fee-holder — he is RAW's henchman, governed by RAW's henchman rules entire, and this module rules nothing about him. What attaches: the XP ledger — expected wage deducted from domain income before the threshold (p.342 + p.423, errata r4 form) — and base loyalty 0 instead of −2, for as long as the fee's service is kept (p.355). What does not attach: no henchman slot (he does not count against 4 + CHA); no slot-chain prerequisite, including p.168's ≥ 50%-of-wage licence to hold henchmen of his own; no wage entitlement (the fee is his pay, p.168); no hireling morale check (the quittance's conditions are the audit — homage at succession, the assize, the render); not the henchman duty economy (p.345's one free ongoing duty at a time, running until revoked — the fee's standing service rests on its own rule, the next row, not on henchman machinery); and not the inner circle's termless service — the mesnie's true henchmen ride without term, the sworn fee-holder is term-bound. A clause not named here does not attach, and may not be invoked elsewhere in this module to settle a question about him. RAW has no partial status. It has henchmen, companions and plain vassals, each a complete package, and it never sells a package by the clause — except once, and that exception is this module's whole warrant: companions "function as henchmen for all purposes… but do not take up henchmen slots" (p.334–6). RAW is silent on what a man carries when he is given some henchman accounting and no henchman slot, because RAW never puts anyone in that position Because a status defined only by what it adds will keep growing, and a clause nobody has to declare is a clause nobody ever checks. Two refusals carry most of the weight, and each is refused for a stated reason. The duty economy (p.345 against p.347) cannot ground the fee's standing service: it is henchman status machinery, describing a true henchman vassal rather than a fee-holder — the next row grounds that service in tenure instead. And p.168's ≥ 50%-of-wage licence is slot machinery, so it cannot decide which knights may take a boy: fosterings run up the ladder, into the great halls that rule excludes. The contract's own warrant is the companion clause, whose entire content is "…but do not take up henchmen slots" — a transplant that disowns the slot system cannot inherit the slot system's prerequisites. So the negative list is normative rather than illustrative, and the closure rule is the operative sentence: to add a clause, add it here, with its precedent and its price. This is the doctrinal form of the rule the code already lives under — one rule, one owner — and it is checkable the same way: a normative citation of henchman status machinery outside these rows is a finding. RAW's henchman wage table (p.168's 25 / 50 / 100 / 200 / 400, and the landed-vassal clause that offsets a wage against domain income) is a price list, cited freely and correctly throughout; only the status clauses are closed here.
The fee's service stands because the fee stands — a tenure held of the lord in perpetuity, whose consideration passed once and in land at enfeoffment, reserves its service as an incident of the tenure, not as a favour that must be renewed. It is bounded by the term — one month of service a year, history's forty days — and it ends only by the process that ends tenures, distraint and then resumption, never at the lord's word. Scope: this rules the standing service of a fee and nothing else — not the man, not any other obligation he may owe, not any unlanded service. A knight without a fee owes what ACKS says he owes RAW's favor⇄duty economy prices ongoing relations between parties whose consideration passes repeatedly — wages, gifts, grants renewed and revoked (p.345 for the sworn henchman, p.347 for everyone else). It has no category for a conveyance with a reserved service, because ACKS assigns land to a holder and then governs him through loyalty and wages rather than through tenure. RAW is silent here, not contrary — and the distinction it lacks is the one this module is about Because the alternative was to keep borrowing p.345, and p.345 is henchman status machinery that the contract row expressly disowns: a transplant that gives up the slot system cannot keep drawing on the slot system's economy — and the fee's single most load-bearing property was resting on exactly that. What it rules over: the standing character of a fee's service, and only that. The lord does not re-purchase the host's attendance each year; he purchased it at enfeoffment, and goes on purchasing it every day he does not resume the land. It is not a better deal than the clause it replaces — it is a different deal, and in two ways a worse one for the lord. RAW's henchman duty runs until revoked, at the lord's word; the fee's service cannot be revoked at all, only distrained and then resumed, by process. And where the henchman's free duty is open-ended in kind, the fee's is bounded to the term. The fee trades the lord's flexibility for the tenant's permanence, which is what tenure is. And it explains the scutage, which p.345 never could: if service were a revocable favour, a lord wanting coin instead of a lance would simply revoke it, and no commutation instrument would be needed. It is because the service is an incident of a standing tenure — not the lord's to cancel — that commuting it requires its own machinery. The module already has that machinery; this ruling is what makes it necessary rather than merely available.
Knights owe service, not tribute — no per-fee tribute line; tribute falls once, on the lord's whole realm RAW tribute cascades to every vassal by realm families (18 × fam0.6, p.343–4) — but the formula was calibrated for baronies and up: on a 12-family fee at ACKS RAW revenues it would take ~80 of 108 gp (74%) — and at the customary rent it is worse, not better: 25 families owe 124 gp against an income of 100, which is confiscatory, because RAW keys tribute to family COUNT and lowering the rate does not move the formula. Tribute is explicitly negotiable ("Adventurers can set the tribute for their own vassals as desired," p.343) Below the barony the render is the lance itself — a ruling inherited from Knightly Realms. The Call-to-Arms duty (troops worth 1 gp/family, p.346) is what cash-vassalage would extract; the fee delivers a 100-gp lance instead.
Service in kind side-steps Tribute Inefficiency Cash tribute decays with vassal count (p.347): 9–16 vassals deliver 66%, 17–63 deliver 50%, 64–216 a third, 16,384+ just 1% (the Drakomir example). Only ≤8 vassals pay in full. One boundary is RAW's own: the printed table lists 16,384 twice — in "16,384 or more" (1%) and in "4,096 – 16,384" (5%). This module resolves the overlap to the stricter 1%; every other boundary is inclusive and matches the printed rows exactly Service never passes through a collector's hands — the knight delivers himself. And the 100% band (≤8) coincides with the henchman cap (4+CHA): RAW's own economics wants the feudal shape — a handful of sworn tribute-vassals, and below them men who pay in person. A knight-heavy realm is poor in coin and rich in lances by design.
The sworn officer cures Tribute Inefficiency at a lawful 12.5% — the Offices section’s fisc oversight The inefficiency bands are unconditional: the loss goes to "crime, corruption, or waste," and nothing in RAW says appointing a steward recovers it. RAW's only officer machinery is the four expense-line magistrates at 12.5% (p.342) — none collects revenue Owned plainly: this buys out a designed scaling limiter, and it is the quietest big change in the module. We rule it as the cure the period kept reaching for and rarely sustained — custodial (salaried) sheriffs were tried in 1236 and 1258 and abandoned both times, while the sheriff's farm and the exchequer audit ran side by side throughout — and because the cure is priced and fragile: it holds only while the officer is sworn or well-held. The corruption dial slides every step of lost loyalty back toward the band, and a hostile officer is the band (Offices section) — a crown that cannot staff loyal men gets RAW back in full.
Service booked at the knight's full wage on the lord's ledger A Call to Arms extracts troops worth 1 gp/family, and an enfeoffed henchman adventures with his lord only when called to council (p.168, 345–6). RAW's military economy is provider-pays: the called vassal must "muster an army with troop wages equal to 1gp per family" at his own cost, while the Troops favor has the lord pay for what he sends down (p.346) — and "scutage does not count as domain income for XP purposes": military transfers are firewalled from XP The fee is a standing favor⇄duty pair — land held against year-round garrison residence and a term-bound host service: one month of service a year in kind (history's forty days, rounded to ACKS's month), at the vassal's cost — provider-pays is the book's own law — with extension at the lord's wages: the muster-roll pay ladder (1, 2, and 4 shillings a day) ↔ 60/100/200 gp, which the pay rolls show fee-holders drawing atop their fees. The duty is discrete and countable because the tenure makes it so, not because a henchman clause allows it: the service is standing because the fee is standing (⚖ the fee's service stands because the fee stands, above), its consideration having passed once and in land at enfeoffment — so the lord asks in any year without buying the call afresh, and the term is what quantizes it to one month of service a year (both the month-long term and the annual cap are the module's feudal doctrine — RAW's own duties have no duration but revocation). The fee-holder is neither a henchman drawing a free ongoing duty (p.345) nor an outsider bargaining call by call (p.347): he stands outside the favor⇄duty frame altogether, which is what a conveyance with a reserved service is. On the balance of the two military systems RAW is with us — "the favors and duties even out; the rules put a standing army and feudal army on equal footing" (p.346–7). The household exception is the henchman bond: the inner circle rides without term. And the full wage buys what p.168 itself prices at full wage: the man's year-round existence, residence, and call — sustainment, not man-days (the crops sell no man above the L1 veteran at any price — and him at a premium, capped at a quarter of hires, p.428–430). Like RAW's scutage, the render never enters anyone's XP ledger.
Squire = watch & train, not a line combatant — 45 gp of medium-horse wage-value on the fee's ledger where a fostered boy actually rides, zero battle BR. Every lance keeps an attendant; not every attendant is a boy RAW has no squire entry at all Start from the horses, because they settle the first half without any convention. A man-at-arms keeps three or four mounts — destrier, palfrey, packhorse — and mail he cannot don unaided, and when he fights someone must hold the remounts. One man cannot do it, so every knight in the field has an attendant, landed or landless, and that is logistics rather than privilege. What varies is who the attendant is, and only one of the two answers is worth 45 gp: a fostered boy of the knightly class (14–21) costs the fee nothing — his wage is his education — and being trained to arms he keeps his knight horsed, rides to war behind the line with the remounts and spare lances, and stands the manor's watch; a hired groom or valet costs coin, stands no watch as a man-at-arms, and earns the fee nothing on the garrison ledger. So the toggle is not asking whether this knight has a servant — he always does — but whether his attendant is a boy of the class who counts as garrison. And the constraint is supply, not permission: all knights may squire, and the class does not hold a boy per fee (the supply of boys, Design chapter, Library). Two questions, and they must not be run together. Does this knight have an attendant? — governed by nobody, it is logistics, and the answer is always yes, landed or landless. Is that attendant a henchman? — governed by ACKS natively: a henchman may hold henchmen of his own only if landed with income ≥ 50% of his wage (p.168), so only if the knight's income licenses one. A squire is a position; a henchman is a status, and for the valet-style squire they never coincide — a hired groom is a retainer, not a henchman, and RAW keeps those categories apart already. So p.168 is correct, kept, and not a transplant: it answers the second question about a man who is an actual ACKS henchman, under ACKS's own rules, with nothing borrowed. What follows falls out cleanly. The sworn fee-holder has a fee, so his income licenses a henchman and his fostered boy may be his own — on a track, levelling, the man who will be a knight. The landless household knight is himself an ACKS henchman with no domain income, so by p.168 he holds none of his own — and he still has an attendant: a hired valet, or a gentle boy who is the lord's charge placed to train in his hall, since the lord's court is the clearinghouse. The henchman bond runs to the lord; the training runs to the knight. And the +45 is garrison value, not status — it rides where a boy of the class actually stands the watch, whoever's henchman he is or is not. The adult fighting esquire is a different man entirely and must not be read off this row: the 60-gp man-at-arms of the esquire's fee, an adult armiger holding land. Kit priced as medium horse (p.169/438); light cavalry's javelin skirmisher maps to the mounted yeoman instead. The squire is not a henchman by definition, and nothing here makes him one: p.168 answers the second question only, about a man who is already an ACKS henchman. Read p.168 as necessary, not sufficient — income licenses a boy, standing and a hall attract one, and the boys pool in a few great halls rather than spreading evenly over fees (the supply of boys, Design chapter, Library). A boy in the earl's hall stands the castle's watch and not a manor's, so a flat +45 per lance is wrong in shape as well as in level. Feudal Realms separates the three quantities this checkbox would otherwise answer at once — supply (a realm budget: boys per household of the class, a convention the realm sets, Hârn's assessed one-per-lance among the settings), placement (halls bid by standing, wardships first, so the great halls fill before a bachelor's manor sees a boy) and credit (whose garrison the value lands on). The last is the one that pays: a fee is quit of the garrison line, so its boy adds to what the fee delivers; the demesne pays that line, so a ward-boy on the castle watch is coin the lord does not spend. Same 45 gp, two different accounts, and a flat per-lance figure books all of it to the second. The ruling stands under either accounting: the boy is watch and train, no place in the line of battle, and the ≥50%-of-wage licence answers only whether he is his knight's henchman.
Leveled knight units priced by the heroic-unit formula, floored at veteran, company-normalized "Heroes" (foray rights) are gated by level — platoon scale NPC L4+ / henchman-of-a-hero L2+; company scale L6+ / L4+ (p.466). The troop tables stop at veteran F1, so RAW prices no L2+ non-hero unit. The formula's divisor is 8 × infantry-per-unit — 960 at company scale, 240 at platoon scale (p.466) We price every leveled unit by the formula, floored at vet HC 0.169, and display all BR ÷960 so knights, troop tables, and the "≈ N companies" line stay comparable. Hero status gates forays, not unit pricing — the Knight Units section flags eligibility per muster.
Aid — a new entry for RAW's Favor/Duty table. The lord may demand an aid on three occasions and no others: ransoming his body, knighting his eldest son, marrying his eldest daughter. The demand is 1gp per family, once, and never repaid. It occupies one duty slot like any other, so a lord who asks it while already asking scutage or a loan is into a Hireling Loyalty roll at RAW's own cumulative penalty. A lord may demand less, as with every duty. RAW invites this. The Favor/Duty table's own text says "the entries on the Favor/Duty table do not exhaust the possible edicts that a ruler might impose on his vassal" (p.345–6). What RAW does not have is this shape: its Scutage is a monthly tax running until revoked, and its Loan is a one-off at 1gp per family that is repaid when the duty is revoked. An aid is a Loan that never comes back — the one form the table lacks. The pricing is not ours either: 1gp per family is RAW's unit for every demand it lists (scutage, loan, gift, Call to Arms), and the loyalty consequence is RAW's own extra-duty rule, unmodified. Because the module needed the crown to have a way of reaching an estate whose assessment it cannot revise, and history's answer was the incidents — of which the aid is the one that recurs. Building it as a Duty rather than as module machinery means it inherits RAW's whole apparatus for free: the duty slot, the favor that offsets it, the loyalty roll, the lord's right to ask for less. The historical rate was 20s the knight's fee (Statute of Westminster I, 1275) — but for two of the three occasions only. The statute fixed the aid for knighting the eldest son and marrying the eldest daughter; it left the ransom where custom had it, on what was reasonable to the case. So the sterling rate prices the two occasions a lord can see coming, and the one he actually dreads is the one no rate was ever set for. At about twice RAW's unit on a bachelor's fee, a Judge who wants the sterling figure should charge two duties' worth and expect the loyalty roll that follows. We take RAW's unit as the default because a rule that costs a loyalty roll every time it is used will not be used. DEBATED
The custom of record — a family yields land + 1 + 0, not land + 4 + 2. Service revenue is 1 and tax is 0 on a customary manor, and customary is the default. Every rural gp on the page is repriced by it; the urban population is held at RAW's own 4 and 2 under either reading, which is the second half of this ruling and not an oversight. RAW gives one schedule: 4 gp of service and 2 of tax per family (RR pp.341–2), motivated as the licence income of a freeman's trades. It does not distinguish a villein population from a burgess one, and prices both at the freeman's rate. RAW's own wording is the argument for the deviation: service revenue is described as the income of freemen's trades, and a villein holding by custom of the manor renders in land and labour, not in coin from a trade he does not practise. So the module runs a customary population at 1 and 0, keeps RAW's own 4 and 2 for the urban population, and puts the choice on a dial that says which reading it is in. Argued in the Custom chapter; the burgess half is the franchise chapter. ⚠ The comparison reading is RAW to the gold piece — this is a deviation the page will run without, on request.
Castle-guard is counted in lances, not days — and what the term does is the charter's business, not the module's. Under a substitution charter (the default) the service is spent once: a lance standing ward is not in the field host that term. Under an abating charter the fee owes the walls and the host, and Magna Carta 1215, cl. 29 abates the ward pro rata by the time served — so the lance rides, and it is the walls that go short in a war year. Both clauses were written, routinely, by the same lords; ward is priced at the module's one calendar either way, the month of service. RAW prices no castle-guard at all. It has a garrison line and says nothing about who stands at the walls, or on what term. The institution is history's — fees bound to a castle owed ward in rotation, and serjeanties clustered at castles because the castle-holder is the one lord land-rich enough to carve them. The count is in lances because the module keeps one calendar: priced by the day at days ÷ 365 a lance reads 10.96 gp/mo against 8.75 — a 25% swing on every ward line, and a second calendar two cards away from the term the rest of the module prices and names. What the two charter forms are for. The substitution reading — service spent once — makes ward a decision rather than a second bill, and it is right about the charter that offers the walls instead of the field. It could not describe the two-clause charter, where a fee owes both; there the pool is the year, not the month, and cl. 29's own final limb settles the collision in the knight's favour — "if we have led or sent him on military service, he shall be excused guard in proportion to the time in service." So the conservation rule holds within a charter form rather than across the institution: substitution conserves the term, abatement conserves the year. It is a hedge, not a dominance, which is why lords wrote both — peace year, the lord has his full ward; war year, the host and bare walls. ⚠ One quantisation is ours: cl. 29 proportions in days and this module answers in months — the rule is Magna Carta's, the rounding is the module's. Priced on the ward; argued at the warded walls.
A settlement is a second population, typed apart from the first — its own revenue line, a flat garrison of 2, no militia, no fee acreage, no density; and the contested III/IV boundary is ruled at 2,500. RAW carries the second population (RR p.352) and propagates the domain's tax setting to it. It also states the III/IV boundary twice, and differently — 2,500 in the Domains chapter, 1,750 in Mercantile Ventures. Two rulings in one row, because they are one decision about typing. The urban lines are held at RAW's own 4 and 2 under either custom of record: the manorial reading is an argument about villeins, a burgess owes none of it, and so the module declines RAW's propagation. The boundary is ruled for 2,500 on witnesses to that side — RAW's own Villages/Towns/Cities table rules the disputed band outright, the Total Investment caps are the band ceilings rung for rung with no rung at 1,750, and JJ's sandbox step uses 2,500 in the step that feeds range of trade. ⚠ And it moves no money: classes V, IV and III all trade at 1.5. The franchise chapter carries both.

⚖ Household doctrine — the rulings the muster adds MODULE

Household doctrine — the rulings the muster adds
RulingWhat RAW saysWhy we rule it
The quota — a fee owes as many lances as it counts fees; a lance is one knight-service, discharged by body: heavy horse whole, a medium-horse serjeant at 2:1 (the assize's mounted serjeants credit ½ each while it is kept), coin at the scutage rate Call to Arms prices the duty in gp and never counts lances (p.346) The full ruling and its historical warrant sit in the ⚖ table in the Library (the servitium debitum; the Assize's mail-per-fee; the 2:1 serviens substitutions). This section applies it: the ledger credits the levy and prices the remainder.
The keep — the domestic tier (valet, groom, armed servant) lives on the holder's living-expense line, below the XP threshold; the fighting household man is a henchman at his full wage, part rendered as the hall's board in kind RAW henchmen draw the full wage; expected living expenses equal the level's wage (p.173) and sit inside the XP threshold (p.423) — servants, stabling, the hall itself Two lines, not one discount. The servant who fights at need is living-expense spending — every knight keeps him, no wage line, and the line sits below the XP threshold. The household henchman costs his wage entire (part in board — the supply rate prices the in-kind share); what makes him affordable is the bond, not the board: 25 gp of L1 henchman replaces 60 gp of hired sergeant, the same discount the fee itself runs on (RR p.168). Historically exact — household knights served for robes, mounts, board, and small annuities, not mercenary wages — and priced without softening: at the parity floor even 25 gp breaks, which is why the standing mesnie awaited the margin and the barony.
The esquire's household — an extrapolation, flagged — the 0-level rung keeps the same domestic tier as the leveled rungs RAW's living-expense rule rides the leveled henchman-wage ladder ("equal to the wages of a henchman of the same level," p.173), and the wage table's own 0-level row is 12 gp (p.168) — there is no esquire-grade row The module treats the 60-gp heavy-cavalry anchor as carrying an esquire-grade domestic establishment on the same basis as the leveled rungs — doctrine, not citation. Mechanically inert: the valet fields no BR, no lance credit, no garrison credit, no henchman slot, no field supply.
The assessment — written at the grant, the charter's count and definition alike; rewritten only at escheat, new enfeoffment, or royal inquest; distraint taxes income directly instead RAW re-prices nothing — domain income is simply current, which is the module's default (assessments current) The record's shape: Domesday and the 1166 cartae wrote counts that then froze for centuries while incomes grew, and the crown's response was never a re-survey but income instruments — distraint at £20/£40. Under ancient, the margin (income − charter anchor) appears on the standing-manor line and funds the household; a realm where the margin is universal has aged into livery. The dial gives the era table teeth.

FAQ — the questions this module gets asked, in playtest and debate

FAQ — the questions this module gets asked in playtest and debate
QuestionAnswer
Can a ruler really count his own person against garrison cost? Said plainly: this is the module's structural break with RAW — one line, bounded, priced. Strict RAW puts a garrison line on every domain and treats it as a floor to be paid (its own aside pictures a ruler "spending only the minimum 2gp," p.342). This module rules the fee quit of that line so long as its service is kept: the lance and the trained levy are the consideration, on the model of charters that made estates quit of geld or castle-guard for service kept, and on RAW's own printed, realm-conditional equivalence — "in some realms, a vassal may send troops instead of gp" (p.346; this module's realms declared such) — exercised standing. The size of the break: at civilized, full militia credit zeroes the line by pure RAW; the entire concession is the frontier increment, ~1–2 gp per family — and it is time-bounded as well as small: a fee walks outlands → civilized as it stocks and fragments (the three counts of a fee, History chapter, Library), so the concession is largest at the grant on a raw march and amortizes to zero as the manor matures — a founder's subsidy that expires, not a standing tax. What the quittance form buys is not a smaller break but a cleaner one — the discharge is contractual, so the knight is never priced onto the line and no gp valuation of the man is ever needed; and it has teeth: a fee in default of the assize is quit for the lance only and hires its missing watch until it re-arms. Asked who actually defends the manor: one knight, his squire, and his armed yeomen (the full ruling: ⚖ doctrine table, Library).
The magistrate keeps 12.5% of a line he oversees; the quit fee books the whole line as income — isn't that minting XP? RAW already mints campaign XP from the garrison line for a military man: the captain of the guard's salary is carved from garrison expenditure, "does not decrease the funds available to pay his troops," and "grants campaign XP" (p.342) — precedent for the kind of move, not the amount. Against the RAW-legal baseline — militia credit maxed — the quittance books 0 extra XP-bearing income at civilized, ~11 gp at borderlands, ~23 at outlands (the 12-family fee at the ~2.1-gp credit ceiling, below — this whole comparison is worked at ACKS RAW revenues, the ledger RAW's own baseline is stated in), beside the captain's lawful 4.5–6 gp on those same lines: between 0× and 4×, and less than RAW at civilized. Nor are the two equally secured: the captain's eighth is free money — troops unreduced, nothing extra delivered — while the fee's income books only while the consideration is delivered: a veteran lance and a trained levy actually standing there, on terms the view of arms audits twice a year. Per gp of XP, one buys the realm a garrison, the other an accountant. And a 12.5% share presupposes a domain with a staff; at fee scale the org chart collapses — captain, garrison, and ruler are one man with one purse. You can't pay a man an eighth of himself.
Is XP double-counted — does the knights' campaign XP subtract from their lord's? No gold piece appears on two XP ledgers. The knight XPs on his own domain income minus expected wage (p.342 — the knight's contract extends this to every dubbed holder, ⚖ table); the lord books nothing from the fee — no tribute, no coin; and the service render, like RAW's own scutage, "does not count as domain income for XP purposes" (p.346). A service realm concentrates less XP up top than a tribute realm — the coin and its XP stay on the land, in the knights. That distribution is the Arthurian texture, chosen on purpose.
Doesn't the knight piggyback on his lord's Personal Authority? No rule shares PA (Personal Authority — RAW's measure of whether a ruler's level is big enough for what he holds; 0 = matched, negative = the domain outgrows the man) — it is computed per ruler, per domain. And the fees sit on the PA-competence diagonal by construction: the PA table's income columns are the GP-threshold bands (verified cell-by-cell against p.348), so each rung's wage-grade reads exactly PA 0 over its own manor — the book's own Designer's Note says rulers advance to PA 0 and stop. Under the knight's contract the land delivers a man one level shy of that mark: every dubbed knight reads PA −1 until the field finishes him, and PA 0 is the badge of the proven knight — the module's texture as law, not a leak. The esquire, outside the contract, ploughs to his grade and reads PA 0 by rents alone. Nothing is borrowed, because nothing is missing.
Doesn't the in-kind garrison inflate knightly income? Run the full RAW ledger (revenue land+4+2, less the three 1-gp cost lines, less garrison, plus militia credit — p.341–2) at RAW's own militia ceiling — 2 per 10 families at the qualifying numbers' best mix, half heavy foot and half bowmen, ~2.1 gp of credit per family, good even uncalled (richer mixes exist on paper, but the yeoman-and-archer mix is the period's) — and it yields land+3 exactly at civilized class. The entire dispute is the frontier increment, ~0.9 gp per family at borderlands and ~1.9 at outlands — call it 1–2; concede it whole and the bachelor's fee moves from 12 families to 13 at borderlands (ACKS RAW revenues; at the customary rent, 25 to 34). What the gold per family buys is a sworn knight in the manor house above the armed peasantry — and p.432 (rebels are drawn from the militia when a domain turns) is exactly why the assize pairs the levy with a resident lord: the counterweight is a term of the same contract.
The enfeoffed knight is no household henchman — why does the wage table bind him? Because the wage table is the market price of a level-L man, and the fee must pay it at every point of contact. At a fee's birth from the household, p.168 applies verbatim: the lord enfeoffs a knight he was already paying, and land replaces wage. At a birth from the market — RAW lets a lord enfeoff non-henchmen outright: "mercenary commanders, adventurers" (p.347) — the fee's income is the recruitment offer, and it must meet the man's open-market wage or he rides on. And at every inheritance the market binds the grade, not the man: an heir on a 96-gp manor doesn't ride off — he stays, poorer, and the estate can no longer sustain the rank's establishment, so the line slides down the kit ladder toward the esquire (the threadbare fee, Design chapter, Library) while standing manors re-grade rather than resize. Netting, offering, retaining: one price — enforced hard at the first two points, and at the third by the slow slide of grade.
Who pays when the levy is called up? Someone does: the provider — RAW's general law (Call to Arms: the vassal musters troops at his own wage cost; Troops favor: the lord pays for what he sends down, p.346). The rung cards price it: afield, the knight pays his yeomen's wages and their plough-teams stand idle. The idle plough is booked at the family's full revenue rate (land+6 under ACKS RAW revenues, land+1 customary — the engine reads the live profile), because RAW's two ledger columns come apart here: p.432 reduces domain revenues by one family per man levied ("produce revenue as if it has [fewer] families"), while p.342's Costs per Family column — liturgies, tithe, maintenance — keeps charging: the family still lives there; only its production marches. Net loss per man is therefore the whole revenue, not the fee's net take. Together, a large fraction of the fee's income for the month of service — at the module's defaults about three-quarters at the bachelor's fee and the whole of it and more at the castellany — plus −2 morale. The share is not a constant: it swings with the land value and the custom of record (swept across both readings and every land value, it runs from under a fifth of a month's income to more than three months of it), so every Ladder card computes its own rung's figure live. Free to keep, dear to call, which is why historical levies were short-term, defensive instruments. And the bill is bounded: the fee owes the term — one month of service a year, the forty days — at its own cost; past it the muster rides on the lord's wages (the pay ladder, 1s/2s/4s ↔ 60/100/200), as the rolls show fee-holders drawing. The knight himself is pre-paid for the term: the fee sustains him year-round — at home always, in the host for the forty days, and beyond them at the lord's coin.
Four fees — one L5 knight, or four knights? Both, and the module says which is which. The wage ladder answers retention: 400 gp of income keeps one L5 man — grade. The quota answers service: four fees owe four lances — count. Historically the count was the law and the grade the social fact, and they were never traded one for the other: a four-fee holder did not send "one better knight" — he sent himself and found three more, or paid. The cards price the finding (scutage, term-hire, the levy's horse), and the Muster section prices why the standing alternative — retained men on wages — belongs to the margin and the barony, not the parity floor. Concentration keeps its real cost visible too: four L3 lances out-rate one L5 on the battle sheet (Units section) — the premium of the great fee is command, quality, and one sworn bond, never bodies.

Played strictly by RAW, a sub-baronial vassal pays his lord in coin, and the arithmetic leaves a low-level man on a big manor — out of the box, ACKS builds a classical realm. This module's structural change is one: the fee renders service instead of coin and is quit of the garrison line for it, at a cost of about one gold piece per family against strict accounting. Around it stand a set of explicit rulings — no per-fee tribute and its inefficiency side-step, service booked at full wage, the assize, the quota with its definition of record, the knight's contract, the squire, heroic-unit pricing, the household's keep and the assessment (Muster section), and the fisc oversight (its corruption dial lives in the Offices section) — each quoted against RAW in the ⚖ doctrine tables (both in the Library). Count the rows of those two tables and the tally is rulings, not one: the difference is that the rest are extensions where RAW prices nothing, not overrides of what it does.

RAW under the hood — every rule this module stands on

Four audits, one per surface: the rule as ACKS II states it, the page it is on, and what this module uses it as. Read them as the working-out behind the RAW marks — the point is that a reader can check a citation without owning the argument that rests on it. Every page reference has been checked against the 2nd printing and its Major Errata.

"A henchman who is given a domain to rule as a vassal does not need to be paid a wage if the domain income is equal to or greater than his wage"RR p.168the fee's constitution — a fee is the smallest estate whose income equals its holder's wage; the manors are this sentence iterated per level

Limits of growth: max families per 6-mile hex — 185 outlands (30 people/sq mi ≈ 6 fam) · 375 borderlands (60 people ≈ 12 fam) · 780 civilized (125 people ≈ 25 fam); at ~5 people per family the ratios fix the hex at ~31 sq mi ≈ 20,000 acresRR p.340the density lever — turns a fee's families into ground (1.5-mile hexes, % of a 6-mile hex) and drives the parceling check: no lord can enfeoff more ground than he holds
