"Non-henchman magistrates might be susceptible to corruption or treachery (Judge's discretion)"RR p.342the corruption dial (doctrine): the unsworn officer skims ¼ / ½ / ¾ of the spread — the gap between the lawful 12.5% and the district's band loss — by loyalty standing (~0 when held by good lordship — favors, offices, marriages; −2 base; −4 beyond range of trade, JJ p.203); hostile = the band returns in full. Between notches: skim share = (2 − loyalty) ÷ 8, clamped 0–1. The two RAW tables are the endpoints, loyalty the dial between them; the skim counts as his income (p.342/423), so corruption levels the man
Landowners & Governors: a governor rules a domain he does not own — collects tax, tribute, and urban revenue, pays garrison and settlement expenses, holds authority, earns full domain XP; the landowner keeps land + service revenueJJ p.405–6the fee-farm pole: a sheriff who farms his shire is a governor; the salaried custodian priced here is a magistrate
Doctrine: RAW's magistrates serve the ruler's own domain and oversee only the four expense lines; no RAW office collects tribute or holds a set district—we add the fisc as a fifth oversight and seat the officer over a district — the sheriff and castle-constable of the medieval record and of Hârn's royal castles

The chapters — the arguments, at length

The long-form arguments, in the order to take them. Castles — what a rung's land actually buys in stone. War — the same question answered in battle ratings, and whether the ladder leaves a lord any choice at all. Money — the gold piece against the pound sterling, and what a ratio across two counting conventions is worth. Custom — the manorial reading, which reprices every gp on the page and is where to start. The franchise — why RAW's 4 gp is right for a burgess and wrong for a villein. Design — the module's own account of itself, including what it declines to build. History — the anchors, the cross-checks, and the places the module deviates from the record on purpose.

Castles — what a rung's land will actually pay for RAW + HISTORY

This page says castle and castellany several dozen times between them and, until this chapter, priced a castle exactly zero times. That is a gap worth closing, because the answer is not the one the vocabulary implies — and it is the finding a reader is most likely to remember.

The ladder, converted to territory and then to stone

Two RAW rules, and nothing else: a domain's minimum stronghold value per 1.5-mile hex (RR p.338) and its population ceiling per 6-mile hex (RR p.340). The families are the module's own rung values at land 6 under the customary reading. Every cell below is computed — hexes = ⌈families ÷ ceiling⌉, then × the class rate — so the table is a function this page can be checked against rather than twelve constants a reader must take on trust.

A castellany's stronghold requirement does not buy a castle. It buys a tower. A bachelor's fee buys a timber hall and a palisade — a ringwork — and that is historically exact. The knightly residence of the 11th–13th centuries was a fortified manor house, a ringwork or a solar tower; the castle proper belonged to a magnate. The arithmetic says outright what the rung note only implies.

And a real castle is an earl's, measurably. Run the same rule backwards: — That is why Caer Gardiren is an earl's castle — only an earl's population can secure one.

Three things the table says that the vocabulary does not

The frontier taxes the knight twice. The same hundred families want — — on top of a higher garrison rate on every one of them. Kaldor is borderlands.

One rung is worse placed than the others, and for a reason worth naming: RAW's living-expense scale is quantised by level while the territory rule is continuous in families, so a rung can carry the stone bill of the tier above while drawing the allowance of its own. RAW's living expenses allow an implicit rent of 1/33 of stronghold value, capped at half the total, so the stone a rung can carry unaided is (wage ÷ 2) × 33. Measured against what its territory actually demands at borderlands: —

⚠ Mind which rung the name lands on. A county knight on this page is the two-fee holding — the terms table: "one the knight bachelor; two the county knight; four the castellan" — and this ladder carries no three-fee, 75-family rung at all. A stone burden quoted against that rung therefore belongs to no rung here, and the finding it carries has to be re-landed before it means anything. That is why every figure above is computed from the ladder rather than transcribed from a table beside it.

Unit capacity ≠ peacetime housing ≠ standing establishment, and RAW supplies two of the three. A keep holds 6 units in a siege and houses a company of 120 in peace (RR p.132, 151). Harlech's actual establishment was 36. ⚠ The third number is the one a reader wants, and it is the one no rulebook prints — which is why the garrison composer treats the first as a refusal and the record's 12–60 as a warning. A cap says what is possible; only the record says what was usual.

⚠ One note on grain, so a discrepancy does not read as a defect. Everything here is computed at RAW's 1.5-mile rates against the per-1.5-mile share of RAW's 6-mile population ceilings. RAW's own 6-mile stronghold figure is not 16× the fine one — 22,500 gp against 24,000 — which is RAW's rounding rather than an error here. At the coarse rate the earl's caput above reads about 2,073 families instead. The fine grain is used because the subject is manors.

War — what a rung's land will actually pay for RAW + MODULE

The castles chapter asked what a rung's land buys in stone. This one asks what it buys in war, and it is a harder question, because the answer is a comparison and this module has never made one. The units tab prices a banner beautifully and cannot help here: it renders one mixture, and the only question a baron actually has is which mixture he should have raised. With this much land — many small fees, or few great ones?

⚠ A validation matrix may not be built to confirm the answer it expects. The design's own sentence is that small fees buy bodies and redundancy while great fees buy command and quality — and a table that reported that whatever the arithmetic said would be worth nothing. So the headline output below is whether there is a trade at all: how many rungs survive with no other rung beating them on every measure. Where one rung wins outright, the matrix says so and names the rungs a lord has no reason to take.

The three bases — and why one comparison is not enough

A rung is only dear or cheap against something held equal, and there are three honest things to hold. Equal land grants one estate different ways. Equal campaign cost spends the same estate's income as coin instead — and that basis charges supply and specialists, which are flat per body and so fall hardest on the mixture with the most bodies. Equal quota reverses the question: the charter fixes the lances and what moves is the bill. The budget at each is derived, not chosen — the module's own ceiling, a barony of families (RR p.343), read through the live land value and custom of record.

The formula's three hidden assumptions, priced

RR p.466 gives BR = (AC+1) × HD × (HD+1) × (1+specials) ÷ (8 × infantry per unit). Three of its terms this module carries as constants, and a comparison across levels is only honest while all three stay common to every row. What they cost if they do not is arithmetic, not caution:

    And the rung that is three levels at one price

    Money — the gold piece against the pound sterling RAW + MODULE

    This page quotes sterling in a dozen places — the £20 minimal fee, the 1436 returns' £24 esquires and £40 knights, Magna Carta's 100-shilling relief — and until now it never said what a pound was worth in gold. It is worth saying, because the module's central figures are gp and half its historical anchors are £: without a rate the two sets of numbers sit on the same page and cannot be compared, which is the condition in which a reader quietly assumes they can.

    The chain has two links, and neither is ours. ACKS's own coin table sets 10sp = 1gp (RR p.123). And ACKS's designer states the historical equivalence directly: 1 silver piece = 1 English silver penny — from which he prices a quarter of wheat at "4gp (3 shillings 4 pence)", i.e. 40d, which checks. Put them together:

    Sterling in ACKS coin — the penny, the shilling and the pound converted
    SterlingIn penceIn ACKS coin
    1 penny (1d)11 sp
    1 shilling (12d)121.2 gp
    1 pound (240d)24024 gp
    1 mark (160d, ⅔£)16016 gp

    Sources. The equivalence is Alexander Macris's, given on Autarch's own site — Starting from the Ground Up…Literally, which sets out "1 medieval English penny = 1 D&D sp; 1 English shilling = 12 pennies = 12sp; and 1 English pound = 20 shillings = 240sp = 24gp" — and restated by him in comments at Blog of Holding. It is not in the rulebook: RR gives the coin table and a purchasing-power table (p.123) and no historical rate at all. So the rate is the designer's, the coin table is RAW, and the reading below is the module's. DEBATED

    One rule before any ratio — count both sides the same way

    A ratio between this module and the record is a ratio only if both sides are counted in the same unit. Divide the module's income by ACKS families and the record's by recorded entries, and the convention below has been applied to one side and not the other: what comes out is not a gap, it is the conversion factor wearing a gap's clothes. Applied to both sides the gap is a single ratio at every denominator — the table two heads down shows it holding at three — so a product of two such figures double-counts the convention and is not a finding. On the same discipline the module is not thin in households: measured in recorded entries it is not thin at all. MODULE

    The rate is not the problem — four anchors, one dial

    Before blaming the conversion, test it. Macris's rate was checked at four independent points — every row below in which the rate actually appears — and it is calibrated at the floor and drifts rich as you climb. The fifth row is not a fifth test: the grain wage is the wheat price divided by the labourer's, both in ACKS's own coin, so no exchange rate enters it and rescaling one could not move it. It is a cross-check on the two anchors that pass, not an anchor.

    The gold-to-sterling rate tested at four independent anchors, with one rate-free cross-check
    AnchorACKSEngland, 13th c.Verdict
    Unskilled labour (RR p.174)1 sp/day = 1d/day1–1½d/day✔ lands
    Wheat (RR p.123)4 gp/quarter = 3s 4d~5–6s✔ cheap by ~1.5×
    Grain wage — days per quarter (derived, not an anchor)40~48✔ lands — rate-free
    Heavy cavalry (RR p.176)60 gp/mo = 20d/dayserjeant 12d, knight 24d1.7× rich
    L3 henchman (RR p.168)100 gp/mo = 33d/dayknight 24d/day on campaign1.4× rich

    A labourer and a loaf are right. Rescaling the rate would fix the fee and break the two anchors that currently work — while the grain wage, carrying no coin, would not move at all and would go on agreeing with the pair it is made of. Two anchors that land, two that drift rich, one dial: over-determined. The rate is not to be touched, and the fault has to be somewhere else.

    One error, one face — the lord's revenue per holding

    It is. The defect is a rate, and a rate reads the same at every denominator you choose — which is the whole of the diagnosis:

    The gap between ACKS RAW revenues and the customary rent, at three denominators
    DenominatorACKS RAW revenuesThe customary rentGap
    Per ACKS family, per month9 gp4 gp2.25×
    Per full tenement, per year£4.50£2.002.25×
    Per recorded entry, per year (÷2.5)£1.80£0.802.25×

    9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 exactly, and it comes from (land+3) ÷ (land−2) at land value 6. What this does not say is that the module's fee is the historical £20 fee. It is not: the £20 fee is about 10 families and yields 40 gp/mo; a customary bachelor's fee is 25 families and yields 100. The module's fee stays 2.5× the benchmark fee in total income, and that is correct. What gets calibrated here is the rate per holding; the size of the grant is set elsewhere, by the body the charter names. The £20 fee does not reach even the 60-gp Domesday rider, let alone the 100-gp Angevin knight — which is the definition of record's business, and its lever already carries it.

    Where the money is invented

    The Judges Journal derives RAW's 12 gp from a modelled farm. Three of its four lines survive contact with the English record; one does not, and the extraction rate does not.

    The Judges Journal's model farm, audited line by line against the English record
    LineACKSEngland
    Crops — 20 ac × 1 qr × 4 gp80 gp = £3.33~15 qr × 5s = £3.75✔ calibrated
    Livestock — 3 cows, ox, pig, 32 sheep83 gp = £3.46~£1✗ 2–3×
    Other labour — 320 days at 1 sp32 gp = £1.33those days were week-work owed, unpaid✗
    The lord's share of the total144 of 195 = 73.8%rent + works + dues ≈ 25–35%✗ 2.4×

    The sheep figure is the checkable one: England's entire sheep population c.1300 — every demesne, monastery and peasant croft — works out to roughly 8–15 per family. ACKS gives every family 32. ⚠ These two columns are not multiplicative. Compounding the endowment factor by the claim factor double-counts, and the product is not a finding. The correction this module makes is to the composition of the 12 gp — the service and tax lines — and not a scaling of the total. DEBATED

    The structural cause — one yield where there were two estates

    A manor had two economies under one lord. RAW has one, and it faces the ruler. Demesne production, tenant rent, labour services, monopoly dues (mill, oven, fold) and taxation are collapsed into a single ruler-facing per-family yield. One number is asked to be a rent, a wage-equivalent, a profit and a tax at once — which is why it cannot be calibrated against any of them individually. HISTORY

    Who bore the risk on a manor, and what RAW does with the question
    Residual claimantBears
    Customary tenant holdingthe tenant, after fixed duesthe initial yield risk
    Directly farmed demesnethe lordproduction and market risk
    A bad year across the whole manor—tenant defaults; arrears transfer much of the loss back to the lord anyway

    ⚠ This table replaces a pull-quote the chapter used to carry — "in ACKS the peasant is the residual claimant; on a manor the lord is" — which was reversed against its own consequences. The slogan was memorable and wrong. Four consequences follow, every one visible in the English record and invisible in RAW: peasants accumulate (a good decade leaves the tenant richer, because his obligation did not move — hence the peasant land market, entry fines, dowries and wills); the lord's income does not track prosperity (grain prices roughly doubled 1180–1300 and assized rents did not move, which is why lords turned to direct demesne farming, tallage and entry fines); risk changes hands (a bad year in ACKS is the peasant's problem, on a manor it is the lord's, and manorial court rolls are largely a register of arrears); and custom is a real constraint — legal power over villeins was near-absolute, practical power was not.

    And the fifth is why this belongs in this module. The remedy is the incident, not the rate. The peasant's assized rent is to his lord exactly what the lord's charter is to the crown: a fixed paper that cannot be revised, with income growing away from it, reached only by event — entry fine, tallage and heriot below; relief, aid and wardship above. The module's own thesis, one level down. Run a manorial superstructure on a fiscal substructure and this is the seam.

    The date, not the error

    Here is the part that makes the whole finding less embarrassing and more interesting. Under ACKS RAW revenues every rung of this ladder already matches its historical band — for the fifteenth century:

    The ladder under ACKS RAW revenues, against the 1436 income returns
    RungKeepIncome (ACKS RAW)SterlingThe record
    Esquire's fee — ½60 gp63 gp/mo£31.51436: ~1,200 esquires averaging £24
    Bachelor's fee — 1100108£541436: ~950 knights at £40+
    Double fee — 2200207£103banneret estates £100–200
    Castellany — 4400405£202small barony, £200+

    The £20 fee is a thirteenth-century threshold — the distraint line, the minimum to live as a knight — and the other four are fifteenth-century observed incomes. Comparing a floor to an average across two centuries gives about 3×, and that is most of what the old 2.7× headline was measuring. So the module was never badly built. It was priced on the later returns and labelled with thirteenth-century vocabulary — and it was demographically thin in every century. The customary rent fixes the second and turns the first into a dial: at the customary rent the same four rungs read £30 · £50 · £100 · £200, which is a thirteenth-century page instead of a fifteenth-century one.

    Worked: what a relief actually costs a fee

    Magna Carta 1215 fixed the heir's relief at 100 shillings for a knight's fee — 120 gp at the rate above. HISTORY Measured against gross income it looks mild — 10% of a bachelor's fee's year at the customary rent, 9.3% under ACKS RAW revenues, against the ~25% a real £5 relief took from a real £20 fee. Measured against what the estate actually clears, which is the quantity every card on this page is built around, it is the second largest capital event in a fee-holder's life — and at the default that measure has no denominator at all. At land value 6, then — the default, and the row this whole passage is worked on:

    Relief by rung at land value 6 under the customary rent — and what it is actually paid out of
    RungFamiliesRelief (fees × 120 gp)Clears, a yearPaid from what?
    Esquire's fee — ½15600borrowing, or the lord's grace
    Bachelor's fee — 1251200borrowing, wardship, selling wood
    Double fee — 2502400the margin, if the manor has grown past its paper
    Castellany — 41004800the margin, a wardship falling in, or debt

    Every rung clears exactly zero, and the fourth column is the finding. At the customary rent the pins divide the net exactly — 60÷4, 100÷4, 200÷4, 400÷4 — so every rung sits on its support floor and the margin is nil. At the default land value, no rung on this ladder can pay its relief out of income at all. A relief is paid by borrowing, by wardship, by selling wood, or by the lord's grace — never from income. That is why relief was the grievance Magna Carta opened with, and it is why the margin — the grown manor, an estate running above its paper (Muster section) — is the only thing that makes a succession survivable.

    ⚠ Pin that to land 6 and leave it pinned. The unqualified form — "under the customary rent no rung can pay its relief at all" — is false off the default: at land value 9 the customary margins are 3 · 5 · 3 · 6 gp/mo, and those estates can accumulate a relief over time. The zero is a divisibility property of net 4 against 60/100/200/400, not a law of the reading. This chapter used to print a "months of clear income" column — 20 · 15 · 34 · 96 under ACKS RAW revenues — and read a trend into it. There was no trend. It was a rounding remainder, and it went to zero on all four rungs at land 7 under those same revenues. The column is retired rather than recomputed. MODULE

    In RAW's own currency of demand — the portable reading. Every duty ACKS lets a lord impose is priced at 1 gp/family: scutage, the loan, the gift, the Call to Arms (p.346). A relief at the parity floor works out at 1.2 × the net per family, because the fee's family count is its anchor divided by that same net — so at the customary default it is 4.8 duties, and under ACKS RAW revenues the same identity gives 10.8. But 1.2 × net is the NOMINAL, and it is exact only where the net divides the anchor — the same divisibility property the paragraph above has just warned about, and it does not hold in both readings. At the customary rent land 6 it holds on every rung (4.80 · 4.80 · 4.80 · 4.80, because 4 divides 60, 100, 200 and 400), and land 3 likewise (1.20 throughout). Under ACKS RAW revenues the family counts round up and the four rungs read 10.29 · 10.00 · 10.43 · 10.67 — near the nominal 10.8, never equal to it, and not steady. Customary land 9 is the same lesson on the other side: 8.00 · 8.00 · 8.28 · 8.28 against a nominal 8.4. The direction is what travels — a richer family is a dearer family and the fee needs fewer of them — and the steadiness is a property of the arithmetic, not of the reading. At the module's own default a relief is five ordinary duties at once, and never repaid.

    That ratio holds only at the parity floor, and the gap is the clearest measure of what the margin buys: a grown manor pays its relief on the charter it outgrew, so a 40-family estate on a one-fee paper pays the same 120 gp spread over more than half again the families — three duties, not five. The Muster section's card computes that ratio for the estate in hand. Reliefs, aids and wardships are how a crown reaches an estate whose assessment it cannot revise.

    Custom — the manorial reading, and how it is derived RAW-INFORMED + MODULE

    Custom — what the dial actually rules

    The custom of record changes two numbers: a peasant family's service revenue from 4 to 1, and its tax revenue from 2 to 0. Urban families are untouched. Start here: one of those two is a house rule and the other is a RAW dial, and the difference matters more than the values do.

    The badge discipline this chapter is written under. The failure a derivation like this is most exposed to is claiming RAW's authority for a module choice, so the badges carry the load and each has a duty: RAW must quote the sentence; RAW-INFORMED must say what RAW supplies and what the module supplies; MODULE is a ruling and must say what it rules over. Every step below is badged to that standard.

    Service 1 — four arguments, ascending

    Provenance, stated before the arguments. RAW identifies skilled freemen and trade rights as the principal basis of service revenue. RAW A customary rural population should therefore yield less service revenue than RAW's commercial profile — the direction, and only the direction. RAW-INFORMED This module assigns that population service 1 rather than 4, keeping a residual for mills and rural trades. MODULE The house rule is not RAW's own sentence, and must not be read as one — RAW says most, not all, is elsewhere agnostic about tenure, and compulsory suit to a lord's mill is not a freeman buying a licence even though both concern milling.

    (a) RAW's own basis excludes it. "Services revenue derives from the services of skilled tradesmen… Most of these services are provided by freemen who offer a portion of their labor to the ruler in exchange for the right to practice their trade on his domain." (RR p.341) A licence fee paid by free tradesmen. A manorial population is villein — and RAW declines to model tenure at all, so the module is filling the one thing RAW says it left blank, not overruling it.

    (b) The manorial instrument is a monopoly, not a licence. HISTORY English lords did not license the miller; they owned the mill and compelled suit to it, paid in multure. Likewise the bakehouse and the assize of ale. The smith usually held by serjeanty — he pays nothing and the lord receives smithing instead of coin, which is land already granted away, not revenue collected.

    (c) The arithmetic, priced from the record. HISTORY A watermill ran 20–40s a year; bakehouse and ale fines a few shillings each. The whole trade complex comes to £2–5 per manor per year, and a fee is two or three manors:

    The fee's service revenue at each setting, against what a manor's trade complex actually yielded
    Fee's service revenuePer manor (2–3 manors)Against the record
    Service 4 — ACKS RAW£50/yr£17–255–10× over, and equal to the fee's whole income
    Service 1 — customary£12.5/yr£4–6✔ in band

    (d) It makes RAW right rather than wrong. RAW priced a free, commercial population and priced it correctly. That population is the urban family, and RAW keeps its 4 gp there. Nothing in this dial touches a borough.

    Tax 0 — a residual allocation, not a claim that lords took nothing

    The derivation, and it is the load-bearing passage of the whole package. MODULE At land value 6 the customary profile is calibrated to a net receipt of 4 gp per full-tenement unit — the historical input, drawn from the manorial record. After the three fixed expenses that leaves exactly one whole gold piece to divide:

    4 = 6 + service + tax − 3 ⟹ service + tax = 1

    RAW says most service revenue comes from skilled freemen and trade rights, and a manor still receives value from mills and rural trades, so the residual is not zero and belongs on the service line. Tax takes what is left, which is nothing. It is falsifiable three ways: move the calibration target and the allocation moves with it; if rural service ought to round to zero then tax becomes 1; if local cash dues demonstrably require another whole gold piece then the target is too low or the decomposition is wrong. The module's one free number is the calibration target — an empirical quantity a reader can check against the record, rather than a rate nobody can audit.

    The booking convention, and only what it claims. RAW-INFORMED MODULE Agricultural week-work is represented through the land line, because that labour produces the demesne output RAW's land line already collects. So labour-rent is not priced twice. That is the whole of the claim, and the strong form does not follow from it: customary rent in general is not already contained in land revenue. Customary tenants commonly owed works and a fixed money rent on the same holding, and the thirteenth-century Extenta Manerii instructs its surveyors to record "how much rent of assize be paid yearly besides the works and customs." Cash rent and labour service were two obligations, and this module folds them into one calibrated receipt rather than resolving them apart.

    The note on resolution — a statement about notation. RAW's domain economy is written in whole gold pieces per family per month, and its smallest possible entry — 1 gp — is ten shillings a year. An English knight's fee of £20 with about 25 recorded entries yielded its lord sixteen shillings per entry per year, and that sixteen shillings is everything: assized rent, the value of works, court perquisites, merchet, heriot, tolls and the mill. The individual dues inside it run one to four shillings apiece. So tax 0 is the statement that no seigneurial due is large enough to earn a line of its own in a ledger written in whole gold pieces — they are collected into the calibrated total rather than resolved separately.

    ⚠ And the claim stops exactly there. That each due is small does not make their sum small — that step is an aggregation fallacy, and this argument does not take it. Sixteen shillings against a ten-shilling digit leaves ample room for the aggregate to reach a whole unit, and part of it does: that is precisely the gold piece the module assigns to services. The claim is about what gets its own line, not about what the dues were worth, so but they did take merchet is answered inside the argument rather than against it.

    The direction of absorption — why service holds the residual, and not tax

    The derivation fixes the sum; this fixes the direction — because absorption is not symmetric. Collapsing two lines into one whole-gold-piece digit means one category absorbs the other, and the surviving line imposes its behaviour on everything folded into it. So "service 1, tax 0 — or tax 1, service 0?" is not a question about labels. It asks which of RAW's two categories the customary receipt is to behave like, and in RAW the two behave differently.

    RAW hangs two mechanics on the tax line and none on the service line. RAW Tax is the line a ruler may raise or lower, at a morale-roll price (p.349), and the line whose setting RAW propagates to his towns (p.352). Service revenue carries no lever and propagates nowhere. Whatever is booked as tax therefore rides the tax dial — a lord could "lower taxes" and erase it, or raise it from a base that already contains it. But the customary receipt is precisely the revenue a lord cannot move: fixed against his will is what the word custom means. A fixed line can absorb variable dues — they simply become part of the fixed receipt. The variable line cannot absorb fixed revenue without making it adjustable: booking the residual as tax would hand the lord a lever over his own mill. MODULE

    It also keeps the lever legible as a move. With the customary receipt on the service line, the tax dial sits at its floor with its whole travel intact: tallage in a bad year is an act, taken at RAW's own morale-roll price, rather than something already spent in the baseline. That is the manorial bargain in one sentence — the lord takes less in coin and is owed more in obedience — and it is why the page names its credit tax morale, the tax line's own modifier and no more.

    The record absorbed in the same direction. HISTORY The folding this allocation models actually happened, and it ran one way: scattered dues and commuted works ossified into fixed customary receipts — that is what rent of assize means, dues assized: fixed, and recorded "besides the works and customs". Drift ran from levy toward custom. The reverse absorption — fixed custom melting back into an at-will levy — is the breach the institution existed to prevent; it had a name, arbitrary tallage, and it was resisted at law and by flight. Booking the customary receipt under tax would model the direction the record shows custom resisting.

    And the audit trail runs one way too. The component the record can price is the trade complex — the £2–5 per manor per year checked above. The tax-side dues are a scatter of one-to-four-shilling incidents with no auditable aggregate. Residual accounting names the line it can measure and lets the remainder fall on the other; invert the allocation and the one surviving line becomes a figure nothing in the record can check — which would spend the falsifiability that is this derivation's whole advantage.

    The anchor of regard — what tax 0 does not earn

    The allocation above has a consequence on the morale table, and for two releases this page got it wrong. RAW adjusts a domain's monthly morale roll by +1 for each gold piece of tax below 2 (p.349). RAW Read literally against a customary profile sitting at tax 0, that paid a standing +2, and the page printed it — on the glance line, in the writ, and in the Dials chapter. It is withdrawn. The dues folded into the calibrated receipt were collected, as the paragraph above concedes in as many words, and a fold that carries the burden cannot also collect the credit for remitting it.

    Three things were wrong with it, and the third is the one that decides the repair.

    (a) A repricing cannot move how people feel. The custom of record is one manor described two ways — same peasants, same dues, two vocabularies. Yet flipping the dial moved printed regard by 2. A modifier that moves when the accounting moves is measuring the accountant.

    (b) The module already reads the neighbouring row by substance. The same table charges −1 per gp of garrison below 2, and a fee spends no coin on garrison at all. The quittance answers that the lance is the garrison, paid in kind — substance, not letter. Reading the garrison row by substance and the tax row by letter would take the favourable half of each, which is not a reading but a preference.

    (c) From RAW's anchor, tallage scores positive. A customary lord who tallages 1 gp a family sits at tax 1 — still below RAW's 2, and so still paid +1 for squeezing his villeins. The first two gold pieces of tallage were morale-positive. That is not a rounding; it inverts the sign of the module's own sentence that tallage is taken "at RAW's own morale-roll price".

    The ruling: the anchor is the custom of record, and nothing else changes. MODULE Regard is measured from what the peasantry expects, which is the custom — so a profile resting at its own custom is at ±0 in both readings: Customary at tax 0, and ACKS RAW at tax 2, each at its own normal. RAW's ±1 a gp is then untouched and prices travel from that anchor: tallage above custom −1 a gp, remission below it +1 a gp. Note the asymmetry, because it is real — downward travel exists only under ACKS RAW, where lowering from 2 remits actual coin. The customary line rests at zero with nothing left on it to remit; a famine-year forgiveness there acts on the folded receipt, not on a tax line that is already empty.

    And this adds no rule, because RAW's tax setting is tallage. An at-will seigneurial exaction above custom is what the word means, and RAW's tax line is seigneurial throughout — merchet, heriot, entry fine, tallage, the court, the tolls and the rent. Even RAW's propagation of the tax setting to the ruler's towns (p.352) matches the instrument: tallage fell on the demesne and its boroughs together. So the act a lord takes is RAW's own tax-rate decision, in the domain turn this module does not model and does not replace. This module supplies the anchor and stops. What was withdrawn here is a number; no mechanic replaced it, and the page carries one rule fewer than before.

    ⚠ Note what the withdrawal does not say. It does not say the customary family was as heavily burdened in coin as RAW's taxed peasant — it plainly was not, and that lighter burden is already priced, in the receipt itself. It says the burden and the relief may not be counted twice: once by folding the dues into a calibrated total, and again by paying a bonus for their absence. And it does not touch the component discipline that the retired credit was at least scrupulous about — a morale figure on this page is one modifier among a dozen and is never a domain's morale total. That rule survives its occasion, and any future tallage clause is held to it.

    What the incidents do and do not carry

    Relief, aid and wardship model extraction upward, from the fee-holder to his liege, and stand in for recurring tribute at that level. They do not replace, duplicate or excuse peasant dues below it. If this module ever wanted incidents to stand literally in place of RAW's smoothed tax line it would have to model the peasant-level incidents — heriots, merchets, entry fines, court receipts — or annualise an equivalent set. It does neither, and the incidents are scoped accordingly.

    Demesne and enfeoffed — the difference is total

    Enfeoffment is the act of alienating the revenue in exchange for service. The families under a knight are gone from the lord's ledger. That is what the word means. HISTORY

    A demesne manor and an enfeoffed manor — identical inside, opposite on the lord's books
    Demesne manorEnfeoffed manor
    Who collects land / service / taxthe lordthe knight
    What the lord receivesall of itnothing recurring
    Instead—a lance when called; castle-guard
    At a death—relief, wardship, marriage
    Revisable?bound by the same custom as any lordno — a grant, not a lease

    The two have identical internal economics. Same land, same service, same tax, same expenses. The only difference is whose purse it lands in. So a feudal lord's income is not families × rate cascading upward; it is (demesne families × net) + service + incidents — which is why the Realms tab shows the demesne and the honour side by side and never sums them into one figure.

    Tax 0 at realm scale — not a rounding at all

    ⚠ This is a claim about the crown, not about RAW's tax line. RAW's tax revenue is seigneurial — coin paid to the ruler by his own peasants — so the absence of a royal land tax is not by itself a reason to zero it. What follows describes where realm income comes from instead; the justification for the dial is the derivation above.

    After Danegeld and carucage lapsed, England had no regular land tax. The king was expected to "live of his own." That absence is why kings needed consent, why scutage and aids mattered, why Magna Carta happened, and why Parliament grew. Tax 0 does not distort the picture; it is the picture. HISTORY And it does not impoverish the realm — it redirects realm income into instruments this module already prices: the demesne (Realms), relief, wardship and marriage (the incidents card), aid (a Duty), scutage (Muster), and justice — the residue of the tax line. The relief that looked light at a tenth of gross becomes load-bearing: it is no longer a decoration on a fat tax base, it is a substantial share of how the lord actually gets paid.

    Sidebar — Package E, the RAW-legal route to the same rate

    The same destination is reachable without the house rule. Set land to 5 — 22.2% of 3d3, an ordinary roll — keep RAW's service 4 and tax 0, and pay the garrison in coin. Net is 4, the fee is 25 families, £50 a year, £0.80 per recorded entry: identical, with zero house rules.

    ⚠ A sidebar, and not a corroboration. "Two disjoint routes agree, so 4 is right" does not follow: E is another parameter combination selected to solve the same target equation, and many combinations can be made to equal 4. Agreement between them is algebra, not evidence. E is also a different ledger — the customary reading describes an enfeoffed holder whose garrison is discharged in kind, E a landholder paying it in coin — so the two do not even describe the same man. It is offered as a configuration for a table that would rather not carry a house rule, and as nothing else. MODULE

    Why the customary reading and not E. E leaves service revenue at £0.80 per entry per year of tradesmen's licences — roughly ten times a real manor's mill-and-oven income — so it is right in total and wrong in its parts. And E has the knight paying £25 a year for a standing garrison on a £50 estate, when English rural policing imposed no standing cash payroll on the lord: frankpledge, the tithing and the hue and cry were obligations of the community, not wage lines. Under the customary reading the militia credit is frankpledge — the community's own armed men discharging the line without coin, exactly as RAW p.341 permits.

    Four arguments that do not support tax 0

    Four plausible-looking defences of the same value, and every one of them fails — all four in the same way, by claiming RAW's authority for a module choice. They are set out because the derivation above has to be told apart from them, and because the failure they share is what the badge discipline at the head of this chapter exists to catch.

    Four arguments for tax 0 that do not work, and why each fails
    The argumentWhy it fails
    "There was no recurring royal land tax on an English manor" RAW's tax line is not a royal land tax. It is explicitly seigneurial — merchet, heriot, entry fine, tallage, the court, the tolls and the rent. The argument does not touch it
    "The module already prices those fees as incidents, so charging both bills inheritance twice" Different levels, different payers, different property interests. A peasant heriot and a knightly relief may both fall at a death, but they are a different deceased paying a different sum to a different recipient, and historically they coexisted. Layered extraction is not double-counting: income on one ledger is an expense on the next
    "The rent is already in the land line" True of labour rent and false in general. Assized money rent coexisted with works on the same tenement — the Extenta Manerii settles it. Saying this is not applying RAW's distinction; it reallocates part of RAW's tax category into land, which is a module choice and must be badged as one
    "The house rule is RAW's own sentence" RAW's wording motivates the cut; it does not supply the value 1. Direction is not magnitude, and borrowing the rulebook's authority for a coefficient it never states is the failure all four share

    The rule that catches all four. A claim that two payments are the same charge must name seven things, not three: flow type, payer, recipient, institutional level, base or consideration, trigger, and substitution relationship. Week-work and assized rent share the payer, the recipient, the level and the tenement, and are still two obligations — they differ on base and on substitution, and those two rows are the whole argument. The first row of the table above fails on level, the third on base; a ratio counted two ways fails on base too. Fill the table before writing the sentence. MODULE

    The franchise — why RAW's 4 gp is right for burgesses and wrong for villeins HISTORY

    The franchise — prose, not mechanics

    No mechanic is added here. This chapter exists to explain why the custom dial has two settings and not a ladder of them — and RAW draws the boundary itself: "If fewer than 75 urban families are ever present in a settlement, the urban settlement dissolves into the hamlets of the peasantry and become peasant families." (RR p.352) RAW

    A manor therefore has no urban families. A manor is service 1, always. There is no service 2. No franchise ladder, no charter fines, no tiers — the thing that would have justified an intermediate setting does not exist inside RAW's own model of a settlement.

    A market was a franchise, not a population effect. In ACKS a market emerges from population. In England it was granted by the crown: it could sit at a village of thirty households and be absent from a large one, and there were over two thousand grants by 1350. That is the deepest difference between the two models of a countryside, and it is worth knowing before you read a market class as a demographic fact. HISTORY

    And RAW gives the class boundary twice, in two chapters, with two different answers. The Domains chapter bands settlements in families and begins Class III at 2,500; Mercantile Ventures defines the same six classes and begins it at 1,750. Every other rung agrees, so it is one contested line and not two ladders. This page reads 2,500, because RAW's own Villages, Towns and Cities table settles the disputed band outright — a small city of 1,250 – 2,499 families is printed there as Class IV — because the investment ladder's caps are the same band ceilings rung for rung with no rung at 1,750, and because the sandbox procedure in the Judges Journal uses 2,500 in the very step that goes on to set range of trade. The errata corrects neither statement. Worth knowing if you carry a settlement between 1,750 and 2,499 families across from another table. RAW

    The spacing rule is a hex rule. The rule cited from Bracton is 6⅔ miles between markets — a third of a day's walk out, a third at market, a third home. ACKS's hexes are six miles. One chartered market per six-mile hex, to within rounding, which is a usable Judge's rule that falls out of the institution rather than the population. DEBATED

    Charters were named to a weekday, and neighbouring markets took different days, so a circuit of markets is a week rather than a map. And selling charters was crown revenue — the same box as reliefs and aids, which is where this chapter rejoins the module's thesis: the crown reaches a countryside it cannot tax by selling it privileges.

    The magnitude is below resolution, at the same scale of institution the tax-0 argument turns on. A modest weekly market was worth £1–5 a year; on the customary rent's 25-family manor that is 0.08–0.4 gp/family a month at this chapter's own coin rate. Under ACKS RAW revenues the fee is 12 families and the same market reads 0.17–0.83. Only a good market — £10–20 a year — reaches 1 gp/family on that 25-family manor, and a market that good implies a settlement, which is exactly where RAW takes over. The same resolution limit, at the same scale.

    The ladder's top rung is an instrument this module already built. A borough bought self-government by paying the crown a fixed annual farm — the firma burgi — which is RAW's fee-farm at the governor pole (JJ p.405–6). A borough is a domain that has bought itself out. The Offices section prices that pole; nothing new is needed here. MODULE

    Design — what this module does, and why MODULE

    What this module does

    ACKS II's Titles of Nobility stop at the 160-family baron; everything beneath is a single undifferentiated "domain." But the layer beneath the baron is where feudal armies actually came from — the knight's fee. This module prices that layer with RAW economics under one declared doctrine — every ruling flagged in the ⚖ table: the henchman wage table fixes what a man of each level must be paid; a fee is the smallest estate whose income pays him (RR p.168 — a henchman-vassal "does not need to be paid a wage if the domain income is equal to or greater than his wage"); the mercenary tables set the recruitment floor. From those inputs alone fall the rung sizes, the powers-of-two "counting in fees" idiom, the lord's profit from enfeoffment, and the XP plateaus. Where the model must choose between ACKS's classical default — free-floating rulers paying cash tribute — and the feudal pattern, it chooses feudal and says so: every such ruling is quoted against RAW in the ⚖ doctrine table, in the Library. History enters as consistency checks: the rungs are derived from the wage table and then measured against the medieval record, never tuned to it — so where they land is corroboration, not proof.

    Lineage

    This is the third generation of an idea. The Wandering Gamist's "ACKS Estates – Nobility" (2017) first worked the knight's fee in ACKS terms: a ~10-family estate as the support unit of a lance, with the decisive observation that feudal service is seasonal — which is why land-for-service beats year-round wages. Helgeran's Knightly Realms systematized it into a whole pyramid: uniform 10-family knightholds under 2nd-level knights netting land+1 at RAW revenues (the garrison still paid in cash, centralized as the baron's 852-gp foot), banners of fifteen fees run as micro-senates, and service in place of tribute below the viscount. This module refines toward the historical record: a graduated scale of manors (esquire to castellan) sized by wage-parity instead of uniform knightholds; the garrison taken in kind (the knight's own lance and trained yeomen in place of the coin line); heritable fees with fosterage demographics closing the XP loop; fidelity through the household rather than the senate; and the cross-checks (History chapter, Library). It states the doctrine as a quittance — the fee is quit of the garrison line so long as its service is kept, the period's own instrument (estates quit of geld or castle-guard for service; quit-rent is the same deal run backward) — and writes the conditions down as the assize of the fee: mail per fee held, levy trained and kitted, view of arms twice yearly, with default priced on every card.

    The engine — levels first, history second

    Be clear about the causality: these manors are generated by ACKS character levels, not by history. The engine is the henchman wage table (RR p.168), which doubles per level — 25 / 50 / 100 / 200 / 400 gp — and one farming fact: a fee-holder who garrisons his own land in kind keeps his whole net per family. The rungs below are worked at ACKS RAW revenues — land + 3, so 9 at average land — because that is the ledger this derivation was written against; under the module's opening customary rent the same wages buy 15, 25, 50 and 100 families instead. Divide wage by net and the rungs fall out: ~7, 12, 23, 45 families. (That 23 misses 2 × 12 by one on purpose: grants come in whole families, so each rung rounds its own remainder up — two bachelor's fees carry two rounding pads where one double fee carries one. The same arithmetic prices two esquire's fees at 14 families against the bachelor's 12: consolidation wastes less remainder, one more reason lords preferred it — and real fee assessments never doubled cleanly either. One cross-current: with fosterage on, every lance brings its own squire, so many small fees carry more squire-value per family than one great fee. But fees are territories, not permanent family-counts — two fees at the bachelor's rung are two manor-territories that will each stock toward ~23 and re-grade (a density fact, and the one figure in this parenthesis the reading does not move) (the parceling check below), so the lord's real choice is how many territories to parcel, and per territory the mature state is the greater fee.) Richer land shrinks these floors, as it should — fees were income assessments, and the hide (the old English tax-assessment unit of land, notionally 120 acres) was itself physically smaller in fertile shires; but a standing manor never resizes, it re-grades: the same estate assesses at more fees and keeps a better knight (see the lever's standing-manor line). Because the wage doubles per level, each rung is twice the one below — which is why the medieval idiom of "holding N fees" maps directly onto levels — the grade each fee retains, its proven holder: ½ fee keeps an L2-grade man, 1 fee an L3, 2 fees an L4, 4 fees an L5 — and onto counts: the same fee-number is the quota of lances the estate owes (the ⚖ quota row; the discharge priced on every card). Grade and count part company above one fee — the wage keeps one better man while the law owes several — and that gap is where scutage, term-hire, and the household live (Muster section). One scope note: these counts are the distraint-century definition's — the definition lever re-counts them per era (a Domesday "fee" is the 60-gp rider's) — while the wage ladder beneath never moves. (What the fee grows unaided is one level shy of that — the knight's contract; the idiom names the man the fee is sized to keep, not the boy it raises. And the later age's fractional fees — tenths and fortieths — are the divorce of fee from knight that the era table dates; the ladder models the marriage, not the divorce.) The manors stop at L5 because the next doubling — 800 gp/mo, the keep of a sixth-level man — is a wage grade no fee reaches, and a level-6 man is a lord and not a knight. It is not the barony: RAW's barony is a tier, 160 families (RR p.343), whose ≈1,120 gp plateaus an L6 against the 1,200 XP threshold. Grade and tier are different in kind, and the module adds no new administrative tier above the barony — though old fee assessments may survive inside baronial domains. History enters as the check: the ratios should land inside the medieval record's own ranges, and the cross-checks (History chapter, Library) show where they hit exactly and where they sit at the edge of the band. A fee is, throughout, a job posting with a fixed salary: its income must match what the man's sword earns on the open market, or he rides elsewhere.

    Making sense for the lord — the other half of the schema

    A rung only exists if the lord profits by granting it — otherwise no fee is ever enfeoffed and the manors are a fantasy. The ledger closes from his side too, and it is two-colored: demesne families garrisoned in coin, enfeoffed families in men — demesne × the garrison rate in cash, plus one lance per fee, and no garrison line under the fees at all. That is the servitium debitum's — the "service owed," a realm's fixed knight-quota — own arithmetic: a quota of knights, never a commuted garrison budget. His cost is the demesne income foregone (land+1 / land / land−1 per family at ACKS RAW revenues, land−4 / land−5 / land−6 customary — in his hands the garrison is paid in cash); the service he receives is the holder's market rate (plus the fosterage squire) — and the fee's two readings agree by construction: N whole fees owe N 100-gp lances, and the anchor is N × 100 (only the half-fee rides above its 50, at history's 60), so the retainer-equivalent is the same figure whether the card counts one graded holder or the quota's lances — and under other definitions of record the identity holds at their own body-price, exactly so under the Survey's 60. At wage-parity fees his net is families × the garrison rate (2/3/4), less the grant's small rounding pad (3–8 gp): the surplus of enfeoffment is the garrison bill he no longer pays. That is why the deal is stable from both sides — the man can get no better wage elsewhere, and the lord turns a profit at every rung, deepest on the frontier where garrisons cost most. It is also why frontier lords historically seeded knights along the marches.

    Three more load-bearing integration points. Tribute: assessed once, in cash, on the lord's whole realm (18 × families0.6, RR p.343–4); knights owe service, not coin, so there is no per-fee tribute line — the same lance garrisons the fee and answers the lord's call. This is doctrine (see the ⚖ rulings table, Library), but RAW rewards it twice over: the tribute formula was never calibrated below ~100 families (at ACKS RAW revenues a 12-family fee would hand over 74% of its income; at the customary rent the 25-family fee owes 124% of its income and the formula does not merely bite, it breaks), and cash tribute decays with vassal count — Tribute Inefficiency (RR p.347) hands the collectors a third of every payment at 9–16 vassals, half at 17–63, and 99% in the Drakomir example's 21,600 — while service in kind never passes through a collector's hands. Only ≤8 vassals pay in full, and that band coincides with the henchman cap: RAW's own economics wants the feudal shape — a handful of sworn tribute-vassals, and below them, men who pay in person. Density: by c.1300 England ran ~1 knight's fee per ~170 recorded entries — about 68 families at the 2.5 convention, which against a customary fee of 25 families says the crown, church and demesne held roughly two thirds un-enfeoffed (dubbed knights were rarer still) — the drivers were demesne retention, the fragmentation of fees, and the fact that a fee's land fed many more households than the one that named it; many fees were held by scutage-paying esquires, widows, and wards — the demesne share — what fraction of a realm its lord keeps in hand rather than enfeoffing — is exactly that dial. This page does not model it: every rung here prices a fee that is enfeoffed and is manned, one at a time. A realm's knight-density is the Judge's own decision, and the historical band is roughly a third to a half of the land enfeoffed, the rest held by crown, church, and demesne. The levy: ACKS's militia rules (2 per 10 families, qualifying numbers, kit and skills passed to heirs — RR p.432) are the Assize of Arms of 1181 in game form — and at land 6 under ACKS RAW revenues the rungs' heavy-foot yeomen even count 0/1/2/4 on the ½/1/2/4-fee rungs, an echo of the statute's hauberk-per-fee scaling (a resonance, not a cross-check — the statute armed the knight, not his ploughmen, and at the customary rent the same land value reads 1/2/5/10 and the echo goes; see the cross-checks table). The module writes this into the assize of the fee on every card — the levy as a term of enfeoffment, audited by the twice-yearly view of arms (Winchester 1285) that the Offices section’s inspection delegation already staffs — and prices default: a fee that lets its levy lapse is quit for the lance only, hiring its watch until it re-arms. And the qualifying numbers enforce the deepest structural rule: the first levied heavy horseman needs a 60-family pool, so the levy cannot make a knight — knights are made by land, footmen by levy.

    Scutage — the quittance run backward

    The fee's standing deal is a coin-obligation discharged by service; scutage is the same equivalence exercised the other way, for the term — the year’s month of service discharged in coin (both directions are printed in the one entry, RR p.346). In the two-colored ledger the fee changes color for one war: its render arrives as coin, and the lord hires a replacement into the host. The exchange always trades down — the lawful floor is the Call-to-Arms quota (1 gp/family, p.346), the market replacement is a 60-gp heavy horseman, and what the host lost was a 100–400 gp wage-grade veteran — which is why lords prefer the men, and why the rates ratcheted for two centuries. Two things scutage never buys out: the assize (readiness is a condition of the tenure, not of a campaign — the view of arms runs regardless), and the XP ledger ("scutage does not count as domain income for XP purposes," p.346 — the coin as XP-inert as the service it replaces).

    Two instruments wear the one word, and this module prices both. RAW's scutage (p.346) is a tax on a tribute vassal: 1 gp per family in his realm, payable every month until the duty is revoked, imposable more than once, and — the clause that governs everything below — it counts as garrison expense for the vassal who pays it. The fee's scutage is a different animal with the same name: a commutation of a standing tenurial service, the year's month of service discharged in coin. The realm is taxed; the fee commutes. Both are printed in the one entry, which is why they are so easily run together — and the realm's monthly form is priced where it belongs, on the vassals card of Feudal Realms, not here.

    Why the fee's render is quantized to the year's month, and why that is not mere smoothing. RAW's monthly rate never travels alone: it is netted against the 2 gp/family garrison line every domain owes (p.341), which is what makes a standing monthly charge bearable at all. A fee has no such line left. It was made quit of its garrison at enfeoffment, by the service itself — the quittance, argued in the ⚖ table on Feudal Manors — so the offset RAW pairs with the monthly rate has already been spent. Carry the monthly rate onto a fee anyway and four things break at once. The fee pays twice for one obligation, in service year-round and in coin every month. The coin/service equivalence collapses, and with it the quota ledger, which rests on a lance and its commutation being the same debt settled two ways. The rate lever inverts: at twelve times the annual figure the RAW anchor would overtop even the requirement in full, so full replacement — the setting that is supposed to be the dear one, the counterfactual where nobody commutes — would become the cheapest on the dial, and the lever would argue the opposite of the history it was built to model. And it would price out scutage's own clientele: the wardships, widows and infirm of the next paragraph are precisely the fees that cannot field a body, and a monthly charge would swallow the minority's whole income — turning the quittance's lawful patch for the incapable into the fastest way to lose the land. The division is doctrine and says so; the quantization is what the quittance leaves behind.

    Who pays it is the elegant part: the scutage-payer's lance stays home, so the natural clientele is history's own — wardships, widows, dotards, the infirm: fees that cannot currently deliver a man. That is the quittance's lawful patch for the minority — the wardship pays coin until the heir can ride, the tenure never lapses, and the manor's watch is meanwhile the best-kept in the realm — its levy and household never leave the yard (the Household muster prices this literally: set the assize serjeants to remain, and the whole obligation settles in coin with no body riding — scutage buys out deployment, never readiness). The household inner circle rides, for their bond is the service (priced, at last, in the Muster section); scutage is the instrument of the enfeoffed mass and the incapable. Commutation also has a geography the model predicts: the quittance amortizes as manors mature (the three counts of a fee, History chapter, Library), so scutage takes hold first in the old, dense core while the young march fees keep real service — and the record agrees: scutage clustered in the settled heartland, and the marches kept genuine knight-service longest. And at realm scale it is the era table's dial: one commuted campaign is a footnote, but a realm where scutage becomes the norm has slid from the distraint century into the indenture century (the era table, History chapter, Library) — service melting into coin, on schedule. The module does not forbid the slide; it prices it and names the destination. Scutage works here as what it was: the escape valve whose overuse is the end of the system.

    What the fee buys that coin cannot

    An army in being, not an army in waiting. In RAW an army is not decided into existence — it is recruited: each realm holds a finite crop of every mercenary type, surfaced only by paid searching and replenished on the scale of seasons (RR p.428). The crops are small — a barony's crop contains no heavy horseman at all, and even a kingdom's 680 heavy horse take three seasons to muster — and the Judges Journal's recruitment vagaries can double the price or empty the market outright. Coin stores value, not readiness. The fee is the period's own solution: it plants a warrior tradition that maintains itself — the knight sits armed, mounted, and obliged on his own ground; his heir squires out and comes home trained; his yeomen pass kit and skills to their sons (RR p.432). A lord of enfeoffed fees rides the week the beacon lights, at the strength the manors price; his cash-rich neighbor is still paying finding fees to learn what troops exist.

    And the realm it builds feels heroic — on purpose. Run a realm's military surplus through fees instead of wage-troops and its host fills with leveled men: banners of L1–L5 knights fight as heroic units among the companies of foot (RR p.466), worth several times their weight in hired horse. In peacetime those same men are out and about — errantry, tournament, escort, feud — because a fee obliges a man, not a garrison post. This is true to the period, and it is a dial on tone: an ACKS campaign run on knightly manors drifts toward Arthurian epic — named riders on every field, and adventure quartered in every manor.

    Fidelity — whose man is he?

    RAW grades a lord's men by their bond, and every loyalty score takes the lord's CHA on top — p.166 applies Charisma to all loyalty scores alike; it is no henchman perk. Nor is base 0 — the same page starts "most henchmen, mercenaries, specialists, and followers" there, so 0 is the default and every −2 in what follows is a penalty some rule has attached. The henchman vassal (base 0) is the household officer — but a lord holds at most 4 + CHA henchmen, so the inner circle is small: the banneret, the castellan, the marshal. At 9th level with a stronghold a magnate attracts companions (RR p.334–6): L1–3 men who "function as henchmen for all purposes" including vassalage, occupy no henchman slot, and start at +2 loyalty — the crown's and the earls' instrument for seating household knights on fees. The dubbed fee-holder stands at base 0 by the knight's contract (⚖ table, Library): the loyalty rides the fee and its service — hold by knight-service and keep the assize, and the base is 0 whoever inherited. The contract grants him no bonus; it declines p.347's −2, exactly as RAW itself declines it for senatorial republics, holding their vassal-rulers at 0 instead of −2 because the institution, not the person, commands the loyalty (p.355). Outside it — the esquire, and the fee in default of its service — stands the plain non-henchman vassal (RR p.347): base loyalty −2, and −4 if his manor lies beyond the range of trade of the lord's largest town (the range itself: JJ p.203 — the trade maps double as loyalty maps). His fee's service still stands — that rides the tenure, not the bond (⚖ the fee's service stands because the fee stands) — but nothing else does: beyond the reserved service he is p.347's non-henchman at one duty per favor, none free, so everything the lord wants above the charter must be continuously bought with good lordship — gifts, offices, monopolies, marriages. The term divides the tiers, too: the household rides without limit — that bond is the oath, not the fee (its price: the Muster section) — while the enfeoffed mass owes the year's month of service, then wages. The negative scores are the medieval texture: enfeoffed fidelity was contractual, not devotional — homage, distraint, and forfeiture all exist because enfeoffed men defaulted. And a pillaged fee is an unpaid knight (going without wages is a calamity → loyalty roll), so frontier defeats cascade into treason exactly as they should.

    Fosterage is where loyalty above the floor is made. The knight's contract is deliberately impersonal: base 0 comes with the fee and its service, whoever holds it and however he came to it. The tiers above that floor — household henchman, companion — are personal bonds, and fosterage is the manufactory: the heir squired out at ~14 — up the ladder, into the hall of his father's own lord — comes home a made man of that household, eligible to be taken as henchman or companion. History ran the same direction, and by law where it mattered most: wardship made custody of the minor heir, and of his marriage, an incident of the tenure itself — the orphaned boy was raised in his lord's hall, and the heiress's husband was that hall's choice. Even the nursery of loyalty rode the fee. A realm that stops fostering keeps its base-0 contract knights; what it loses is the next reign's supply of men worth more than the minimum — the fosterage lever is fidelity manufacture as much as XP delivery. And the better bonds cannot scale: the henchman cap holds the hall to 4 + CHA sworn men, so a baron takes his castellans and double-fee knights as henchmen and they hold the bachelors — subinfeudation (RR p.343, the Quintus example) is the only legal shape for a realm of sworn men. Knightly Realms solved the same scarcity the other way: banners of fifteen fees organized as micro-senates (RR p.355), knights voting, base loyalty 0 — equally RAW. Choose by flavor: the household, or the hundred-court.

    The supply of boys — and why they pool. MODULE The doctrine table rules that all knights may squire and that the binding constraint is the supply of boys (⚖ squire = watch & train). Here is the arithmetic behind it, with its inputs on the table, because it is a derivation from assumptions and must not borrow the record's authority. In a stationary population the knightly class holds roughly 7 × k ÷ G boys of squiring age per fee: a seven-year window (14–21), a generation length G ≈ 30, and k ≈ 1.4 sons reaching adolescence for each one that inherits — which is what a class carrying ~20% failure of male lines per generation must produce to hold station. That is about one boy for every three fees, and the plausible parameter box runs 0.20–0.56. The third digit is not the point and should not be quoted: every plausible input gives well under one boy per lance, and canon's spear assesses exactly one — paper against muster, arriving from a third independent direction.

    And the scarce boys cluster — which the record confirms, with one correction to where. HISTORY If supply is the binding constraint, henchman-squires should pool on the knights who can license them — and three independent sources say they did. History: placement ran up the ladder, into great halls — the royal court, earls, bishops, substantial barons — which functioned as the training schools of the class, best attested for the 13th–15th centuries, this module's distraint-era target. The word itself: Edward IV's Black Book of the Household (c.1471–2) establishes "Henxmen" — young gentlemen educated in the royal household — under a salaried Master of Henchmen who taught them riding, arms and manners; ACKS's term and the medieval institution are the same word for the same thing, and the institution is a household one. Canon, independently: Kaldor 17's royal salary table carries a Master of Squires at 324d/mo — above a Constable of Keeps at 300d, on canon's own chart, no exchange rate required — and, in the same table, "Squires (unpaid)". Columbia put the Black Book's structure in the royal household without comment: an officer to run the boys, and the boys on no wage, which is the module's his wage is his education confirmed from outside. ⚠ The correction: they cluster on households, not on incomes. p.168 licenses a henchman at income ≥ 50% of wage, which every rung of the ladder clears — so the rule spreads squires across essentially all fee-holders, while the record pools them in a few dozen great halls and leaves most landed knights with none. Read p.168 as necessary, not sufficient: income licenses a boy, standing and a hall attract one. The mean of ~1 boy per 3 fees is right for the realm and wrong as a picture — the distribution is skewed, not spread. That is a shape consequence, not only a level one: a boy in the earl's hall stands the castle's watch, not a manor's, so watch-and-train value concentrates where the boys are and does not spread evenly over manors, which is exactly what a flat +45 per lance assumes. Recorded as a known simplification rather than fixed, because fixing it means modelling household placement — and the mechanism that would do it is wardship, already in this module, since a ward is the lord's charge by law and the law is what moves the boys upward.

    Levels drive everything — and the XP loop closes

    The rung sizes are retention prices: the fee that matches a level's wage. ACKS's XP rules then close the career loop — and the dubbing decides which ledger his land grows him on. A dubbed knight is on the knight's contract (⚖ table, Library): his expected wage comes off domain income before the XP threshold applies (RR p.342 + Major Errata r4; the wage is "expected" — imputed whether or not coin changes hands), so his fee raises him to one level below what it retains — the bachelor's fee pays an L3 but only grows an L2 under either reading, since both sides of that comparison are wage grades and neither is a family count — and the last level must be won in the field. The esquire, undubbed, keeps RAW's plain vassal ledger (income − threshold, p.423) and ploughs to his fee's full grade — the one man on the ladder whom land alone completes, in four or five quiet years. Fosterage is how the field reaches the heir before he inherits either way: squired out at ~14, he comes home L1–L2 and grows into his grade. Domain XP alone is glacial — which is the correct result: knights are made by war; the fee only keeps them. (Why the esquire's exemption is no favor to the knights, and what it produces, is the Library’s History chapter’s distraint section.)

    The threadbare fee — below parity

    What happens when a fee's income slips under its holder's wage — the manor pillaged, the land value fallen, a line seated above its means? Not a vanishing. RAW already prices the state as a gradient: income below the expected wage is the "without wages" calamity (p.166–7), and a calamity forces a loyalty roll, decaying the score by −1 each time — a slow bleed, not a cliff. The fidelity tier is the tolerance dial: the sworn knight at base 0 absorbs shortfalls that would break a −2 stranger, and the household man rides them out longest — good lordship is measured in the arrears a man will bear. Meanwhile the manor pays part of his rank in kind: RAW's living-expenses list counts an implicit rent of 1/33 of the stronghold's value, the servants, the stabling (p.173) — which is why a threadbare knight lives like a richer man than his ledger shows, and clings to land no wage table justifies. Held long enough, sub-parity resolves the way the retaining rule says: the line slides down the kit ladder — the destrier unaffordable, the mail unrenewed — until the manor keeps an esquire in a knight's hall. That slide is distraint's whole clientele: men on knight's land, below knight's estate, dodging a rank they can no longer carry. The poor knight is not an exception the model tolerates; he is a state it prices.

    History — the anchors, the cross-checks, the record HISTORY

    How history is used here

    History enters this module as consistency checks, never as input: the rung sizes were derived from the ACKS wage table alone, then checked against the medieval record — corroboration where they land, not proof. This chapter holds the record side — the anchors, the cross-checks, the century readings, the deliberate departures — and grades every claim by how hard its source is. Three grades recur: table-verified (checked cell-by-cell against ACKS II's printed tables, 2nd printing plus Major Errata r4), statute / record (a dated instrument of the period, with manuscript variance disclosed where it exists), and scholarship (standard secondary figures, flagged where not independently re-verified). The full grading sits in Sources & confidence at the bottom — no two claims here are asserted at the same strength unless they deserve it.

A typical English manor of 20–40 recorded entries is 8–16 families, which brackets the customary esquire's half-fee (15) and sits below the bachelor's (25). Estate-bannerets held £100–200/yr — 5–10× the £20 fee, 2.5–5× the £40 distraint line; this rung is 3.75×, inside the band. Men of this weight also filled the great ministerial posts — constable of a royal castle, sheriff — but the office was a revocable commission, staffed from this bench precisely because the fief made its man worth commissioning. (RAW prices office-holding separately — see the Offices section: magistrates at 12.5% of the lines they oversee, RR p.342; the fee-farm pole maps onto the Judges Journal's landowner/governor split, JJ p.405–6 — the fixed-render farm itself is the module's historical gloss on it.) "Banneret" here is a role, not a rank — the senior knight entrusted with a banner — which is also the historically correct usage: banneret was a battlefield promotion (cutting the pennon square), not a peerage.

Knighthood ends exactly where lordship begins, in both systems, independently.

"The £↔gp ratio (£20 ↔ 100 gp)" is not a coin rate at all: it is an identification of the module's bachelor's fee with the historical £20 fee, and the two are not the same estate — at the declared rate the £20 fee is about 10 families and 40 gp/mo, while a customary bachelor's fee is 25 families and 100, and the module's fee is deliberately 2.5× the benchmark. The rate itself is £1 = 24 gp, declared once in Money and derived from RAW's coin table and the designer's penny equivalence — neither of them chosen here, and neither of them fitted to this table.

    Comparison — Cuxham, Oxfordshire

    None of the module's numbers were tuned to Cuxham. The rung family counts were derived from the ACKS wage table before this example was chosen; what follows sets a real manor beside the model. One case is a comparison, not a calibration. One real manor, walked end to end. Cuxham is the best-documented small manor in England — P.D.A. Harvey's A Medieval Oxfordshire Village (1965) rests on a near-continuous run of account rolls kept after Walter de Merton bought the manor (1268) for the college that bears his name. Before that it was an ordinary gentry estate of the honour of Wallingford: Foliots from before 1166, then Chenduits, then sold to pay a knight's debts. Every figure below is from the modern VCH Oxfordshire (2016), which digests Harvey's own tables; the one thing open sources could not settle is graded as such.

That count is a holdings count, so it does not convert — but the module's own side does: at the customary rent 23 families is just under a single knight's fee (25). What is not reconciled here is 13 cottagers against 8 cottages, and this module has not gone back to the manorial rolls to settle it. It is flagged rather than smoothed, because the one thing a comparison table must not do is make two sources agree by choosing a word. And the well-documented £40 years are the Merton College years: an institutional demesne under exceptional management, in precisely the phase when Cuxham supported no knight. The disclaimer at the head of this section is the important one, and it is repeated here on purpose: these figures were never a target the module was fitted to.

    Source typing — why every count on this page now names its unit

    "Recorded household" is retired as a general term. Use recorded entry. A Domesday entry can be a tenant holding, a household head, a smallholding, a dependant, or a servus counted individually. They are not one observation type, and calling them all households smuggles a conversion into the noun — which is exactly how this page came to publish a 5.6× gap that was really 2.25×, by dividing the module's income by ACKS families and the record's by entries.

    The convention, and the scope rule that bounds it. One ACKS peasant family ≈ 2.5 recorded entries; the band is 1.5–3.5. Apply it when converting a source that counts people under a roof. Never apply it to a source that counts holdings. Never apply it inside the engine — it lives at the point of citation and nowhere else, which is why no computed field on this page contains the number 2.5. MODULE
