    Six fields, not a number. Every comparison in this Library carries raw count · source unit · conversion · converted range · date · numerator definition. Worked, for the row above:

    Cuxham, 1086 — raw count 15 recorded entries, mixed status · conversion 1.5–3.5 entries per tenement · converted 4.3–10 families, central 6 · lordly value £6 · numerator whole-manor value, Domesday valuation

    Propagate the range, not the point. 2.5 is a central estimate. A card that says "£0.80 per entry" where the underlying band spans £0.57–£1.33 is claiming a precision the conversion cannot carry. The customary rent's calibration lands on £0.80 as a chosen point inside a wide range — the evidence itself runs £0.40 (Cuxham 1086) to £1.74 (Cuxham, 13th-c. tenants against 14th-c. profit). No comparison made across this conversion may be called an exact match; the strongest available verdict is lands inside the band.

    Two things Cuxham's figures need said on their face, both visible in the table above. First, the 23-tenant count is 1279 and the ~£40 net profit is chiefly early-14th-century accounting: dividing one by the other is a cross-period ratio and must say so on its face. Second, that £40 is a whole-manor numerator — directly farmed demesne, tenant rents and works, mill and appurtenances, market sales. It can benchmark total estate return; it cannot by itself set the service and tax lines, and the service-1 argument does not lean on it.

    The diagnostic, if you are ever unsure whether a conversion has been applied twice: any figure implying more than about 30 acres per recorded entry has had the convention misapplied. 15–25 acres is a correct mixed manor of yardlanders, half-yardlanders and cottars; 47–60 means it was applied to a tenement count that was already right; 120–150 means a tenement count has been divided.

    The three counts of a fee — grant, stock, fragment

    Ask "how many families is a knight's fee?" and the record returns three numbers — 12, 20, 23. They are one process observed at three moments, and each count has its own derivation. 12 is the grant floor — the least the grant can be: wage-parity (100 gp ÷ 9 gp/family at ACKS RAW revenues; 25 families at the customary rent, and the three counts below are a ratio argument that survives either), the leanest estate that retains its knight. The floor is where the lord's incentive points, since every family enfeoffed is demesne alienated forever — and the record shows grants trending toward it: Domesday's milites on 1.5–2 hides, the Cartae Baronum's "new enfeoffment" fees running smaller than the old, new fees carved from waste and march-land as territory to grow into. A young fee under-fills its assessment — tilling ~360 of the notional 600 acres — exactly as Domesday manors did (Cuxham, above: 15 recorded entries in 1086). 20 is the stocked survey: the 5-hide fee divided into whole holdings — 600 geld-acres at the virgate every full peasant household tills, and RAW's own farm agrees: 30 acres per family (JJ p.406; the 20-crop + 10-fallow maths of JJ p.434 is the virgate), so 600 ÷ 30 = 20. A ceiling of whole holdings, not a headcount — the assessor's idealization, exactly as notional as the 120-acre hide itself. 23 is the standing manor: population keeps growing after the slots fill, so the slots themselves split — virgates halve into half-yardlands, cottagers settle the margins with a garden and their labor — and households multiply past the virgater ceiling while each grows poorer. The manor's income rises through it: more rents and court profits from more heads, and above all the demesne worked cheap by the labor the crowding created (Cuxham 1279: 3 free tenants, ~7 half-yardlanders, 13 cottagers — 23 households, double-fee income, rents a mere £5 of the ~£60 gross; the rest was the demesne's corn).

    The three counts of a fee — grant, stock and fragment, stage by stage
    StageFamiliesSettled groundOf a 6-mi hexTilledDensity reading
    Granted12~640 ac settled of a ~1,060-ac territory3.2% settled — ~5% with its waste360 ac — 60% of capacity~88 ac/fam on the full territory — toward the outlands end
    Stocked20~1,060 ac5.3% (≈ 0.85 of a 1.5-mi hex)600 ac — every virgate whole53 ac/fam — the borderlands constant exactly
    Fragmented23+~1,060 ac + assarts~5.5%~600 ac, subdivided — half-yardlands of 15, cottages of scraps≈46 ac/fam and falling — drifting to the civilized end, where Cuxham sits

    All three counts are correct answers to different questions — what does the lord grant? what does the survey idealize? who actually lives there? To pick one and call the others wrong is to mistake a process for a quantity. The counts also read as a wealth dial: land-rich yeomen at the grant, the standard-holding ideal at stock, a full manor of poor households under a rich lord at fragmentation. Per-family revenue holds near RAW's standard throughout, because the ACKS family is a revenue unit, not a holding size — the cottar delivers his value through the demesne's wage-book rather than his own plough — which is why the family-count keeps working exactly where holding-counts break down.

    The dial turns itself. Read the last column again: grant → stock → fragment walks the density dial — outlands → borderlands → civilized — on one estate, over two centuries. And RAW walks alongside: a domain advances in class at these same thresholds — 185 families makes borderlands, 375 civilized, given a road, a nearby town, and morale (p.340) — so the classes are earned by stocking plus connection, not painted on the map. The era table below is that same walk read as history; the density lever in the Dials section is the same walk read as geography. And the walk does mechanical work. The quittance amortizes: at the civilized reading, full militia credit alone equals land+3 by RAW, so the module's one structural break — largest at the grant, ~2 gp/family on a raw march — has decayed to zero by the time the manor is old: a founder's subsidy that expires, not a standing tax. Commutation becomes endogenous: as the quittance's value fades and the levy pool grows, the old dense core is exactly where service-in-kind stops paying and scutage begins, while young march fees keep real service — and the record agrees: scutage clustered in the settled heartland, and the marches kept genuine knight-service longest. A realm, finally, is a portfolio of stages — grant-stage marches reading outlands, an old core reading civilized — which is what the density lever's "settled-hex, never a national average" caveat means in time as well as space. One boundary rides along: RAW's class has a danger face (the garrison rate) as well as a density face (the caps); the arc walks the density face, and the danger face follows only as the march pacifies around the fee — the two usually travel together, since no one stocks a manor under active raids, but a dense fee on a hot border is dense and dangerous. Assarting likewise stretches the footprint and slows the walk. This is a reading of RAW's classes, not a discovery inside them — but what it produces is the module's strongest kind of claim: played forward, domain-seasons deliver the eras in sequence, no dial set by hand — the dynamics reproducing the record's order, not merely its states.

    The era table — the ladder read as history, dial the century

    The rungs are ranks at any one moment; they are also the path the knightly class itself climbed across three centuries. Each era of English knighthood sits at a different setting of the module's dials — land value, grant size, household-versus-enfeoffed mix, and how much of the render is commuted to coin. The ladder prices eras as readily as ranks.

    The era table — each century of English knighthood as a setting of these dials
    EraThe knight of the recordOn this ladderThe dials
    Post-Conquest
    1066–1100    		 Harvey's ordinary miles: a mailed professional barely above the peasantry, many still quartered in the lord's hall; fees of 1.5–2 hides (~200 acres) 4–6 families, 24–42 gp — F0–L1: sub-floor half-fees on wasted land; the esquire's fee is their settled descendant — the Domesday miles was an esquire in all but name Land 3–4 (war-wasted in the harried shires, pre-clearance everywhere); small grants; almost all household tier — first-generation henchman bonds, castle-guard raw; assessments fresh — the Survey itself is one
    Norman & Angevin
    12th century    		 The hall empties onto the land; the fee quotas crystallize (Cartae Baronum — the barons' 1166 returns listing their knights' fees); scutage (attested from Henry I) becomes the commutation lever; kit inflates until knighthood is an income class — the £20 income yardstick itself is the next century's, born with income-based distraint (1241) The bachelor rung fills: L2–L3; the 100-gp veteran floor emerges as the rank's running cost Land climbs with clearance and peace; second-generation heirs pass from the household circle to the knight's contract — base 0 riding the fee, the personal bond gone; fosterage develops as the manufactory of the next household men; the cartae freeze the counts — the first margins open (assessments ancient)
    The distraint century

    A campaign can therefore set its century. Post-Conquest is this module at poor land and small household grants; the high ladder is the thirteenth century; a realm that commutes to scutage and indenture is the fifteenth. The dials hold the eras apart in combination too: a 40-family estate at land 6 seats an L4 county knight; at land 3 it can still pay an L4 but no longer grows one; and seating an L2 on it builds a thirteenth-century estate under a Domesday-grade man — an estate two centuries older than its holder, a pairing the record never produced. The one thing the ladder refuses to model is the divorce of fee from knight — fees fragmenting into tenths and fortieths, held by heiresses, wards, and burgesses — which the record shows happening from the mid-13th century on. That history is not denied; it is dialed: the demesne share — the Judge's own — and the scutage section are where it lives.

    The lance, before and after — a vocabulary note that doubles as a cross-check

    The module's lance is the earlier, informal sense: the knight himself, his fostered squire, the remounts. The fifteenth century wrote the word into statute — the Burgundian lance fournie (1468: a man-at-arms, a coustillier, a page; the Ordinance of Abbeville, 1471: those three plus three mounted archers and three foot) — and the paybook, read against this module, corroborates three of its rulings from the far end of the arc. The page rode unpaid and out of the line — the squire-as-train ruling, in a state document. The fighting second rider — the coustillier: brigandine, light lance, the langue-de-bœuf at his belt — was a separately paid combatant, never the boy: the module's split between the fostered squire and the fighting man-at-arms, kept by a quartermaster. And the nine-man lance is recognizably the fee’s month-of-service muster written into a paybook — knight, squire, and trained yeomen re-purchased as man-at-arms, page, archers, and foot once tenure had melted to coin: the era table's slide, visible in a single unit's roster. The missing link is the 1351 French ordinance's gros valet — the armed servant in a habergeon — the threshold's armed servant on his way to becoming a paid line. One rule keeps count and crew straight, there and here: the ordinance counted lances, and the coustillier rode inside one — nine men, one lance. The quota counts the same way: a double fee owes two lances, and built Burgundian-fashion that is two men-at-arms, two coustilliers, two pages, counting as exactly two — the crew multiplies with the count, never against it. (Kaldor sits in the distraint century; ordinance vocabulary appears on this page only where flagged — the Muster section’s coustillier gloss points here.)

    Distraint — the word, precisely

    The module leans on this word, so define it. Distraint is the period's ordinary legal remedy: the seizure of a man's goods — chattels driven off, profits impounded — to compel performance of an obligation, no court judgment required, only the right. The assize is enforced by it (a defaulted fee is distrained at the view); so are rents, suits, and services of every kind. Distraint of knighthood is that remedy pointed at rank: from 1224 the crown ordered sheriffs to distrain fee-holders, and from 1241 any man of £20/yr in land (later £40), until they took up the arms and dubbing of a knight — compulsion by inconvenience, with respite purchasable by fine (the Fine Rolls carry the receipts). In the module's terms — a reading the module makes, not language any writ used — it is two resets in one: an income instrument that taxes the assessment lag without resurveying the manor, and a definition reset that forces the current standard of knighthood — kit, harness, and ledger — onto the man himself (the definition lever, Dials section). The record shows the income instrument plainly; the definition reset is the module's synthesis of what the compulsion did. The next section shows why the crown needed it.

    The esquire's ledger — distraint of knighthood, out of the arithmetic

    This section documents the module's strangest convergence, because it is easy to miss and it is among the strongest evidence the reconstruction has: the rules generate, rather than assume, the central social drama of the thirteenth century. Under the knight's contract (⚖ table, Library), the dubbing is a real exchange. The dubbed man's expected wage comes off his domain income before the XP threshold, so his fee grows him only to one level below its grade — the last level must be won in the field — and in return his base loyalty rises from a stranger's −2 to a sworn man's 0. The esquire signs nothing: RAW's plain vassal ledger applies, nothing is deducted, and his fee completes him — the £24 man ploughs to L2 in four or five quiet years, the only figure on the ladder whom land alone finishes.

    Now price the choice as a man on a £20 fee would price it. Take the spurs, and you accept slower growth, a war-debt for your final level, mail and remounts to maintain, and a bond that binds you closer to your lord's call. Refuse them, and your estate finishes you by itself while your obligations stay a plain vassal's. Any rational fee-holder dodges the dubbing — and that is precisely what the record shows: knightly numbers falling through the thirteenth century, men in knight's harness on knight's incomes declining the rank, until the crown began compelling them to take it up (distraint of knighthood — addressed to fee-holders from 1224, to £20 incomes from 1241). In the module's terms, the crown's side of the ledger explains the compulsion: it is not buying the man's prowess — he fights in the same harness either way — it is buying the contract: the sworn base-0 loyalty and the priced, auditable service package that the plain vassal never owes. The record adds two threads the module does not price, and they only deepen the story: the crown happily sold exemption — fines for respite of knighthood were a revenue stream in their own right — and men fled the rank as much from its administrative burdens as from its cost, for juries, the grand assize, coroners' and tax commissions all fell on the county's knights. Refusing an honor because it is priced like an office: the module and the record agree on the behavior.

    How much of this was designed in? Less than it looks, but not none. The parts are all RAW's — the wage deduction is the henchman-vassal clause (p.342, in its errata'd form); the loyalty step rests on RAW's own precedent that an institution can hold non-henchman vassals at base 0 (p.355 — written for republics, transplanted here to tenure by knight-service, ⚖ table); the thresholds are the p.423 table — and no distraint rule was written anywhere: men dodge the dubbing because the arithmetic pays them to, and the crown compels because it cannot afford the dodge. Both transplanted clauses were chosen with this history in view, so the claim carries a condition: take these two transplants, each made on RAW-precedent grounds, and the century follows. It also follows by different means than it did in England — XP and loyalty in the model, respite fines and jury burdens in the record — so what comes back is the pressure, not the paperwork. Still, a wage table has no opinion about knighthood, and run forward it returns men refusing an honor and a crown with cause to compel them. The compulsion itself is no mechanic — it is lordship, done with the module's own instruments: dubbing written into the grant, required at succession before homage is taken, or excused for a respite fine. The rest of this chapter checks the model against numbers; this section checks it against behavior — and behavior is the harder test.

    The recovered layer — bastard feudalism and the affinity

    The politics below the chroniclers' eye-line has a name: since K.B. McFarlane (1945 on) historians call it bastard feudalism DEBATED — lordship exercised through retained men rather than tenure: annuities, livery, and maintenance in place of homage and land. It was recovered late for a concrete reason — high politics survives in chronicles, while the gentry's world survives in court rolls, deeds, and private letters, and only 20th-century county studies (Carpenter on Warwickshire, Saul on Gloucestershire, Wright on Derbyshire) rebuilt the picture shire by shire. One structural fact drives it: power was personal, not institutional — no police, no bureaucracy at the village, royal courts that could not enforce their own judgments — so protection and justice were private goods, produced by networks of lordship. From that the whole economy follows: a market in good lordship (protection, offices, and backing at law, traded for service, counsel, and presence); livery as the advertisement of whose man would come if you were crossed — legislated against from 1390 precisely because it was load-bearing; arbitration and the loveday settling most disputes under the implicit weight of both parties' followings; and worship — standing — as the network's credit rating. The texture survives best in the Paston letters: Margaret Paston sending for crossbows to hold a manor house, the Duke of Norfolk besieging Caister (1469) over an inheritance, a rising family's frantic shopping for a lord great enough to protect it. Nibley Green (1470) — two retinues settling a Berkeley inheritance by pitched battle — and Sir Thomas Malory, the chivalric author indicted as ambusher and extortioner, mark the operating reality against the ideal.

    In the module's terms the era is a dial-state, not a new system: assessments ancient, the margin universal, and the obligation migrated from the enfeoffed population to the retained one — the Muster section prices the retained man, and the era table dates the slide. The comparative literature reads the same machine wherever the state runs thin — private protection generally (Gambetta's study of the Sicilian mafia is the nearly exact parallel), the political machine, the big-man polity (Sahlins) — with one break: the medieval bond was dressed in homage, law, and religion, and was thought legitimate. The engine — weak state → private protection → power measured in men → wealth that must become followers to be safe — is the same.

    The thread — land and lordship, coming apart

    The sections above — the era table's slide, distraint, the esquire's ledger, the recovered layer — and the esquire's rung on the Ladder are limbs of one thesis this chapter can now state in a sentence: the fee is the land half of a bundle coming apart, and the esquire is what a fee-holder looks like after it has. The feudal grant fused property with function — land carrying justice, service, and office. The centuries pull the halves apart, and always upward: the assizes draw pleas into the royal courts, scutage detaches the service as coin, distraint is the crown chasing men who keep knight's land while shedding the knight's function, and the affinity rebuilds lordship on retainer with no land in the bond at all. RAW tells the same story run in reverse (JJ p.407): republics set governors over landowners, the office's upkeep-lands turn hereditary, and the landed lord emerges — fusion on the way in; this chapter is the separation on the way out. The arc also explains a design choice: the module never applies the Judges Journal's landowner/governor split (JJ p.405–6) to the manor, because at manor scale the bundle never came apart — demesne, rents, and the manor court stayed fused in the lord of the manor into the modern era, while what separated migrated up to the crown, where the Offices section prices it.

    Hârn — the first application HÂRN

    This module was built for Hârn, and Hârn is also the test it had to pass. The arithmetic came from ACKS II and from English tenure; the setting was written decades ago by other people from other sources. Where the two agree, nothing here was tuned to make them — which is why this tab is evidence and not decoration. It runs in three parts: what canon's institutions turn out to be in the ladder's terms, the numbers at manor and kingdom scale, and canon's own two rules — a second tradition that assesses knight service exactly twice and leaves the two unreconciled, as this module does.

    Kaldor is modeled on 12th–13th-century England, so most of the fit is inheritance — the manors were derived from ACKS RAW, and Hârn's canon institutions land on their rungs without adjustment. In the era table's terms (History chapter, Library), Kaldor sits squarely in the distraint century: consolidated fees, honorable and costly dubbing, service still rendered in kind, and crown offices staffed from the great-fief bench. The density dial says the same thing a second way: Kaldor's 350 families per settled hex sits just below the borderlands cap — a realm still stocking, its marches active (the three counts of a fee, History chapter, Library) — which is exactly canon's Kaldor: colonized centuries ago, not yet full.

    Double fee (23 fam) at ACKS RAW    		 ⚠ The ordinary Hârnic manor is the single fee, and reading it as the double one is a revenue error rather than a setting fact. Canon’s 23–34 tenant households sit almost exactly on the customary single fee of 25 — so the ordinary Hârnic manor owes one knight, which is what Kaldor 21 says it owes. The margin that pays for squire, yeomen and remounts is the manor’s growth past that paper, not a second fee. See Canon’s two rules.
    Esquires (mostly unlanded household men)Esquire’s fee — 15 fam at the customary rent, 7 at ACKS RAW Canon Hârnic esquires serve in households; the esquire's fee seats a landed man-at-arms where the poorer marches want one — the constable's sergeant with dirt under his nails.
    Yeomen (double tenancy, 60 days' service, own kit)Trained militia ACKS trained militia to the letter — kit and skills pass to heirs (RR p.432), and their wage-value counts against the garrison even uncalled. The levy lines on every rung card ARE the yeomanry.
    Squires (fostered out at ~14 — canon practice)Watch & train — 45 gp wage-value Kitted as medium horse (knights ride heavy, mounted yeomen light) and worth 45 gp of wage-value in the lance's service — but in the line of battle he does not stand: squires are the lance's train. The fosterage lever is canon practice made mechanical.
    The great vassal knight (a multi-manor fief)Castellany — 100 fam at the customary rent, 45 at ACKS RAW Four fees in one pair of hands — the greatest man who is still anyone's knight: the old vassal family holding several manors of its baron or of the crown, inherited as one fief. Hârn's constables of royal castles are the neighboring, different thing — appointed officers, nearer sheriffs than lords — and crowns commission them from exactly this bench. When he leads a banner men call him a banneret: a role, not a rank. Hârn has no banneret rank, and neither does this module.
    The Hârnic baron (a handful of manors)The 160-family ceiling Demesne manors plus enfeoffed fees — how a real barony splits between them is the demesne share, and the barony floor values at ~13⅓ fees either way (cross-checks, History chapter, Library).

    The numbers — manor, then kingdom HÂRN

    Two scales, and the second is the one that matters. A single manor can be made to fit anything; a kingdom's whole fief table cannot. The manor below is the one canon itself chose to demonstrate its levy on, and the kingdom figures are measured off canon's tables by the tools in this folder rather than counted by hand, so that the parse and not a transcription is what the argument rests on.

    Worked example — Touvant Manor, canon's own pick

    Kingdom of Kaldor demonstrates its levy on a named manor (Kaldor 21): "The knight of Touvant Manor (Heru), has 2220 acres and thus owes 1mh (himself), 1lh (a squire), plus five yeomen (2mf and 3lf) and scutage for 120 acres." The fief table (Kaldor 30) fills in the rest: Endrunel Hundred, held in fee simple by clan Plaganel under Heru Keep and the Earl of Osel — 2,220 gross acres · land quality 1.21 · 37 households. Because canon chose this manor itself, running it through the module is a like-for-like test nobody picked for convenience.

    ⚠ Touvant is an illustration, and must not be used as the calibration. Among 574 individually-listed Kaldoric knight's manors — parsed from the subinfeudation pages, and a different corpus from the 686 manor rows counted for tenure below: this one is the manors with a knight attached, that one is every lay row in the fief tables — it sits at the 75th percentile for households, the 87th for acres and the 94th for land quality: a large, rich manor, and a poor single point to fit a rate to. The fit that matters is pooled. Across 64 holdings in three kingdoms — 50,758 households — the customary rent fits canon's own acreage rule at 0.99, and ACKS RAW revenues are excluded in every one of the 64. Nothing in the corpus comes within 1.66× of the RAW rate. The argument below rests on those 64 holdings; Touvant is where it can be watched working. HÂRN

    And Kaldor stays at land value 6. Canon grades Touvant's land 21% rich, which reads as a case for land 7 and is not one: no canon source ties service or scutage to land quality — only to gross acres — and land 7 makes the fit worse. Land quality does not enter.

    The acreage row below is the load-bearing one. Canon's 2,220 acres over 37 tenant holdings is 60 acres apiece, against this page's Kaldor dial of 57 — both sides are holdings, so the 2.5 convention does not apply and there is nothing to convert. Canon says so itself: Kaldor 22's legend reads "Each household averages 20 tenant acres." It is the single strongest canon check in the corpus, and it stands under either custom of record.

The example has the knight serve in person and commute only the 120-acre remainder — £1. The whole-manor £18.5 is this module's hypothetical, legitimate because Gardiren 29 permits full commutation, but it is not canon's valuation of anything. Priced in canon's own coin it is 4,440d a year against the 2,304d canon pays a medium-horse knight (Kaldor 17) — the buy-out costs about twice the man, which is exactly why canon shows the blend and not the buy-out DEBATED

    Same manor, two bookkeepings, one render: knight, squire, yeomen by size, coin for the fraction, a term counted in days. The one thing canon flattens that the module grades is the knight himself — canon mounts every manor's knight alike, while the module reads a 37-household estate as a weightier man (L4) than a 14-household one. The fief tables side with the grading in practice: constables and sheriffs are commissioned from exactly the multi-manor bench (see the castellany row above).

    Kaldor at kingdom scale

    Kaldor's ~17,000 families yield a feudal host of armored men in the meaningful hundreds — consistent with how the Kingdom of Kaldor module portrays its musters. A Kaldoric Succession Crisis tabulates the whole kingdom's feudal levy by shire (pp. 16–19, 64 rows): 636 knights, 545 lay and 91 church. Against that census, the customary rent puts the kingdom's capacity at 1.25–1.30× what canon actually enfeoffs; ACKS RAW revenues put it at 2.8–2.9×. A realm that has enfeoffed 80% of what it can bear is ordinary. One that has enfeoffed 35% is not. Manor acreage uses 57 acres per family for Kaldor against this page's baronial default of 47.

    ⚠ Hârn does not canonically run hot, and a reading that says it does is reading the revenue rate. Put ACKS RAW revenues on canon's ground and the module runs 2.23× above it — in all 64 holdings, across three kingdoms — which arrives looking like a setting that seats a knight on nearly every manor. It is not: it is the rate, wearing a setting explanation. Mind the unit on the other side of that comparison too: "1 fee per 170 households" is an English figure in recorded entries, which is about 68 families per fee — and since a customary fee is 25 families, that ratio says the crown, the church and the demesne held roughly two thirds un-enfeoffed, which is the standard picture rather than a contrast. HISTORY

    The tenure contrast is real; it is the magnitude that has to be got right. Across canon's own fief tables — 30 lay holdings, 686 manor rows, 20,049 households — Kaldor's enfeoffed clan manors carry 56% of listed households (423 of the rows, 62% counted by row), against England's roughly one third. Hârn really does carry more enfeoffed land per household than England did. What it does not carry is a knight on nearly every manor.
    ⚠ Both figures in that sentence are in stated units, and they are different units. The 56.1% is a household share; the 423 is a manor-row count — quoting them as though one were computed over the other is the mistake this row exists to prevent. Both come from the runnable parse of the fief tables rather than a hand count, and the parse names a fifth class a coarser reading folds away — hundred-moot vills, 3.9%, which are neither enfeoffed nor an officer's. The full split by households is enfeoffed 56.1 · liege-official 25.4 · keep demesne 13.6 · moot 3.9 · guild 1.1. HÂRN

    Canon's two rules — a second tradition with the same architecture HÂRN

    The strongest single piece of evidence on this page, and the reason the Hârn tab is not an appendix: canon assesses knight service two ways at once and never reconciles them — which is the module's charter-against-muster model, arrived at independently, decades earlier, from different sources.

    This module built charter against muster from English evidence and its own doctrine: a paper obligation fixed at a grant, and a countryside that grows away from it. That is an argument, and arguments can be convenient. So it is worth knowing that a second tradition — written decades later, by different authors, from different sources — contains the same architecture and quantifies the gap. Hârnic canon assesses knight service two ways, both live at once, and never reconciles them, because the tension is the point.

    Canon's two assessments of knight service, and the module's name for each
    CanonWhat it measuresThis module calls it
    The manor rule "each manor provides one knight… one squire" (Kaldor 21); "all manors can provide one knight and one squire" (Melderyn 29, the realm rule) — a headcount fixed by the unit of tenure, insensitive to yield the charter
    The acreage rule £1 per 120 acres, £10 per spear ⇒ 1 knight per 1,200 gross acres (Gardiren 29); "each listed settlement is obligated to provide one mounted knight… per 1,500 gross acres" (Chybisa 20) — an assessment on the resource, which re-counts as the land is measured the current assessment
    The gap between them the mean Kaldoric knight's manor runs 1,681 gross acres. Against the 1,200-acre spear that is 1.40, where the paper says 1 the margin — the grown manor

    The acreage rule closes on itself, which is how you know it is a rate and not a slogan. A light foot costs 300 gross acres (Kaldor 21). At £1 per 120 acres that is £2.50, and four of them are £10 — one spear, at Gardiren's own price. The £10 spear and the £1-per-120-acres scutage are one rate written twice, in two books, and they agree.

    ⚠ Melderyn's "roughly one knight per 1200 acres" is not a third acreage rule, and must not be cited beside Gardiren's 1,200 and Chybisa's 1,500. It is not a realm assessment. On Melderyn 29 that sentence belongs to the Order of the Lady of Paladins — "the keeps held by the Lady of Paladins have roughly one knight per 1200 acres plus one man-at-arms per 300 acres" — a single military order's garrison standard for its own two keeps. Melderyn's realm rule is on the same page and is a manor rule, already cited in the row above; measured against that page's own fief table (838 manors over 1,388,160 acres) Melderyn actually runs about 1,657 acres to the knight, which is looser than Gardiren's 1,200, not tighter. Two senses sit on one page, and only one of them is a realm density — a trap worth naming, because taking the wrong one imports a keep's garrison standard as a kingdom's assessment. HÂRN

    Two holdings where canon does the module's work for it

    Both are worked examples of machinery this page already ships, preserved in print with the dispute intact.

    Vemion — both rules applied to identical ground. Minarsas 29 assesses the holding at 120 spears. Kaldor 21 lists 60 manors for the same four holdings. The two books agree on the acreage — 133,700 — to the digit, and 133,700 ÷ 1,200 is 111. So one book is keeping the current assessment and the other the paper, on the same land, in the same century. That is the two-definition model the Muster section computes, sitting in canon as a discrepancy nobody resolved.

    Neph — three counts of one obligation, and canon names the deficit itself
    SourceCountThe module's word for it
    Gardiren 29, the levy table77what the muster actually produces
    The crown's obligation100the charter
    The acreage rule on 144,755 acres120.6the current assessment

    Muster < charter < current assessment — the module's exact ordering, and canon states the adequacy deficit in its own prose: "the earl does not have sufficient vassal knights to meet his full obligation" (Gardiren 29). The Muster section calls that the make-good, and prices the remedies. Canon leaves it standing, which is the more realistic ending.

    What this is evidence of, and what it is not

    It is not independent evidence about England. HârnManor was itself built from English manorial data, so both traditions descend from one source and cannot confirm each other about the record. What it is: two systems built from that tradition, decades apart, arriving at the same architecture — a fixed paper obligation, a resource assessment that outgrows it, and a muster that meets neither. That is a structural finding rather than a numerical one, and it is the stronger of the two things Hârn contributes to this page. HÂRN

    Two things must travel with any levy priced against canon. First, a spear is four yeomen in Gardiren and five in Minarsas, and only the four-yeoman version closes the scutage arithmetic above, so this page computes with four. ⚠ The five-yeoman spear is neither a different unit nor an error — and it is the best canon evidence the argument has. Reading it as an error presupposes that the £10 prices bodies. It does not. Minarsas 29 assesses 120 spears of seven men each (knight, squire, five yeomen) and prints the scutage as £1,200 — £10 the spear, the identical rate Gardiren attaches to a six-man one. The money is fixed per spear while the bodies move. And canon gives the reason in its own words: "Because the earl's manors are larger than normal, each spear is set at one knight, one squire, and five yeomen." That is this page's grown manor, in print, in a second book — a paper unit holding still while the ground under it grows. Second, the yeoman rate is realm-specific: one per 300 acres in Kaldor and Chybisa, one per 600 in Melderyn, with the knight rate unchanged. A levy computed with Kaldor's yeoman rate on Melderyn's ground is out by a factor of two, and nothing in the books flags it. HÂRN
